# Ouroboros + Venom (O+V): A Governed Architecture for Autonomous Self-Development

> **Prepared by:** Derek J. Russell
> **Report date:** 2026-04-16
> **Last updated:** 2026-10-13. See **§93. Developments (May 14 – October 13, 2026)** for the local-model era, the first autonomous landings and the Trinity learning loop, and **§92** for April 17 – May 13. The original §1–§91 substrate is unchanged; both addenda are appended per the policy in Appendix F, and §93.16 lists the earlier text they supersede.
> **Repository:** `github.com/drussell23/JARVIS` (formerly `JARVIS-AI-Agent`, which redirects)
> **Canonical technical reference:** `docs/architecture/OUROBOROS.md` (2,774 lines)
> **This paper:** research-paper treatment of the above — plain-English explanation, analogies, architectural narrative, visual diagrams, honest evidence-backed claims.

---

## Abstract

Ouroboros + Venom (O+V) is the autonomous self-development engine at the heart of the JARVIS Trinity AI Operating System. It is the mechanism by which the system detects its own improvement opportunities, reasons about code changes, generates patches, validates them against tests, applies them to disk, commits them under an autonomous signature, and learns from the outcome — without a human engineer in the driver's seat for most operations.

The paper describes O+V at three levels simultaneously. For non-technical readers, each section opens with a plain-English **Big Picture** paragraph using analogies drawn from biology, medicine, manufacturing, and everyday life. For software engineers, the technical detail — phase semantics, FSM transitions, budget allocations, safety invariants — is presented in full with source-file citations. For researchers interested in autonomous AI systems, the design principles are connected back to a coherent architectural philosophy: a deterministic skeleton with an agentic nervous system, governed by a constitutional document (the Manifesto), and supervised by a metacognition layer (Trinity Consciousness).

Battle-test evidence is treated with equal seriousness. The paper includes a full postmortem of sessions A through W — the 11-day arc during which O+V evolved from a shadow-mode exploration scorer to producing its first end-to-end autonomous multi-file `APPLY` on 2026-04-15 (Session W: four Python test modules autonomously generated, validated, repaired, written to disk, committed, 20/20 pytest green). The paper is honest about what is proven (enforcement, persistence, Iron Gate semantics) and what is not yet proven (durability per Manifesto §6, broader scope beyond new-file creation, load-bearing workarounds on three deferred latent bugs).

The architecture is open — the full source is at `github.com/drussell23/JARVIS-AI-Agent`, every file cited in this paper is browseable at the referenced line numbers, and every battle-test session has its own debug log preserved in `.ouroboros/sessions/`. The goal is that a researcher or engineer can read this paper, clone the repo, and reproduce any claim end-to-end.

---

## How to Read This Paper

This is a **comprehensive research-paper treatment of O+V**, written to work simultaneously for three audiences:

1. **Non-technical readers — business partners, investors, research peers, newcomers to autonomous AI.** Each section opens with a **Big Picture** callout in plain English, using everyday analogies (apprentices, immune systems, dining rooms, mentorship loops). You can read just these callouts end-to-end and come away with the full narrative of what O+V is, how it works, and why it matters.

2. **Software engineers — anyone who might read, extend, or adopt ideas from the O+V codebase.** Every technical section cites source files, line numbers, configuration variables, and FSM transitions. A glossary is included as Appendix A. All environment variables are indexed in Appendix B.

3. **Researchers — anyone studying autonomous AI, governance architectures, or self-improving systems.** The paper connects implementation details back to design principles (the seven Manifesto principles) and provides honest evidence — what is proven through battle tests, what remains unproven, and what the deliberate deferred trade-offs are.

The paper is **intentionally long** — approximately 150 pages — because O+V is genuinely intricate. A cursory treatment would not do the architecture justice. However, the structure supports **skim reading**: every Part opens with a Big Picture paragraph and a brief contents summary, so a reader can navigate directly to the parts relevant to their interest.

**The canonical technical reference** remains `docs/architecture/OUROBOROS.md` in the repository. This paper is a companion document — it adds narrative, context, and accessibility, while pointing at OUROBOROS.md for the deepest technical detail and at the battle-test session logs for the raw evidence.

# PART I — Vision and Context

> **Big Picture:** This Part explains what Ouroboros + Venom is — in plain English first, then in technical terms, then in the context of the philosophical document (the Manifesto) that shapes every design decision. If you only read the first three sections of this paper, you will come away with the complete conceptual picture.

## §1. What O+V Is, In Plain English

> **Analogy:** Imagine hiring a junior software engineer who works 24 hours a day, never gets tired, and costs almost nothing per task. This engineer reads the team's codebase, notices what needs fixing, writes the fix, tests it against the existing test suite, checks in the result, and learns from whether it worked. A senior engineer reviews the junior's work when the stakes are high; when the stakes are low, the junior is trusted to act autonomously. Over time, the junior develops opinions about which parts of the codebase are fragile, remembers which past attempts failed, and asks clarifying questions when the direction is ambiguous.
>
> That is what Ouroboros + Venom is. It is an autonomous software engineer that lives inside your codebase, with the discipline of a senior professional and the scale of a machine. The word "Ouroboros" — the serpent eating its own tail — captures the self-referential nature: JARVIS uses O+V to improve JARVIS.

### §1.1 What it *does*

Every few seconds, a set of 16 autonomous sensors scans the codebase for specific classes of improvement opportunities. One sensor watches the test suite and fires when a test fails. Another looks at code complexity and flags overly-tangled functions. A third reads the most recent commits and notices documentation that has drifted out of sync with the code it describes. Yet another scans for `TODO`, `FIXME`, and `HACK` comments left by human engineers. These sensors are event-driven — they do not poll on a schedule; they react to events in the file system and the version control system.

When a sensor fires, it produces a **signal**: a structured description of a potential change, including the target files, a goal (a sentence describing what should happen), an urgency level, and metadata about where the signal came from. The signal enters a **pipeline**. The pipeline is the heart of O+V.

The pipeline has **eleven phases**. At each phase, the operation is either permitted to proceed, queued for later, escalated for human review, or rejected outright. The phases handle, in order: classifying the operation's risk level, routing it to the correct model provider (cheap inference for routine work, expensive reasoning for critical work), expanding the context the model will see, reasoning about the implementation strategy, generating the actual code change, validating that change against the test suite, gating it through deterministic safety checks, approving it (automatically for low risk, human-in-the-loop for higher risk), applying it to disk, verifying the applied change still passes tests, and completing the operation with a postmortem entry.

Between the phases, a **metacognition layer** (Trinity Consciousness) records what happened and predicts what will happen next time. It remembers which files have been trouble before, notices when the same failure is recurring across operations, predicts regression risk before a change is attempted, and during idle time speculatively pre-computes improvements that might be valuable later.

The whole thing runs with an explicit budget — cost per operation, cost per day, wall-clock time per phase, and human-approval time limits. When budgets are exhausted, the system falls back gracefully rather than burning resources or asking the human to intervene at 3 AM.

### §1.2 What makes it different

Three things distinguish O+V from a typical AI coding assistant.

First, it is **proactive, not reactive**. A chatbot answers when asked. A copilot suggests when invoked. O+V *initiates*: it decides for itself what to work on next, based on what the sensors have detected, what the human has prioritized, and what the metacognition layer predicts will be most valuable. There is no prompt box. There is no "generate me a fix for X." There is a running organism, and its decisions are observable through a rich terminal interface and a persistent thought log.

Second, it is **governed, not free**. The autonomy is contained inside a deterministic safety skeleton called the Iron Gate. The Iron Gate is not an AI. It is a set of hard-coded rules — AST parsers, command blocklists, exploration-depth scorers, file-path protectors, cost ceilings — that no model can override. When a model tries to edit a file outside the repository, the Iron Gate blocks it. When a model tries to run a destructive shell command, the Iron Gate blocks it. When a model produces output containing non-ASCII characters that might corrupt a file, the Iron Gate blocks it. The agentic intelligence provides flexibility; the deterministic skeleton provides safety. The model cannot deceive the skeleton because the skeleton is not listening to language — it is reading file paths, token types, and exit codes.

Third, it is **accountable**. Every operation has an identifier. Every phase transition is written to an append-only ledger. Every model call is recorded with its cost. Every applied change becomes a git commit with a structured message that attributes the work to the autonomous system, names the operation ID, notes the risk tier, and cites the provider used. If something goes wrong six months later, the full causal chain can be reconstructed from the ledger and the git history.

### §1.3 Why the name

**Ouroboros** is the ancient symbol of a serpent consuming its own tail — a closed loop of self-reference. The name captures the architectural fact that the system is the subject of its own improvements. JARVIS uses O+V to refactor JARVIS, to add features to JARVIS, to write tests for JARVIS, and to document JARVIS.

**Venom** is the agentic execution layer — the subsystem that gives the provider (the language model) the ability to read files, search code, run tests, and revise its output across multiple turns. The name is taken from the Marvel symbiote — a nervous system that attaches to a host, granting the host abilities the host could not exercise alone. The analogy is deliberate: Ouroboros is the governance skeleton; Venom is the fluid intelligence layered on top.

Together, **Ouroboros + Venom** means "disciplined self-improvement." The discipline comes from Ouroboros. The self-improvement comes from Venom. Neither works without the other.

## §2. What O+V Is, In Technical Terms

> **Big Picture:** This section re-states the same system in technical vocabulary. If you are an engineer, this is the section that situates O+V inside a system architecture you can reason about. The plain-English framing in §1 is the *what*; this section is the *how*.

O+V is a six-layer event-driven pipeline running as a governed coroutine tree inside the JARVIS backend process. The layers, from top to bottom, are:

1. **Strategic Direction** (`strategic_direction.py`) — a boot-time service that reads the Manifesto (`README.md`) and architectural documents, extracts the seven core principles, and injects a ~2,500-character strategic context digest into every generation prompt. This layer answers the question "where are we going?" and ensures the model generates Manifesto-aligned code, not generic fixes.

2. **Trinity Consciousness** (`backend/core/ouroboros/consciousness/`) — a metacognition layer comprising four core engines (HealthCortex, MemoryEngine, DreamEngine, ProphecyEngine) and three awareness-fusion engines (Contextual Awareness Intelligence, Situational Awareness Intelligence, Unified Awareness Engine). This layer answers "why evolve?" and feeds cross-session episodic learning back into the pipeline.

3. **Event Spine** (`backend/core/ouroboros/governance/intake/`) — the `IntakeLayerService` (Zone 6.9) and 16 sensors plugged into a unified event bus. This layer answers "when to act?" Signals arrive event-driven (filesystem changes via `watchdog`, test-result JSON from a pytest plugin, post-commit hook metadata, webhook deliveries, voice commands) rather than via polling loops.

4. **Ouroboros Pipeline** (`backend/core/ouroboros/governance/orchestrator.py`) — the deterministic governance skeleton running the 11-phase FSM. This layer answers "what to do, safely." It owns no domain logic — only phase transitions, error handling, retry bookkeeping, and ledger writes. Every unhandled exception routes to `POSTMORTEM`. Every phase transition writes a `LedgerEntry` to an append-only JSONL log.

5. **Venom Agentic Loop** (`tool_executor.py`, `repair_engine.py`) — the multi-turn tool-use layer. A `ToolLoopCoordinator` wraps each generation call. The provider (Claude or DoubleWord) is given a tool manifest; it can call `read_file`, `search_code`, `edit_file`, `run_tests`, `bash`, and twelve other tools across multiple turns within a single generation. When validation fails, the L2 Self-Repair Engine attempts up to five iterations of fix-test-classify-revise within a 120-second wall-clock timebox.

6. **ChangeEngine + AutoCommitter** (`change_engine.py`, `auto_committer.py`) — the persistence layer. When the pipeline decides to APPLY, the ChangeEngine writes the patch to disk with pre-APPLY snapshots for rollback. When VERIFY passes, the AutoCommitter creates a structured git commit with an `Ouroboros+Venom` co-author signature, an operation identifier, a risk tier, and an integrity hash.

The pipeline runs inside a `BackgroundAgentPool` of three workers (default; configurable via `JARVIS_BG_POOL_SIZE`). Operations are dequeued from a 16-slot `PriorityQueue` keyed on a composite score (source tier, urgency boost, file-count penalty, confidence bonus, dependency credit). The pool guarantees bounded concurrency and provides worker watchdog timeouts configurable per route (IMMEDIATE 60s, STANDARD 120s, COMPLEX/BACKGROUND 180s, plus grace and tool-loop overhead).

Provider routing is deterministic — a pure-code `UrgencyRouter` at the ROUTE phase maps `(urgency, source, complexity)` to a `ProviderRoute` enum in under a millisecond with zero LLM calls. The five routes (`IMMEDIATE`, `STANDARD`, `COMPLEX`, `BACKGROUND`, `SPECULATIVE`) each define a cascade contract — which provider is primary, whether a fallback exists, what the cost target is. Adaptive recovery within the cascade is handled by a `FailbackStateMachine` that classifies failures into modes (`RATE_LIMITED`, `TIMEOUT`, `SERVER_ERROR`, `CONNECTION_ERROR`, `CONTENT_FAILURE`) and uses exponential backoff with failure-mode-specific timing.

The system is *not* monolithic. Each layer has a clean interface and is independently testable. The pipeline orchestrator imports the providers via a `CandidateProvider` protocol; it does not know whether a given provider is backed by Claude, DoubleWord, a self-hosted Prime instance, or a test mock. The consciousness bridge is optional — if disabled, the pipeline runs without metacognition; the ops still complete, just without reputation-driven risk assessment. The Venom tool loop can be disabled with `JARVIS_GOVERNED_TOOL_USE_ENABLED=false`, at which point the system degrades gracefully to single-shot generation.

All of this runs under one overriding architectural commitment: **no hardcoded model names**. Every model reference is resolved at runtime from `brain_selection_policy.yaml` or an environment variable. This makes the system model-agnostic; when a new inference provider is on-boarded, the code does not change — only the policy file does.

## §3. The Seven Manifesto Principles

> **Big Picture:** Every engineering team has values — usually unwritten. The JARVIS Trinity has them written down as seven principles, and those principles are actively injected into every AI generation call as prompt context. The model is literally reminded of the team's architectural philosophy every time it writes code. This section states the principles in the form they appear in the source code, with a plain-English gloss of what each one means in practice.

The seven principles are quoted verbatim from `strategic_direction.py`. They are numbered and named here for ease of reference throughout the rest of the paper.

### Principle 1 — The Unified Organism

> *"Tri-partite microkernel. Single entry point."*

JARVIS is not a collection of scripts — it is one organism with three parts (Body, Mind, Soul) that communicate via well-defined protocols. The organism has a single entry point; you do not start ten services to run JARVIS; you start JARVIS, and JARVIS orchestrates everything else.

In O+V terms: the governed loop service is a single coroutine tree. It is not spawned by a supervisor and forgotten; it is owned, observed, and shut down cleanly as part of the unified process lifecycle. When the organism shuts down, every in-flight operation is either completed, explicitly cancelled, or recorded as aborted. No silent leaks.

### Principle 2 — Progressive Awakening

> *"Adaptive lifecycle. No blocking boot chains."*

The system comes online *adaptively*. If a dependency is slow, the system does not hang — it marks the dependency as degraded, continues booting, and hot-swaps the dependency in when it becomes ready. There is no twenty-second blocking wait at startup.

In O+V terms: providers can be `INACTIVE`, `STARTING`, `ACTIVE`, `DEGRADED`, `STOPPING`. The GovernedLoopService runs `_oracle_index_loop` as a background task; it does not wait for the codebase index to finish before accepting operations. If the index is stale, operations run with stale-index warnings; they do not fail.

### Principle 3 — Asynchronous Tendrils (Disciplined Concurrency)

> *"Structured concurrency. No event-loop starvation. Zero polling. Pure reflex."*

All I/O is `asyncio`. Nothing blocks the event loop. Nothing polls. The system reacts to events via message passing, not timers. When a file changes, a filesystem watcher publishes an event; a sensor subscribes; the sensor decides whether the event is actionable; if it is, a signal is pushed into the intake router. No five-second `while True: sleep(5); scan()` loops anywhere.

In O+V terms: the DW 3-tier event-driven architecture (Part VI, §34) is a direct expression of this principle. Tier 0 is real-time SSE streaming (zero polling). Tier 1 is webhook-driven batch (zero polling). Tier 2 is adaptive-backoff polling — used only as a safety net when webhooks are unavailable, and even then with exponential backoff plus jitter, not fixed-interval polling.

### Principle 4 — The Synthetic Soul

> *"Episodic awareness. Cross-session learning."*

The organism has memory. Not parameter-weight memory — *episodic* memory. It remembers that file X failed three operations ago. It remembers that the operator rejected a change to file Y yesterday with a specific reason. It remembers which routing decisions have worked on which classes of problem.

In O+V terms: the MemoryEngine writes `FileReputation` records to `~/.jarvis/ouroboros/consciousness/` with a 168-hour TTL. The UserPreferenceMemory persists typed memory entries across sessions. The LastSessionSummary reads the previous session's `summary.json` at CONTEXT_EXPANSION so the new session inherits context. Cross-session learning is first-class, not an add-on.

### Principle 5 — Intelligence-Driven Routing

> *"Semantic, not regex. DAGs, not scripts. The cognitive forge."*

Decisions are made by reasoning about *meaning*, not pattern-matching on *strings*. A regex that dispatches work based on the presence of the word "refactor" in a signal description is a crude proxy for what the routing layer should actually do: reason about the signal's semantic content, its likely complexity, its risk profile, and the appropriate provider tier.

But — and this is the nuance — routing itself should be *deterministic code*, not another model call. The deterministic fast-path (`UrgencyRouter`) executes in under a millisecond with zero LLM calls, by consulting lookup tables derived from the intelligence layer's offline analysis. The model reasons about *what* the change should be. The deterministic code decides *which provider* will do the reasoning.

### Principle 6 — Threshold-Triggered Neuroplasticity (Ouroboros)

> *"Detect gaps. Synthesize. Graduate."*

When the system detects a gap in its own capabilities, it does not merely log a `TODO`. It synthesizes a candidate fix, validates it, and — if the fix works reliably over multiple attempts — graduates the capability into a permanent part of the organism. The Ouroboros loop is the mechanism: detect → generate → validate → apply → verify → learn → graduate.

The graduation threshold is deliberately conservative: three consecutive successes for a capability class (configurable via `JARVIS_GRADUATION_THRESHOLD`). One success is a data point. Three successes is a pattern.

### Principle 7 — Absolute Observability

> *"Every autonomous decision is visible."*

The organism's decisions are not a black box. Every operation has a visible thought log (`.jarvis/ouroboros_thoughts.jsonl`). Every heartbeat is rendered in the SerpentFlow CLI. Every model call's cost is tracked and summed. Every commit carries an `Ouroboros+Venom` signature identifying which subsystems contributed. If something goes wrong, the full causal chain from signal to side-effect can be reconstructed from disk.

In O+V terms: five-phase `CommProtocol` messages (`INTENT → PLAN → HEARTBEAT → DECISION → POSTMORTEM`) provide structured observability for every operation. The `SerpentFlow` CLI renders these messages using the same visual language Claude Code popularized, adapted for O+V's proactive nature. A human can sit in front of the terminal and watch the organism think.

### The Zero-Shortcut Mandate

Beyond the seven principles, the Manifesto contains one overriding *mandate*:

> **"No brute-force retries without diagnosis. No hardcoded routing tables. Structural repair, not bypasses."**

When something fails, the answer is not to retry harder or to special-case the failure. The answer is to understand the failure, to fix the structural cause, and to ensure the failure cannot recur for the same reason. This mandate is invoked repeatedly through the battle-test postmortems (Part XII): when an issue was discovered, the fix was never "retry five more times." It was always "instrument the FSM, find the true root cause, and rewrite the contract."

## §4. Why This Was Built

> **Big Picture:** There is a specific reason autonomous software engineering is worth building, and it has nothing to do with replacing human engineers. The goal is to make maintenance work — the grinding 80% of an engineer's time spent on small fixes, test repairs, doc updates, and refactors — happen while the engineer is doing something else. This section makes that case in concrete terms.

The thesis that motivates O+V is not "AI will replace programmers." The thesis is: **most of the work programmers do is maintenance, and most of that maintenance is proceduralizable by a disciplined autonomous agent.**

Consider a typical week for a senior engineer on a mature codebase. They spend maybe eight hours writing genuinely novel code — the code that required their actual judgment, their taste, their architectural intuition. They spend the other thirty-two hours on: investigating flaky tests, updating docs that drifted out of sync, fixing lint warnings, bumping dependency versions, writing tests for edge cases they spotted during code review, renaming a symbol across the codebase, refactoring a duplicated pattern into a utility, triaging GitHub issues, and responding to alerts.

The thirty-two hours are *not* wasted. They are the work that keeps a codebase habitable. But they are also *prescriptive* — the engineer knows what needs to happen; the question is only whether they have the time to do it. An autonomous agent with enough discipline to not cause damage, enough taste to produce patches that feel hand-written, and enough observability to be audited after the fact, could do most of that thirty-two hours while the engineer sleeps.

The key constraint is *discipline*. A human engineer doing maintenance work is disciplined by fear — fear of breaking the build, fear of triggering a pager, fear of being called out in code review. An autonomous agent has no such fear. The discipline must be structural — baked into the system. That is what O+V is: structural discipline for autonomous code generation.

The seven Manifesto principles are the philosophical embodiment of that discipline. The eleven-phase pipeline is the structural embodiment. The Iron Gate is the unconditional-safety embodiment. Trinity Consciousness is the episodic-learning embodiment. Every design choice in O+V exists in service of the following invariant:

> *The organism may do any procedurally-describable maintenance work, autonomously, at any hour, under its own budget — but it may never do work the human would not have sanctioned, cannot be audited, or cannot be rolled back.*

This is the bargain O+V offers. In exchange for structural discipline, the organism is granted procedural autonomy. That is the bargain the Manifesto codifies, the pipeline enforces, and the battle-test log (Part XII) has been incrementally validating one session at a time.

<div class="engage" id="engage-part-i">
<p class="engage-kicker">Conceptual questions</p>
<details class="cq"><summary>1. Principle 5 says decisions should be "semantic, not regex", yet the router that picks a provider is plain deterministic code. Why is that not a contradiction?</summary>
<p>The paper splits the work in two. The model reasons about what the change should be, which is the semantic part. Deterministic code decides which provider does that reasoning, using lookup tables derived from the intelligence layer's offline analysis. Routing runs for every operation, so making it a model call would add cost and latency and would make the route non-reproducible. Keeping routing deterministic preserves the ledger's ability to replay a signal and get the same route. See §2 and §3 (Principle 5).</p>
</details>
<details class="cq"><summary>2. Why does the paper stress that the Iron Gate "is not an AI"? What would be lost if the safety checks were themselves model calls?</summary>
<p>The Iron Gate is a set of hard-coded rules: AST parsers, command blocklists, path protectors, cost ceilings. Because it reads file paths, token types and exit codes rather than language, a model cannot talk its way past it. If the safety layer were another model, it could be persuaded, could disagree with itself across runs, and could fail in the same ways as the generator it is meant to check. The design pairs flexible agentic intelligence with a skeleton the intelligence cannot negotiate with. See §1.2.</p>
</details>
<details class="cq"><summary>3. How do the three distinguishing traits in §1.2 (proactive, governed, accountable) depend on each other? What happens if you keep proactivity but drop the other two?</summary>
<p>Proactivity means O+V decides for itself what to work on, with no prompt box. That is only acceptable if the actions are bounded (governed) and reconstructable afterwards (accountable). Without governance, a self-initiating agent could edit files outside the repo or run destructive commands. Without accountability, nobody could trace a bad change months later through the ledger and structured commits. The closing invariant in §4 states the bargain directly: procedural autonomy is granted only in exchange for structural discipline, with work that is sanctioned, auditable and reversible. See §1.2 and §4.</p>
</details>
<p class="engage-kicker">Quiz</p>
<div class="quiz" id="quiz-part-i">
<div class="mcq" data-answer="3">
<p class="mcq-q">1. According to §1.1, how many autonomous sensors and how many pipeline phases does O+V have?</p>
<ol class="mcq-options" type="A">
<li>7 sensors and 6 phases</li>
<li>12 sensors and 5 phases</li>
<li>16 sensors and 11 phases</li>
<li>24 sensors and 8 phases</li>
</ol>
<details class="mcq-why"><summary>Show answer</summary>
<p><strong>C.</strong> §1.1 describes a set of 16 event-driven sensors feeding a pipeline of eleven phases. The six figure is the number of architectural layers in §2, and seven is the number of Manifesto principles.</p>
</details>
</div>
<div class="mcq" data-answer="1">
<p class="mcq-q">2. Why does the paper say a model cannot deceive the Iron Gate?</p>
<ol class="mcq-options" type="A">
<li>It checks file paths, token types and exit codes, not language.</li>
<li>It asks a second, larger model to audit every response.</li>
<li>It only runs after a human has approved the change.</li>
<li>It keeps the model's output hidden until tests pass.</li>
</ol>
<details class="mcq-why"><summary>Show answer</summary>
<p><strong>A.</strong> §1.2 says the skeleton "is not listening to language"; its rules are deterministic checks on paths, tokens and exit codes, so persuasive text has nothing to act on.</p>
</details>
</div>
<div class="mcq" data-answer="4">
<p class="mcq-q">3. Under Principle 6, what is the default threshold before a capability graduates into a permanent part of the organism?</p>
<ol class="mcq-options" type="A">
<li>One successful operation with passing tests</li>
<li>Five successes within a 120-second timebox</li>
<li>Human sign-off on a review pull request</li>
<li>Three consecutive successes for that capability class</li>
</ol>
<details class="mcq-why"><summary>Show answer</summary>
<p><strong>D.</strong> §3 sets the graduation threshold at three consecutive successes, configurable via <code>JARVIS_GRADUATION_THRESHOLD</code>: "One success is a data point. Three successes is a pattern."</p>
</details>
</div>
<div class="mcq" data-answer="2">
<p class="mcq-q">4. A provider call keeps failing. What response does the Zero-Shortcut Mandate require?</p>
<ol class="mcq-options" type="A">
<li>Retry with exponential backoff until the call succeeds</li>
<li>Diagnose the failure and fix its structural cause</li>
<li>Add a special case that skips the failing input</li>
<li>Escalate the operation to a human immediately</li>
</ol>
<details class="mcq-why"><summary>Show answer</summary>
<p><strong>B.</strong> §3 quotes the mandate: "No brute-force retries without diagnosis... Structural repair, not bypasses." The fix is to understand the failure and make sure it cannot recur for the same reason.</p>
</details>
</div>
</div>
<p class="engage-kicker">Problem set</p>
<div class="pset" id="pset-part-i">
<div class="problem">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Problem 1 (trace).</strong> A unit test starts failing on a quiet Sunday. Using only §1.1 and §2, follow this event from detection to a git commit. Name each of the six layers it touches, in the order it touches them, and say what each layer contributes.</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>Start with the layer that answers "when to act?", and remember that two layers feed the pipeline with context rather than sitting in the signal's direct path.</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p>The Event Spine (layer 3) sees the failure through the pytest plugin's test-result JSON; a sensor turns it into a signal with target files, a goal and an urgency. The signal enters the Ouroboros Pipeline (layer 4), the deterministic 11-phase FSM that logs every transition to the ledger.</p>
<p>During generation, Strategic Direction (layer 1) has already injected its roughly 2,500-character Manifesto digest into the prompt, and Trinity Consciousness (layer 2) supplies memory and regression predictions between phases.</p>
<p>At GENERATE, the Venom Agentic Loop (layer 5) lets the provider read files, search code and run tests over several turns; if validation fails, L2 Self-Repair gets up to five iterations in 120 seconds.</p>
<p>Finally the ChangeEngine (layer 6) writes the patch with pre-APPLY snapshots, and once VERIFY passes the AutoCommitter creates a commit carrying the Ouroboros+Venom signature, operation id, risk tier and integrity hash. See §1.1 and §2.</p>
</details>
</div>
<div class="problem">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Problem 2 (design).</strong> A contributor proposes replacing the <code>UrgencyRouter</code> with a small LLM that reads each signal's description and picks the provider, arguing this is more "semantic". Using §2 and §3, write a short critique: what would the change cost, and which guarantees would it weaken?</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>§9's reasons are previewed in Principle 5 and in §2's description of the router's speed and cost.</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p>Today the router maps (urgency, source, complexity) to a route in under a millisecond with zero LLM calls (§2). An LLM router would add a model call to every operation, which costs money and eats into per-phase time budgets.</p>
<p>It would also make routing non-deterministic. Principle 5 says the model should reason about what the change is, while deterministic code decides which provider does the reasoning; this keeps the route reproducible from the signal alone.</p>
<p>The contributor might cite the mandate's "No hardcoded routing tables". The paper's answer is that the router's tables are derived from the intelligence layer's offline analysis, not hand-typed guesses. So the better fix, per Principle 5, is to improve that offline analysis while keeping the online decision deterministic. See §2 and §3.</p>
</details>
</div>
<div class="problem">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Problem 3 (analysis).</strong> §4 says a senior engineer spends about 8 of 40 weekly hours on novel code. (a) What share of the week is maintenance, and does it match the "grinding 80%" in the section's summary? (b) The invariant at the end of §4 forbids three kinds of work. For each, name one mechanism from Part I that enforces it.</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>The three forbidden kinds are work that is unsanctioned, unauditable, or not reversible. Look at §1.1, §1.2 and §2 for matching mechanisms.</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p>(a) Maintenance is 32 of 40 hours, which is 80 percent, matching the summary's figure.</p>
<p>(b) Unsanctioned work: the risk tiers and approval step in the pipeline; low-risk work is autonomous but higher-risk work goes to a human, as the "senior engineer reviews when stakes are high" analogy in §1 describes, and the Iron Gate blocks forbidden actions outright (§1.2).</p>
<p>Unauditable work: every phase transition is written to an append-only ledger and every change becomes a structured git commit naming the operation id, risk tier and provider (§1.2).</p>
<p>Irreversible work: the ChangeEngine takes pre-APPLY snapshots for rollback before writing a patch (§2). Together these let the organism act "at any hour, under its own budget" without violating the invariant. See §4.</p>
</details>
</div>
</div>
<p class="engage-kicker engage-kicker-adv">Advanced conceptual questions</p>
<details class="cq-adv"><summary>A1. The §4 invariant forbids work "the human would not have sanctioned", yet §1.2 says O+V decides for itself what to work on. By October (§93.7) goals found by Goal Discovery are signed automatically by <code>synthesize_and_sign()</code>. Is that still sanction, or has proactivity quietly eaten the invariant?</summary>
<p>In the April design, sanction was spread across the pipeline rather than given per item. Sensors proposed work (§1.1), the risk ladder set a tier (§9.1), and only Orange work waited for a human (§14.1). Green and Yellow work was sanctioned by policy: the operator had agreed in advance to what those tiers allow.</p>
<p>§93.7 makes that policy explicit and narrows it. Every source of work, including model-invented proposals, must pass through one signer ("There is no second sanction path"). Goal Discovery may only sign evidence-only work, such as ambient red tests and uncovered modules. The Sentinel auto-approves only up to a tier ceiling, and BLOCKED work, Order-2 self-modification and anything touching the cage always escalate.</p>
<p>A defensible position is that this is still sanction, but sanction of a class of work rather than of each item. The operator signs a rule ("evidence-only goals below this tier"), not each goal. The weakness is that a rule can admit items the operator would have refused. §93.14 records four wrong landings out of 91: one hollow, one with no intended change, one that dropped content and one that flattened text.</p>
<p>The evidence that would settle it is the rate at which auto-signed goals produce landings the operator later reverts or repairs, compared with operator-sanctioned goals. If auto-signed work is reverted much more often, the class-level rule is too wide and the invariant is being honoured in form only.</p>
</details>
<details class="cq-adv"><summary>A2. Principle 6 says three consecutive successes make "a pattern" (§3), and §78 adds "under comparable conditions". Why would that bar still fail to show that the Reactor learning loop of §93.11 made the model better?</summary>
<p>Principle 6 measures <em>repeatability</em>: can a capability succeed again and again under the same conditions (§3, §78)? It does not compare against a baseline. A model that was already able to write a passing test file would pass three times in a row whether or not training changed anything.</p>
<p>§93.11 shows the gap in practice. The first adapter beat the incumbent 4/6 to 3/6 on the handoff's greedy comparison. The project's own notes reject this as evidence of learning: only three answers contributed, the gradient norm was about 1e-4, and the margin was one greedy flip. On a held-out benchmark of 30 tasks drawn from human commits with hidden tests, the adapter solved 0, with a mean gain of 0.03.</p>
<p>So the learning question needs a controlled comparison that Principle 6 does not demand: the same held-out tasks, the incumbent as control, and a gain that exceeds run-to-run noise. The operator's standing rule, that no training-derived change is pushed until a held-out gain is shown (§93.11), is that missing clause. Graduation asks "does it keep working?" The learning loop must also ask "does it work better than before?"</p>
</details>
<details class="cq-adv"><summary>A3. §1.2 says the model "cannot deceive the skeleton because the skeleton is not listening to language". §93.3 reports that about 8.8% of LLM-generated adversarial mutations escape the static cage. Does the second result refute the first?</summary>
<p>Not directly. The two claims are about different things. §1.2 is about <em>persuasion</em>: the gate does not read arguments, so no wording can talk it into allowing a path or command. Nothing in §93.3 suggests the escapes worked by persuasion.</p>
<p>§93.3 is about <em>visibility</em>. The North Star attributes the residue to <code>eval</code>, <code>exec</code>, <code>subprocess</code> and <code>pickle</code> called on strings built at runtime. A gate that reads file paths, token types and exit codes can only judge structure that is present in the text it reads. A string that becomes code only when it runs is invisible to it by construction. So "cannot be deceived" is true, while "cannot be evaded" is false at about twice the 4.4% gate.</p>
<p>This also explains the stated remedy: OS-level runtime containment, not more AST rules (§93.3). It fits the April design's own split, where execution was meant to happen inside a sandbox with process isolation (§5.3), and the October PID-namespace containment for test runs (§93.8). The paper notes that no re-measurement after the later hardening was found, so the open evidence is the escape rate with runtime containment in place.</p>
</details>
<p class="engage-kicker engage-kicker-adv">Challenge problems</p>
<div class="pset pset-adv">
<div class="problem problem-adv">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Challenge 1 (quantitative).</strong> §4 imagines an agent doing "most of" a senior engineer's 32 weekly maintenance hours. Test this against §93.10. Givens: the 6.03 h soak <code>bt-2026-10-05-012717</code> made 6 substantive landings, with "1.34/h in the first 2.98 h" and nothing landing in a window from 22:24 to 00:29. The 1.97 h soak <code>bt-2026-09-26-143412</code> made 3 substantive landings. There were 91 autonomous landings dated 2026-09-06 to 2026-10-10, of which 84 were test files. (a) Compute the substantive rate in the second part of the 6.03 h soak. (b) What fraction of that soak was the idle window? (c) Compute the average daily landing rate over the 91-landing period. (d) Say which of the §4 maintenance tasks this evidence covers.</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>Treat the 1.34/h figure as a substantive rate, multiply it out to get landings in the first part, and subtract from 6. Count calendar days inclusively for (c).</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p>Assumption: the "1.34/h in the first 2.98 h" note sits in the substantive-per-hour column, so it is read as a substantive rate.</p>
<p>(a) Substantive landings in the first part: 1.34 × 2.98 ≈ 3.99, so about 4. The remaining 6 − 4 = 2 landed in 6.03 − 2.98 = 3.05 h, which is about 0.66 per hour. That is roughly half the early rate. This is the "supply wall" that PRD §34 records: after about four hours on uncovered modules, yield is bounded by the supply of landable work, not by the model.</p>
<p>(b) From 22:24 to 00:29 is 2 h 5 min, or about 2.08 h. 2.08 / 6.03 ≈ 0.345, so about a third of the soak landed nothing.</p>
<p>(c) 2026-09-06 to 2026-10-10 inclusive is 25 days in September plus 10 in October, which is 35 days. 91 / 35 = 2.6 landings per day. Test files alone give 84 / 35 = 2.4 per day.</p>
<p>(d) §4 lists flaky-test investigation, doc drift, lint, dependency bumps, edge-case tests, renames, refactors, issue triage and alerts. The evidence covers one item strongly (writing tests: 84 of 91), docs weakly (2 landings, one repaired by hand), and production fixes thinly (5 landings, one reverted). §93.14 says production-code landings at cadence are "not demonstrated".</p>
<p>Conclusion: the rate is real but narrow. It covers a slice of one §4 task, it is limited by work supply, and it is far from "most of" 32 hours. Check: 4 + 2 = 6 matches the table, and 1.00 per hour over 6.03 h also gives about 6.</p>
</details>
</div>
<div class="problem problem-adv">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Challenge 2 (adversarial).</strong> The §4 invariant says the organism may never do work that "cannot be rolled back". Build an operation that respects every file-level rule yet breaks this invariant in spirit: a generated test file whose body calls <code>pkill -f jarvis</code> (an event §93.8 records really happened). The target path is ordinary, the content is ASCII, and the model explored first. Go through the April layers in §1.2, §5.3, §12.4 and §15 and decide which, if any, stops it. Then name what the October paper added.</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>Ask what each layer actually reads. Does the bash blocklist see a test file's body? What does a <code>RollbackArtifact</code> restore?</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p>Walk the layers in order.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Protected paths (§9.1 Rule 0).</strong> A new file under <code>tests/</code> matches none of <code>.env</code>, <code>credentials.*</code>, <code>.git/</code> or supervisor files. It passes.</li>
<li><strong>GENERATE Iron Gates (§12.4).</strong> The exploration-first and ASCII checks look at the model's behaviour and the bytes of the content. Both pass by assumption.</li>
<li><strong>Bash blocklist (§1.2, §12.3).</strong> This gates the <code>bash</code> <em>tool call</em>. Here the dangerous command is inside a test that VALIDATE or VERIFY runs as part of a normal test run. The blocklist does not inspect test bodies, so nothing in the paper says it would fire.</li>
<li><strong>Rollback (§15.1, §15.2).</strong> <code>RollbackArtifact</code> snapshots and restores <em>files</em>. Killing a process is not a file change, so there is nothing for it to restore.</li>
<li><strong>Sandbox (§5.3).</strong> April's answer was to run tests inside Reactor with process isolation. That is the only layer that could stop it, and only if the isolation stops a test from signalling processes outside its sandbox.</li>
</ul>
<p>What happened: §93.8 records that the candidate test killed the daemon. So in the environment that ran it, no layer stopped it. The paper does not say why the §5.3 isolation did not apply there. The fix was containment at the OS level: test runs now execute in a PID namespace (<code>6b00b8adf5</code>), so the test cannot see the daemon's process to kill it.</p>
<p>Lesson: the invariant's "rollback" is defined over repository state, but executing candidate code has side effects outside the repository. Only runtime containment covers those. This matches §93.3's conclusion for the cage. Check: a PID namespace leaves every file-level rule unchanged, so this fix closes the gap without weakening any other layer.</p>
</details>
</div>
</div>
<p class="engage-kicker engage-kicker-x">Connections</p>
<div class="pset pset-x">
<div class="problem problem-x">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Connection 1 (Queueing theory).</strong> §2 says operations run in a <code>BackgroundAgentPool</code> of 3 workers and are taken from a 16-slot <code>PriorityQueue</code>. The paper gives no measured service time, so assume each operation holds a worker for 120 s, the STANDARD watchdog limit. Treat this as a worst-case planning figure, not a measurement. (a) What is the pool's maximum throughput? (b) What is utilization if signals arrive at 1 per minute? (c) Arrivals jump to 2 per minute. How long until the queue fills, starting empty? (d) Once it is full, use Little's law to estimate how long a newly admitted operation spends in the system.</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>Capacity is workers divided by service time. In a full, saturated system, the rate at which operations are admitted equals the rate at which they leave, so Little's law uses throughput as the arrival rate.</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p>(a) Each worker finishes one operation per 120 s, so three workers finish 3 / 120 = 0.025 operations per second. That is 1.5 per minute, or 90 per hour.</p>
<p>(b) Utilization is arrival rate over capacity: rho = 1 / 1.5 = 0.67. The system is stable. The queue empties between bursts, and a newly arriving operation usually finds a free worker or a short wait.</p>
<p>(c) At 2 per minute, rho = 2 / 1.5 = 1.33, which is above 1. The queue grows at 2 - 1.5 = 0.5 operations per minute, so 16 slots fill in 16 / 0.5 = 32 minutes.</p>
<p>(d) Once the queue is full, 16 operations wait and 3 are in service, so L = 19. Only 1.5 per minute leave, so only 1.5 per minute can be admitted. Little's law, W = L / lambda, gives 19 / 1.5 = 12.7 minutes. The other 0.5 per minute (30 per hour) cannot enter. §2 does not say what happens to them.</p>
<p>What this says about the architecture: a bounded pool and a bounded queue turn overload into a bounded delay (about 13 minutes under these assumptions) instead of a backlog that grows without limit. The cost is that someone must decide what to drop or defer. That is why the queue is a priority queue keyed on source tier, urgency and confidence (§2): under saturation, the score decides who gets one of the 19 places.</p>
</details>
</div>
<div class="problem problem-x">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Connection 2 (Probability and statistics).</strong> Principle 6 (§3) graduates a capability after three consecutive successes (<code>JARVIS_GRADUATION_THRESHOLD</code>), on the grounds that "one success is a data point; three successes is a pattern." Assume attempts are independent and each succeeds with a fixed probability p. (a) What is the chance of three straight successes for p = 0.5, 0.8 and 0.95? (b) Treat three straight successes as evidence against the null hypothesis p = 0.5. What is the one-sided p-value? How many consecutive successes would push it below 0.05? (c) Ten capability classes, each a coin flip (p = 0.5), each make one run of three attempts. How many would you expect to graduate by luck?</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>Under independence, the probability of n straight successes is p to the power n. Expected graduations are the number of classes times the per-class probability.</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p>(a) p^3 = 0.125 for p = 0.5. It is 0.512 for p = 0.8 and 0.857 for p = 0.95. So a mediocre capability graduates one time in eight, and even a 95%-reliable one fails the bar about one time in seven.</p>
<p>(b) Under H0 (p = 0.5), three straight successes occur with probability 0.125, so the one-sided p-value is 0.125. That is not significant at the 0.05 level. Four straight gives 0.0625, still not enough. Five gives 0.5^5 = 0.03125, which clears 0.05.</p>
<p>(c) 10 x 0.125 = 1.25 expected false graduations from ten coin-flip classes.</p>
<p>What this says about the architecture: three in a row is "conservative" compared with one success, as §3 says. Read as a statistical test, though, it is a weak filter. It trades evidence for speed. The threshold is configurable, so the evidence bar is an operator's choice, not a fixed property of the design. Real attempts are also not independent (the same file, model and prompts recur), which makes a short streak even weaker evidence than this calculation suggests.</p>
</details>
</div>
<div class="problem problem-x">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Connection 3 (Markov chains).</strong> Connection 2 looked at a single window of three attempts. A capability that keeps trying gets many windows. Model the Principle 6 rule (§3) as a Markov chain. The state is the current streak of consecutive successes: 0, 1, 2 or 3. State 3 (graduated) is absorbing. Each attempt succeeds independently with probability p. Success moves the streak up by one, and failure resets it to 0. (a) Write the transitions. (b) Find the expected number of attempts until graduation, as a function of p. (c) Evaluate it for p = 0.5, 0.8 and 0.95. (d) What is the probability that a p = 0.5 capability eventually graduates if attempts are unlimited?</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>Let E_i be the expected number of attempts to reach state 3 from streak i. Each E_i equals 1 plus p times the next state's E plus (1 - p) times E_0. Solve from E_3 = 0.</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p>(a) From state i (i = 0, 1, 2): go to i + 1 with probability p, and to 0 with probability 1 - p. State 3 goes only to itself.</p>
<p>(b) E_2 = 1 + (1 - p) E_0. E_1 = 1 + p E_2 + (1 - p) E_0. E_0 = 1 + p E_1 + (1 - p) E_0. Substitute and solve. The standard result for a run of k successes is E_0 = 1/p + 1/p^2 + ... + 1/p^k. For k = 3 that is 1/p + 1/p^2 + 1/p^3.</p>
<p>(c) p = 0.5: 2 + 4 + 8 = 14 attempts. p = 0.8: 1.25 + 1.5625 + 1.953 = about 4.8 attempts. p = 0.95: 1.053 + 1.108 + 1.166 = about 3.3 attempts.</p>
<p>(d) From every transient state, the chain reaches the absorbing state with positive probability within three steps. So absorption is certain: probability 1. A coin-flip capability graduates after about 14 attempts on average.</p>
<p>What this says about the architecture: a streak threshold separates good capabilities from bad ones by how fast they graduate, not by whether they graduate. Unlimited retries make graduation certain for any p above 0. For the threshold to work as a filter, it needs a companion limit: a bounded number of attempts, a time window, or a failure count that blocks graduation. The paper's Zero-Shortcut Mandate against brute-force retries without diagnosis (§3) points the same way.</p>
</details>
</div>
</div>
</div>
<!-- engage:end -->

# PART II — The Trinity Architecture

> **Big Picture:** Before we descend into the details of the pipeline, we need to understand the *body* O+V lives in. JARVIS is not a monolith — it is a three-part organism. Each part has a distinct role, a distinct codebase, and a distinct hosting environment. O+V runs in the Body layer, but it reaches into the Mind and the Soul. This Part establishes the three parts and the Multi-Repo Saga pattern that lets O+V coordinate work across all three.

## §5. The Three-Part Organism: Body, Mind, Soul

![Figure 1 — The JARVIS Trinity. O+V runs in the Body layer, reaches into the Mind (J-Prime) for heavy reasoning, and invokes the Soul (Reactor Core) for sandboxed execution. The three parts communicate via explicit protocols, never shared memory, carrying tracing data for full causal reconstruction.](figures/fig01_trinity_architecture.png)

> **Analogy:** Think of a Formula 1 racing team. The car (the Body) is what physically races. The driver (the Mind) makes split-second decisions on how to race. The strategy engineers back at the factory (the Soul) reason about race strategy, long-term trade-offs, and what the car should do next lap. Each part is essential; none can replace the others; and they communicate via clear protocols (radio comms, telemetry streams, pit stops). JARVIS is architected the same way.

### §5.1 JARVIS — The Body

**Role:** Real-time perception and action on the operator's machine.

**Codebase:** `github.com/drussell23/JARVIS-AI-Agent` (this repository).

**Runs on:** macOS, as a local process with privileged access to screen, keyboard, audio, and filesystem.

**Contains:**
- Vision pipeline: `backend/vision/` — screen capture, OCR, visual-language-action models, frame server.
- Voice pipeline: `backend/voice/` — voice I/O, wake-word detection, text-to-speech.
- Ghost Hands: `backend/ghost_hands/` — focus-preserving UI automation (moves the mouse and types without stealing focus).
- Core Contexts: `backend/core_contexts/` — five execution contexts (Executor, Architect, Developer, Communicator, Observer).
- **The O+V pipeline itself**: `backend/core/ouroboros/` — because self-development happens on the Body's codebase.
- The unified supervisor: `unified_supervisor.py` — a 102,000-line monolithic kernel that owns process lifecycle across Zones 0 through 7.

The Body is where real-time work happens. When you speak to JARVIS, the Body hears you. When JARVIS types on your keyboard, the Body types. When O+V generates a patch, the Body writes it to disk.

### §5.2 J-Prime — The Mind

**Role:** Self-hosted model inference, heavy reasoning, cross-session cognitive state.

**Codebase:** Separate repository (`JARVIS_PRIME_REPO_PATH`).

**Runs on:** Google Cloud Platform virtual machines with GPU acceleration.

**Contains:**
- `PrimeClient`: HTTP protocol for model invocation with schema enforcement.
- Self-hosted model weights (when available) for cost-optimized heavy reasoning.
- Cross-session memory that is too large to fit on the operator's laptop.

In the provider cascade (Part VI), J-Prime is Tier 2. It is used when available but is not required — if J-Prime is `unhealthy`, the CandidateGenerator promotes DoubleWord to primary. The architecture is deliberately resilient to J-Prime being offline.

### §5.3 Reactor Core — The Soul

**Role:** Sandboxed execution runtime.

**Codebase:** Separate repository (`JARVIS_REACTOR_REPO_PATH`).

**Runs on:** Can be local (development) or remote (production).

**Contains:**
- Execution sandboxes for code that Venom's tool loop wants to run.
- Isolated environments for validating candidate patches.
- Resource limits, process isolation, syscall filtering.

When Venom's `run_tests` tool is invoked, it runs inside Reactor. When the Iron Gate permits a `bash` command, the command executes inside Reactor, not on the Body's shell. This separation is what makes the Iron Gate's containment guarantees meaningful.

### §5.4 Communication Between the Three

The three parts talk via explicit protocols, not shared memory.

- **Body ↔ Mind:** HTTP/WebSocket over TLS. The Body sends generation requests to the Mind; the Mind streams results back. The protocol carries operation identifiers so the Body's ledger and the Mind's telemetry can be correlated.
- **Body ↔ Soul:** Sandbox invocation protocol. The Body hands the Soul a patch to validate; the Soul runs tests in an isolated environment and returns structured results.
- **Mind ↔ Soul:** Uncommon. Usually mediated through the Body, but the architecture permits it for capability-graduation workflows.

The communication protocol carries **tracing data**: every request has an operation identifier and phase identifier; every response carries the context necessary to reconstruct the causal chain. This is Principle 7 (Absolute Observability) manifesting at the inter-part boundary.

## §6. Zone 6.8 — The Governed Loop Service

> **Big Picture:** The Governed Loop Service is the *process lifecycle manager* for O+V. It is not the pipeline itself — the pipeline runs as a coroutine tree inside it. The Service is what turns the pipeline on and off cleanly, what handles the in-flight operations when the process is shutting down, and what ensures that every operation is either completed or gracefully abandoned. It is the boring infrastructure that makes everything else not-boring work.

**Source:** `backend/core/ouroboros/governance/governed_loop_service.py`.

**Zone:** 6.8 in the unified supervisor's numbering scheme.

The Service is instantiated by the supervisor at Zone 6.8 boot-time. It owns:

- **Provider wiring:** it constructs `DoublewordProvider`, `ClaudeProvider`, and (if available) `PrimeProvider`, passing them configured API keys, cost caps, and retry budgets.
- **Orchestrator construction:** it builds a `GovernedOrchestrator` with the providers and an `OrchestratorConfig`.
- **Health probes:** a 30-second health loop polls each provider and records whether the provider is healthy, degraded, or in `QUEUE_ONLY` mode.
- **The file-touch cache:** `_file_touch_cache` — a three-touches-per-ten-minutes-window counter per file. If a file has been modified three times in ten minutes by O+V, further modifications are hard-blocked until the window resets. This is a concurrency guard.
- **The active brain set:** `_active_brain_set` — the set of usable provider endpoints discovered during the boot handshake. Providers that failed the handshake are excluded.
- **The Oracle index loop:** a background coroutine that continuously indexes the codebase's symbol graph. The index is used by `get_callers`, `list_symbols`, and `list_dir` tools. If the index is stale (more than 300 seconds old), context expansion emits a warning rather than blocking.
- **The repo registry:** `_repo_registry` — the map from repo key (`jarvis`, `jarvis-prime`, `jarvis-reactor`) to local path. Used for multi-repo operations.

### §6.1 The Service State Machine

The Service itself has a deterministic state machine:

```
    INACTIVE ──→ STARTING ──→ ACTIVE
                     │             │
                     └──→ FAILED   ├──→ DEGRADED
                                   │
                                   └──→ STOPPING ──→ INACTIVE
```

**INACTIVE** is the cold state. **STARTING** happens during boot. **ACTIVE** is steady-state healthy. **DEGRADED** is steady-state with some providers unhealthy but operations still flowing. **STOPPING** is a cooperative shutdown — in-flight operations are given a grace period to complete before being cancelled. **FAILED** is a terminal failure state that prevents further operations.

Transitions are logged to the ledger and emitted as structured events. An operator watching the CLI sees precisely when the Service transitioned.

### §6.2 The `submit()` Interface

All operation submission flows through a single method:

```python
async def submit(self, envelope: SignalEnvelope) -> OperationContext:
    """Delegate to orchestrator. Never blocks on I/O longer than necessary."""
```

The Service does not do any pipeline work itself. It delegates to the orchestrator. This separation is deliberate: the Service is the lifecycle manager, not the pipeline. An upgrade to the pipeline (e.g., adding a new phase) does not require modifying the Service.

<!-- engage:begin -->
<div class="quick-check" id="qc-6">
<p class="qc-label">Quick check · §6</p>
<details class="qc"><summary>1. Why does <code>submit()</code> delegate all pipeline work to the orchestrator instead of doing any itself?</summary>
<p>The Service manages lifecycle; it is not the pipeline (§6.2). Keeping the two apart means a pipeline upgrade, such as a new phase, needs no change to the Service.</p>
</details>
<details class="qc"><summary>2. What happens to in-flight operations when the Service enters STOPPING, and how does that differ from FAILED?</summary>
<p>STOPPING is a cooperative shutdown: in-flight operations get a grace period to complete before they are cancelled, and the Service then returns to INACTIVE. FAILED is a terminal state that prevents any further operations (§6.1).</p>
</details>
<details class="qc"><summary>3. The Oracle's symbol index is more than 300 seconds old. What does context expansion do, and why?</summary>
<p>It emits a warning and continues instead of blocking. The index is rebuilt continuously by a background coroutine, so slightly stale structural data is preferred over stalling the operation while waiting for a fresh index.</p>
</details>
</div>

<p>It should undo the Body edit. The Saga pattern walks already-applied patches in reverse order and reverts each through <code>ChangeEngine.rollback()</code>, a step called compensation. ## §7. Multi-Repo Operation — The Saga Pattern

> **Big Picture:** Real work in the Trinity often spans multiple repositories. A change to an HTTP contract must land in both the Body and the Mind simultaneously — if only one side is updated, the contract is broken. The Saga pattern is how O+V coordinates these multi-repo changes atomically, with rollback if any part fails.

**Source:** `backend/core/ouroboros/governance/saga/`.

### §7.1 The Problem

Imagine a sensor detects that the API contract between JARVIS Body and J-Prime has drifted. The fix requires editing `jarvis/backend/protocols/prime.py` (Body side) *and* `jarvis-prime/api/v1/schemas.py` (Mind side). If O+V applies only the Body change, the Mind will reject requests. If O+V applies only the Mind change, the Body will send stale requests. Both must land, or neither.

### §7.2 The Solution

The Saga pattern wraps multi-repo operations in an atomic transaction with compensation. The pipeline produces a `schema 2c.1` candidate — a patch dictionary keyed by repo, with per-repo `RepoPatch` objects. The `SagaApplyStrategy` applies them in dependency order, with each `RepoPatch` recording an undo descriptor.

If any single `RepoPatch` fails validation or application, the Saga enters **compensation**: it walks the already-applied patches in reverse order and reverts them via `ChangeEngine.rollback()`. The end state is either **fully applied** or **fully reverted** — never partially applied.

The `CrossRepoVerifier` runs *after* all repo patches have been applied but *before* commit. It executes cross-repo tests to validate that the union of the patches is consistent. If the cross-repo verification fails, the Saga compensates even though every individual patch validated in isolation.

Schema versions carried by the pipeline:

| Schema | Use |
|---|---|
| `2b.1` | Single-repo patch (the common case) |
| `2b.1-noop` | Target change is already present; fast-path to COMPLETE |
| `2c.1` | Multi-repo patch (Saga) |
| `2d.1` | Execution-graph operations (L3 self-repair with parallel work units) |

### §7.3 Where Sagas Fit in the Pipeline

From the orchestrator's perspective, a Saga is just a candidate with `schema: 2c.1`. The pipeline phases (CLASSIFY through COMPLETE) run once per operation, not once per repo. Only the APPLY phase knows it is handling a Saga — it dispatches to `SagaApplyStrategy` instead of the single-repo `ChangeEngine.execute()`.

This is a design choice: the pipeline's 11 phases remain uniform. Multi-repo complexity is encapsulated in the apply strategy. A reader of the orchestrator source code can understand the phase flow without needing to understand Saga semantics.

<!-- engage:begin -->
<div class="quick-check" id="qc-7">
<p class="qc-label">Quick check · §7</p>
<details class="qc"><summary>1. When a Saga compensates, why does it revert the already-applied patches in reverse order?</summary>
<p>Patches are applied in dependency order, each recording an undo descriptor. Walking back in reverse undoes dependents before the things they depend on, via <code>ChangeEngine.rollback()</code>. The guaranteed end state is fully applied or fully reverted, never partial (§7.2).</p>
</details>
<details class="qc"><summary>2. Every <code>RepoPatch</code> validated on its own. Why can the <code>CrossRepoVerifier</code> still force compensation?</summary>
<p>Each patch being valid in isolation does not mean their union is consistent: for example, a contract both sides must agree on. The verifier runs cross-repo tests after all patches are applied and before commit. If they fail, the Saga compensates anyway.</p>
</details>
<details class="qc"><summary>3. What does schema <code>2b.1-noop</code> signal, and what does the pipeline do with it?</summary>
<p>It means the target change is already present. The operation takes a fast path to COMPLETE instead of applying a redundant patch (§7.2 table).</p>
</details>
</div>
<!-- engage:end -->

<details class="cq"><summary>2. The Governed Loop Service only delegates <code>submit()</code> to the orchestrator and does no pipeline work itself. What does this separation buy?</summary>

The pipeline's phases live in the orchestrator. Because of the split, adding or changing a phase does not require touching the Service. It also keeps responsibilities clear: the Service ensures every in-flight operation is completed or gracefully abandoned, while the orchestrator owns phase transitions. See §6 and §6.2.</p>

<details class="cq"><summary>3. Why is the <code>CrossRepoVerifier</code> needed if every repo patch has already passed validation on its own?</summary>

Only tests that run across the union of patches can check that agreement. So the verifier runs after all patches apply and before commit, and if it fails the Saga compensates even though every individual patch was valid. See §7.1 and §7.2.</p>
</details>

<p class="engage-kicker">Problem set</p>
<div class="pset" id="pset-part-ii">
<div class="problem">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Problem 1 (trace).</strong> A Saga carries a <code>2c.1</code> candidate with patches for <code>jarvis</code>, <code>jarvis-prime</code> and <code>jarvis-reactor</code>, applied in that dependency order. All three apply, but the <code>CrossRepoVerifier</code> fails. Trace what happens next, in order, and state the final state of each repo.</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>Compensation walks the applied patches in a specific direction, using the undo descriptor each <code>RepoPatch</code> recorded.</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p>Each <code>RepoPatch</code> recorded an undo descriptor when it was applied (§7.2). The verifier runs after all patches apply but before commit, so nothing has been committed yet.</p>
<p>Its failure triggers compensation even though each patch validated alone. The Saga walks applied patches in reverse: first <code>jarvis-reactor</code>, then <code>jarvis-prime</code>, then <code>jarvis</code>, each reverted with <code>ChangeEngine.rollback()</code>.</p>
<p>All three repos end in their pre-operation state: "fully reverted", never partially applied. The rest of the pipeline treats this as one operation, since only APPLY knew it was a Saga (§7.3). See §7.2.</p>
</details>
</div>
<div class="problem">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Problem 2 (design).</strong> A contributor suggests that every pipeline phase should loop over repos, so CLASSIFY, GENERATE and VALIDATE each run once per repo in a Saga. Using §7.3 and §6.2, argue for or against this, naming what the current design protects.</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>Ask who would need to understand Saga semantics under each design.</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p>The current design runs the phases once per operation and lets only APPLY dispatch to <code>SagaApplyStrategy</code> (§7.3). That keeps all 11 phases uniform and lets a reader follow the orchestrator without knowing Saga semantics.</p>
<p>Looping every phase over repos would spread multi-repo logic into every phase, so every phase author would need to handle partial progress across repos. It would also split one operation into several partial ones, which works against the single all-or-nothing result the Saga guarantees.</p>
<p>The same principle appears in §6.2: the Service delegates to the orchestrator so that pipeline changes do not ripple into lifecycle code. Encapsulating complexity in one place is the pattern. The argument favours keeping the current design. See §6.2 and §7.3.</p>
</details>
</div>
<div class="problem">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Problem 3 (code reading).</strong> Open <code>backend/core/ouroboros/governance/governed_loop_service.py</code>. (a) Find the <code>ServiceState</code> enum and compare its members with the diagram in §6.1. (b) Search for <code>_file_touch_cache</code> and find the cooldown guard. What are its window and hit-count constants, and which phase does a blocked operation advance to?</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>The guard sits under a comment beginning "Cooldown guard"; look at the <code>return</code> inside the loop.</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p>(a) <code>ServiceState</code> has six members: <code>INACTIVE</code>, <code>STARTING</code>, <code>ACTIVE</code>, <code>DEGRADED</code>, <code>STOPPING</code> and <code>FAILED</code>. These match the six states in the §6.1 diagram.</p>
<p>(b) The guard sets <code>_COOLDOWN_WINDOW_S = 600.0</code> (ten minutes) and <code>_COOLDOWN_MAX_HITS = 3</code>. For each target file it keeps a deque of timestamps keyed by the resolved path, drops entries older than the window, appends the current time, and blocks if the count exceeds 3. So the fourth touch inside ten minutes is the one blocked, which matches §6's "three touches" description.</p>
<p>A blocked operation calls <code>ctx.advance(OperationPhase.CANCELLED)</code>, so in code the "hard block" takes the form of a cancellation, and a warning is logged naming the file and op id. See §6.</p>
</details>
</div>
</div>
<p class="engage-kicker engage-kicker-adv">Advanced conceptual questions</p>
<details class="cq-adv"><summary>A1. §5.2 calls J-Prime an optional Tier 2 that the architecture is "deliberately resilient" to losing. §93.6 makes it the only lane, with paid lanes switched off by declaration. What second-order effects follow when the optional Mind becomes the single point of failure, and should the system still "degrade gracefully"?</summary>
<p>In April, resilience came from the cascade: if J-Prime was unhealthy, DoubleWord was promoted, and Claude sat behind it (§5.2, §12.1). With <code>JARVIS_PAID_LANES_ENABLED=false</code>, Claude and DoubleWord are not even constructed (§93.6). There is nothing to fall back to.</p>
<p>Three effects follow. First, failure classification matters more. §93.5 shows a 402 read as an outage, which produced 125 false awaken triggers in one session. With one lane, a misclassified failure leaves nowhere to send the work. Second, the Mind now shares a single GPU with the Soul: training takes the card through an exclusive lease, so the lane is also unavailable whenever learning runs (§93.6, §93.11). Third, Principle 2's habit of "mark degraded and continue" (§3) stops making sense, because there is no lesser lane to continue on.</p>
<p>A defensible position is that, with one lane, the right behaviour is to refuse and queue, not to degrade. October's design leans this way. Capability assurance refuses to run an operation below its declared envelope rather than degrading silently (§93.12). The cost governor already queues work rather than executing it when the budget is gone (§8.2, clause 5). The rehearsal tier records what was exhausted and when it lifts, but it is default off (§93.5). The evidence that would settle it is whether ops queued during an outage or lease later land at the same rate as ops that never waited.</p>
</details>
<details class="cq-adv"><summary>A2. §5.3 defines Reactor Core as the sandboxed execution runtime and says that separation "is what makes the Iron Gate's containment guarantees meaningful". §93.11 describes JARVIS-Reactor as the training repository. If the Soul's job changed, where did containment go, and what happened to the "uncommon" Mind-to-Soul channel of §5.4?</summary>
<p>In April, the Soul was where code ran: <code>run_tests</code> and permitted <code>bash</code> executed inside Reactor, with resource limits, process isolation and syscall filtering (§5.3). By October, §93.11 says the Soul, "JARVIS-Reactor, the training repository", had been "architecture on paper", and it now trains a GRPO LoRA adapter on what O+V recorded. The §93.16 corrections table does not list this change, so the reader has to reconcile the two descriptions.</p>
<p>Containment did not disappear. It moved to mechanisms the October text names on the Body side. Operations execute in a sovereignty worktree (§93.7). Test runs execute in a PID namespace (§93.8). A resource-aware execution lock stops a test suite from out-of-memory-killing a soak (§93.8). Modules that execute on import are quarantined (§93.8). So the §5.3 claim survives in purpose but not in location.</p>
<p>The Mind-to-Soul channel that §5.4 called "uncommon", allowed "for capability-graduation workflows", became central. The Training Lifecycle Handoff leases J-Prime, verifies the VRAM release, trains, converts and publishes the adapter to J-Prime's registry, then activates it or rolls back (§93.11). The second-order effect is contention: Mind and Soul now compete for one GPU, and the lease is the protocol that keeps them from both holding it.</p>
</details>
<details class="cq-adv"><summary>A3. The Saga guarantees "fully applied or fully reverted" at APPLY (§7.2). §93.7 adds later stages: accumulation branches, a promotion gate that can quarantine a landing, and fast-forward-only promotion to local <code>main</code>. Does Saga atomicity survive these later stages?</summary>
<p>The Saga's guarantee is scoped to APPLY and the <code>CrossRepoVerifier</code> before commit (§7.2, §7.3). Once each repo's change is committed, the paper's atomicity argument has done its job. §93.7 then describes promotion as a per-branch pipeline: accumulation onto <code>ouroboros/battle-test/&lt;ts&gt;</code>, a promotion gate checking provenance, coverage and vanished public symbols, quarantine on failure, and fast-forward to local <code>main</code>.</p>
<p>The paper describes that path for JARVIS and does not say whether promotion is coordinated across the three repos. If the gate quarantined the Body half of a contract change while the Mind half was promoted, local <code>main</code> in the two repos would disagree. That is the very partial state §7.1 exists to prevent, recreated one stage later.</p>
<p>A cautious position: until promotion is shown to be repo-aware, a cross-repo landing should be treated as atomic only up to commit. The evidence that would settle it is either code showing the promotion gate groups commits by operation ID across repos, or a test that quarantines one half of a <code>2c.1</code> landing and checks what happens to the other.</p>
</details>
<p class="engage-kicker engage-kicker-adv">Challenge problems</p>
<div class="pset pset-adv">
<div class="problem problem-adv">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Challenge 1 (adversarial).</strong> A <code>2c.1</code> Saga renames a request field from <code>user_id</code> to <code>uid</code> in <code>jarvis/backend/protocols/prime.py</code> and in <code>jarvis-prime/api/v1/schemas.py</code>, the two files from §7.1. Both patches validate on their own, both apply, and the <code>CrossRepoVerifier</code> passes. But a module in <code>jarvis-reactor</code> also reads <code>user_id</code>, and it is not in the Saga. Find every layer in Parts II and III that might catch the third consumer, and decide honestly whether any of them does. Then propose, and label as a proposal, the smallest change that would.</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>Look at what CONTEXT_EXPANSION does with a path outside the repo (§10.1, step 4), and at which tests VERIFY selects (§16.1).</p>
