<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p>Go through the candidate layers.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>CONTEXT_EXPANSION (§10.1).</strong> Suggested paths are resolved against the repo root, and paths outside the repo are rejected by the Iron Gate. Even if the model guessed the Reactor consumer, expansion could not add it to context. The model is structurally unable to look across the boundary through this phase.</li>
<li><strong>Saga application (§7.2).</strong> Compensation only covers repos that appear in the patch dictionary. Reactor is not one of them, so nothing there is applied or reverted.</li>
<li><strong>CrossRepoVerifier (§7.2).</strong> It "executes cross-repo tests to validate that the union of the patches is consistent". It catches the break only if its test selection includes Reactor tests that touch the field. The paper does not say how that selection is made, and the scenario says it passed.</li>
<li><strong>VERIFY (§16.1).</strong> It runs a scoped set of tests that exercise the <em>changed</em> files. The Reactor consumer is unchanged, so its tests are not in scope.</li>
<li><strong>Stale-exploration guard (§15.3).</strong> It compares hashes of the target files only. It is irrelevant here.</li>
</ul>
<p>Honest conclusion: as described, no layer is guaranteed to catch it. The design would ship a contract break into the third repo and leave it for a later sensor, such as a test-failure signal, to find.</p>
<p>Proposal (not in the paper): when a candidate changes a symbol named in a cross-repo contract, the CrossRepoVerifier's scope should be every repo in the Service's <code>_repo_registry</code> (§6), which already lists <code>jarvis</code>, <code>jarvis-prime</code> and <code>jarvis-reactor</code>, not just the repos in the patch. A cheap first step is a deterministic search for the old field name across all registered repos before GATE, failing closed on any hit outside the Saga. This is a structural check, not a model call, so it fits Principle 5 (§3). To check the proposal, plant exactly this scenario and confirm the operation ends in POSTMORTEM rather than COMPLETE.</p>
</details>
</div>
<div class="problem problem-adv">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Challenge 2 (systems design).</strong> Under the October constraints (one 32 GB GPU, no paid lanes), the Service state machine of §6.1 has no honest way to say "the only lane is lent to training". Givens from §93.6 and §93.11: J-Prime cold-loads in 15 s to 18.9 GiB resident; the lease releases 21,236 MiB; Reactor holds the 30B at 15.64 GiB resident while training. (a) Show with the numbers why serving and training cannot share the card. (b) Explain why neither DEGRADED nor FAILED describes a lent lane. (c) Design the missing behaviour and justify it against Principle 2 and §8.2.</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>Re-read the definitions of DEGRADED and FAILED in §6.1 word for word. Then look for an existing "queue rather than execute" rule in Part III.</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p>(a) Serving needs 18.9 GiB and training needs 15.64 GiB, a total of 34.54 GiB. A 32 GB card holds at most 32 GiB even on the most generous reading, and less (about 29.8 GiB) if GB means 10^9 bytes. Either way, the two jobs do not fit together, which is why the lease is exclusive. The lease frees 21,236 MiB (about 20.7 GiB), which is more than the 15.64 GiB that training needs. Returning to service costs at least the 15 s cold load.</p>
<p>(b) §6.1 defines DEGRADED as "some providers unhealthy but operations still flowing". With one lane lent, no generation can flow, so DEGRADED would mislead the operator. FAILED is "a terminal failure state that prevents further operations". A lease is planned and temporary, so marking it terminal would be wrong, and it would block the return.</p>
<p>(c) Proposal (not in the paper): add a non-terminal state, for example <code>LEASED</code>, entered from ACTIVE when the training lease is granted and left back to ACTIVE when J-Prime's reload is confirmed. While LEASED:</p>
<ul>
<li>Intake keeps accepting signals, but the pool does not dispatch GENERATE. This mirrors §8.2 clause 5, where an exhausted budget queues the next operation instead of running it.</li>
<li>In-flight operations either finish before the lease is granted or are recorded as aborted, never leaked (Principle 1, §8.1).</li>
<li>The transition is written to the ledger and shown in the cockpit, which already has a GPU-lease lock screen (§6.1, §93.9).</li>
</ul>
<p>Justification: Principle 2 forbids blocking boot chains and hanging on a slow dependency. LEASED does not hang; it states plainly that one resource is away and resumes when it returns. It also matches capability assurance, which refuses to run below the declared envelope rather than degrading silently (§93.12). To check the design, run a training handoff during a soak and confirm three things: no operation reaches GENERATE while LEASED, no operation is lost, and queued operations dispatch within roughly the cold-load time after release.</p>
</details>
</div>
</div>
<p class="engage-kicker engage-kicker-x">Connections</p>
<div class="pset pset-x">
<div class="problem problem-x">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Connection 1 (Graph theory).</strong> A Saga (§7.2) carries three <code>RepoPatch</code> objects: P_prime (a J-Prime schema), P_jarvis (the Body client for that schema) and P_reactor (a Reactor runner that calls the Body client). The declared dependencies are that P_jarvis needs P_prime, and P_reactor needs P_jarvis. (a) Draw the dependency DAG and give every valid apply order. (b) Drop the second edge, so P_reactor is independent. How many valid orders are there now? (c) With the original DAG, P_reactor fails to apply. List the compensation steps. (d) All three apply, but the <code>CrossRepoVerifier</code> fails. List the compensation steps and count the total <code>ChangeEngine</code> calls. (e) Show that undoing in reverse order never leaves an applied patch without its dependency, while undoing in forward order can.</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>A valid apply order is a topological sort. During compensation, look at the set of patches still applied after each step, and ask whether that set is closed under "depends on".</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p>(a) The edges are P_prime to P_jarvis to P_reactor, a chain. A chain has exactly one topological order: P_prime, P_jarvis, P_reactor.</p>
<p>(b) With only the edge P_prime to P_jarvis, P_reactor can go in any of three positions relative to the fixed pair. That gives 3 valid orders: (R, P, J), (P, R, J) and (P, J, R).</p>
<p>(c) P_prime and P_jarvis are already applied. Compensation walks them in reverse: roll back P_jarvis, then roll back P_prime. That is 2 rollbacks, after 2 successful applies and 1 failed apply.</p>
<p>(d) All three are applied, so compensation rolls back P_reactor, then P_jarvis, then P_prime. That is 3 applies plus 3 rollbacks: 6 <code>ChangeEngine</code> calls, ending fully reverted, as §7.2 guarantees.</p>
<p>(e) Applying in topological order means the applied set is always a prefix of that order. A prefix of a topological order is closed under dependencies: every applied patch has its prerequisites applied. Removing the last element of a prefix leaves a shorter prefix, so reverse-order undo keeps that invariant at every step. Forward-order undo would first remove P_prime while P_jarvis is still applied: a Body client pointing at a schema that no longer exists. That is exactly the broken-contract state §7.1 warns about.</p>
<p>What this says about the architecture: the dependency DAG fixes the apply order, and its reverse fixes the undo order. Every intermediate state of the Saga is then internally consistent, not just the two end states.</p>
</details>
</div>
<div class="problem problem-x">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Connection 2 (Formal verification: invariants).</strong> §6 says the <code>_file_touch_cache</code> allows three O+V modifications per file per ten-minute window, after which "further modifications are hard-blocked until the window resets". Suppose the property you want is I: "no file is modified more than 3 times in any 10-minute interval." The paper does not say whether windows are fixed (aligned to boundaries) or sliding, so analyse both. (a) Under fixed windows, build a trace that satisfies the cache but violates I. What is the most touches possible within a few seconds? (b) Under each design, what is the most touches in any 60-minute interval? (c) Which design makes I an invariant?</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>A fixed-window counter forgets everything at the boundary. An arbitrary 60-minute interval that does not start on a boundary overlaps seven fixed windows.</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p>(a) Fixed windows, boundaries at 10:00 and 10:10. Touch the file at 10:09:58, 10:09:59 and 10:09:59.5. That is 3 touches in window one, all allowed. At 10:10:00 the counter resets, so touches at 10:10:00, 10:10:00.5 and 10:10:01 are also allowed. That is 6 touches in about 3 seconds, violating I.</p>
<p>(b) Sliding window: any 60-minute interval splits into six consecutive 10-minute intervals, each holding at most 3 touches. That gives at most 18. Fixed windows: an interval starting mid-window overlaps seven windows (a partial first one, five whole ones, a partial last one). Each can put 3 touches inside the overlap, so up to 21.</p>
<p>(c) Only the sliding design, which keeps per-file timestamps and counts those in the last 600 s, makes I hold in every state. The fixed design enforces a weaker property: at most 3 per aligned window, which allows bursts of 6 across a boundary.</p>
<p>What this says about the architecture: the cache is a concurrency guard against O+V repeatedly reworking the same file. Whether it meets that intent depends on an implementation detail the description leaves open. Writing the guard's property down as an invariant shows exactly which detail matters, and gives a test to check it against: the boundary-burst trace in (a).</p>
</details>
</div>
</div>
</div>
<!-- engage:end -->

# PART III — The Eleven-Phase Pipeline

> **Big Picture:** The pipeline is the heart of O+V. Every operation passes through the same eleven phases, in the same order, with the same contract at each boundary. The phases are *deterministic* — they transition based on explicit conditions, not on model output. The *content* of what happens at GENERATE is agentic and probabilistic; the *decision* about whether GENERATE's output proceeds to APPLY is deterministic. This is the key architectural choice that makes O+V safe while still being autonomous.

## §8. The Eleven Phases — Overview

![Figure 2 — The 11-phase pipeline. Every operation traverses the same phases, in the same order, with the same contract at each boundary. Square brackets indicate phases that may be skipped for trivial operations. Every unhandled exception routes to POSTMORTEM.](figures/fig02_pipeline_flow.png)

The eleven-phase flow:

```
CLASSIFY → ROUTE → [CONTEXT_EXPANSION] → [PLAN] → GENERATE → VALIDATE
                                                              │
                                                              ▼
           COMPLETE ← VERIFY ← APPLY ← APPROVE ← GATE
```

Square brackets indicate phases that may be skipped for trivial operations (single-file, short-description changes).

Each phase has a **contract**: the inputs it receives from the previous phase, the outputs it produces for the next phase, the failure modes it can emit, and the retry budget it is governed by. The contracts are enforced by the orchestrator; a phase cannot transition to an arbitrary next phase — only to phases the contract permits.

### §8.1 Terminal and Non-Terminal Phases

| Phase | Terminal? | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `CLASSIFY` | No | |
| `ROUTE` | No | |
| `CONTEXT_EXPANSION` | No | |
| `PLAN` | No | |
| `GENERATE` | No | |
| `GENERATE_RETRY` | No | |
| `VALIDATE` | No | |
| `VALIDATE_RETRY` | No | |
| `GATE` | No | |
| `APPROVE` | No | |
| `APPLY` | No | |
| `VERIFY` | No | |
| `COMPLETE` | **Yes** | Success |
| `POSTMORTEM` | **Yes** | Failure — always reached, never skipped |
| `CANCELLED` | **Yes** | User-initiated cancellation |
| `BLOCKED` | **Yes** | Short-circuited at CLASSIFY (e.g., protected path) |
| `FAILED_PERMANENT` | **Yes** | Unrecoverable error — sink state |

Every operation ends in a terminal state. The orchestrator's guarantee is that **no operation is leaked** — if an exception unwinds the call stack without being handled, the FSM's `__exit__` handler transitions to POSTMORTEM before re-raising. Every terminal transition writes a `LedgerEntry`.

### §8.2 The Governance Contract

The phases are what gives O+V its structure, but the *governance contract* is what gives it its safety. The contract has five clauses:

1. **Every phase transition is logged.** No silent transitions.
2. **Every unhandled exception routes to POSTMORTEM.** No silent crashes.
3. **Retries are bounded by config.** No infinite retry loops.
4. **BLOCKED operations short-circuit at CLASSIFY.** No wasted work on a pre-rejected op.
5. **Cost is tracked continuously.** Every phase transition carries a cost update. When the daily budget is exhausted, the next operation is queued rather than executed.

These five clauses are not advisory. They are enforced by the orchestrator's code structure. A contributor who adds a new phase must wire it into the contract; otherwise the phase will not be reachable from the FSM.

## §9. CLASSIFY & ROUTE — Risk and Urgency

> **Big Picture:** The first two phases exist to answer two deterministic questions: "how dangerous is this change?" (CLASSIFY) and "which model provider should handle it?" (ROUTE). Neither phase calls a model. Both use lookup tables, heuristic code, and cached metadata. The goal is to spend zero inference cost deciding whether an operation is cheap or expensive — the deterministic fast-path is a cost-optimization on top of a safety-optimization.

### §9.1 CLASSIFY — The Risk Engine

**Source:** `backend/core/ouroboros/governance/risk_engine.py`.

**Purpose:** Assign a `RiskTier` and a `ChangeType` to the incoming signal.

The `RiskTier` enum has four levels:

| Tier | Color | Auto-Apply? | Example Triggers |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SAFE_AUTO` | Green | Yes, silent | Single-file, non-core, non-security |
| `NOTIFY_APPLY` | Yellow | Yes, visible | New files, multi-file changes, core orchestration paths |
| `APPROVAL_REQUIRED` | Orange | No, blocks for human | Security-sensitive, breaking API changes |
| `BLOCKED` | Red | Never reaches APPLY | Supervisor files, credentials, governance-engine internals |

The tier is assigned by evaluating the signal against a rule ladder — twelve rules, evaluated in order, with the first matching rule assigning the tier. Rule 0 is protected-path detection: if any target file matches `.env`, `credentials.*`, `.git/`, or the supervisor's core files, the tier is `BLOCKED` and the operation short-circuits immediately. Rule 1 is security-sensitive pattern detection (API keys, secrets). Rules 2–11 handle increasing specificity: file count, line count, path class, change-type class, intent-description keywords, consciousness-driven escalation.

Consciousness-driven escalation is the interesting one: if `ConsciousnessBridge.assess_regression_risk()` returns `HIGH`, the operation's tier is elevated by one step (Yellow → Orange, Green → Yellow). The MemoryEngine knows that the target files have failed often before; the ProphecyEngine predicts the operation is risky; the risk engine listens.

### §9.2 ROUTE — The Urgency Router

**Source:** `backend/core/ouroboros/governance/urgency_router.py`.

**Purpose:** Stamp a `ProviderRoute` onto the operation based on `(urgency, source, complexity)`.

The five routes:

| Route | Strategy | Intended Cost/Op | When |
|---|---|---|---|
| `IMMEDIATE` | Claude direct (skip DW) | ~$0.03 | Test failures, voice commands, runtime-health critical |
| `STANDARD` | DW primary → Claude fallback | ~$0.005 | Default cascade for normal-priority work |
| `COMPLEX` | Claude plans → DW executes | ~$0.015 | Multi-file architectural, heavy tool loops |
| `BACKGROUND` | DW only, no Claude fallback | ~$0.002 | Opportunity mining, doc staleness, TODOs |
| `SPECULATIVE` | DW batch fire-and-forget | ~$0.001 | Intent discovery, proactive exploration, dream-engine |

The router is pure code. No LLM call. Latency under one millisecond. It consults two deterministic lookup tables:

- `_IMMEDIATE_SOURCES`: frozen set of source names whose high-urgency signals always route to IMMEDIATE (`test_failure`, `voice_human`, `runtime_health`).
- `_BACKGROUND_SOURCES`: frozen set whose signals always route to BACKGROUND regardless of urgency (`ai_miner`, `exploration`, `backlog`, `architecture`, `todo_scanner`, `doc_staleness`).

And one deterministic complexity check:

- `_COMPLEX_COMPLEXITIES`: frozen set (`heavy_code`, `complex`) — architectural operations route to COMPLEX regardless of urgency.

If none of those apply, the signal falls through to STANDARD. The fall-through default is the cheapest cascade that still has a Claude safety net.

**Why deterministic and not model-driven?** Three reasons:

1. **Determinism** — the routing must be reproducible from the signal envelope alone. If you replay a signal, you get the same route. Non-determinism in routing would break the ledger's causal reconstruction guarantee.
2. **Cost** — a routing model call would itself cost money. Routing happens for *every* operation; inferencing every routing decision would double the bill.
3. **Latency** — agent workloads have tight per-phase budgets. A routing model call would consume budget the generation phase needs.

<!-- engage:begin -->
<div class="quick-check" id="qc-9">
<p class="qc-label">Quick check · §9</p>

<p>With first-match rules, order is precedence. If a later rule such as "single-file, non-core" fired first, a change to <code>.env</code> or a supervisor core file could be classed Green. Putting protected paths first makes BLOCKED win, and the operation short-circuits immediately (§9.1).</p>
</details>
<details class="qc"><summary>2. What triggers consciousness-driven escalation, and how far can it move a tier?</summary>
<p>It fires when <code>ConsciousnessBridge.assess_regression_risk()</code> returns HIGH, reflecting the MemoryEngine's file history and the ProphecyEngine's prediction. It raises the tier one step: Green to Yellow, or Yellow to Orange (§9.1).</p>

<details class="qc"><summary>3. A high-urgency signal arrives from <code>todo_scanner</code>. Which route does it get, and which provider will run it?</summary>
<p>BACKGROUND. <code>todo_scanner</code> is in <code>_BACKGROUND_SOURCES</code>, which routes to BACKGROUND regardless of urgency. That route is DoubleWord only, with no Claude fallback (§9.2).</p>
</details>
</div>
<!-- engage:end -->

## §10. CONTEXT_EXPANSION — Bounded Exploration Before Generation

> **Big Picture:** Before the model writes code, it helps to have seen the code. Context expansion is where O+V identifies which files the model should read *before* generation, so it is not writing blind. But exploration must be bounded — letting the model wander the codebase would be expensive and slow. The context expander is a two-round, five-files-per-round, lightweight-prompt service that the model uses to nominate additional context.

**Source:** `backend/core/ouroboros/governance/context_expander.py`.

**Hardcoded governance limits:**

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| `MAX_ROUNDS` | 2 |
| `MAX_FILES_PER_ROUND` | 5 |
| `MAX_FILES_PER_CATEGORY` | 10 |

The phase runs only when `context_expansion_enabled=true` in the orchestrator config (default `true`). For trivial operations (single file, short description), the orchestrator skips expansion entirely via a fast-path heuristic.

### §10.1 The Expansion Loop

Each round:

1. **Build a lightweight prompt** — description, target filenames, no file contents. The goal is to spend as few input tokens as possible to get expansion suggestions.
2. **Call `generator.plan(prompt, deadline)`** — a plan-oriented model call that returns `expansion.1` schema JSON.
3. **Parse the response** — extract a list of file path suggestions with per-file justifications.
4. **Resolve the paths** — each suggestion is resolved against the repo root. Paths outside the repo are rejected (Iron Gate). Paths that don't exist are silently skipped (the model may hallucinate).
5. **Accumulate** — confirmed paths are added to `ctx.expanded_context_files`.

The loop stops early if: the response is empty, the JSON is invalid, no paths confirm, or the generator raises.

### §10.2 Why Two Rounds?

The two-round limit is a deliberate compromise. One round captures first-order relationships (files imported by the target). A second round captures second-order relationships (files imported by the files imported by the target). A third round would be mostly noise — the useful signal is concentrated in orders one and two.

### §10.3 Stale-Index Tolerance

Context expansion consults the Oracle (`backend/core/ouroboros/oracle.py`) for structural neighborhood data. The Oracle maintains a NetworkX graph of the codebase, indexed asynchronously by `_oracle_index_loop`. If the index is more than 300 seconds stale (checked via `Oracle.index_age_s()`), the context expander emits a warning but does not block. Stale data is better than no data.

## §11. PLAN — Model-Reasoned Implementation Strategy

> **Big Picture:** Before generating code, the model reasons about *how* to implement the change. This phase mirrors what Claude Code does internally, exposed as an explicit phase so the reasoning is observable and auditable. For trivial operations, planning is skipped — the overhead would exceed the value. For architectural operations, planning is required — the coordination across files is what makes the change tractable.

**Source:** `backend/core/ouroboros/governance/plan_generator.py` (`PlanGenerator`, `PlanResult`).

### §11.1 The `plan.1` Schema

The model produces structured JSON conforming to the `plan.1` schema:

| Field | Type | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `approach` | string | 1–3 sentence strategy summary |
| `complexity` | enum (`trivial`/`moderate`/`complex`/`architectural`) | Self-assessed complexity |
| `ordered_changes` | list of `FileChangeDescriptor` | Dependency-ordered list of changes |
| `risk_factors` | list of string | Specific actionable risks |
| `test_strategy` | string | Verification approach |
| `architectural_notes` | string | Cross-cutting concerns |

The `ordered_changes` list is the most important field. It tells the GENERATE phase which files to change in which order, with per-file rationale.

### §11.2 When Planning Runs, When It Doesn't

Planning runs when:

- The operation involves more than one file (`JARVIS_PLAN_TRIVIAL_MAX_FILES`, default `1`).
- The description is longer than a trivial threshold.
- Complexity was classified as `moderate` or higher at ROUTE.

Planning is skipped when the operation is trivial — single-file, short description, low-complexity classification. The orchestrator short-circuits through PLAN with an implicit "default approach" entry.

### §11.3 Soft Failure

Planning failures are **soft** — if the plan call times out or returns invalid JSON, the pipeline falls through to GENERATE with no plan injected. This is a deliberate choice: planning is *helpful* but not *required*. A failed plan should not block a routine operation.

### §11.4 Prompt Injection

The plan is injected into the GENERATE prompt under an `## Implementation Plan` section. The code-generation model sees the plan's strategy summary, the ordered changes, and the risk factors. This ensures coherent execution across multi-file operations — file 3 is written knowing what files 1 and 2 committed to.

### §11.5 Coherence Validation

Before the plan is injected, it is validated for coherence:

- **File overlap:** planned files must overlap with target files. A plan that omits all target files is incoherent.
- **Acyclic dependencies:** if the plan declares that file A depends on file B and B depends on A, the plan has a cycle. Cycles are rejected.
- **Ordering:** the file order must be a topological sort of the declared dependencies.

Validation failures downgrade the plan to "default approach" rather than blocking the pipeline.

### §11.6 Observability

SerpentFlow renders the plan phase as:
- `🗺️  planning` during execution.
- `🗺️  planned [complexity=moderate]` on completion, with the complexity badge visible.

The plan itself is recorded in the ledger under the `PLAN` state entry — `ctx.plan_result` is serialized with the `ordered_changes` structure so a postmortem reader can reconstruct what the model intended before GENERATE began.

<p>The planned files must overlap the target files, the declared dependencies must be acyclic, and the file order must be a topological sort of those dependencies (§11.5). A failure downgrades the plan to "default approach"; it does not block the pipeline.</p>

## §12. GENERATE — The Agentic Heart

> **Big Picture:** This is where the model actually writes code. But unlike a single-shot "here's a prompt, give me a completion" call, GENERATE with Venom is a multi-turn conversation in which the model can read files, search the codebase, run tests, and revise its own output across multiple iterations. This turns generation from a one-shot gamble into a process of exploration, drafting, and verification — the same process a human engineer uses. This phase consumes more than half of the total operation wall-clock on architectural changes, and that's by design.

**Sources:**
- `backend/core/ouroboros/governance/providers.py` — `ClaudeProvider`, `PrimeProvider`.
- `backend/core/ouroboros/governance/doubleword_provider.py` — `DoublewordProvider`.
- `backend/core/ouroboros/governance/tool_executor.py` — `ToolLoopCoordinator`.
- `backend/core/ouroboros/governance/candidate_generator.py` — cascade routing.

### §12.1 The Cascade

At GENERATE time, the provider decision has already been made at ROUTE. Depending on route:

- **IMMEDIATE**: call Claude directly; skip DoubleWord entirely.
- **STANDARD**: call DoubleWord primary; on failure, cascade to Claude.
- **COMPLEX**: call Claude for planning; call DoubleWord for execution (current topology has DW sealed from COMPLEX pending SSE stability; see `brain_selection_policy.yaml`).
- **BACKGROUND**: call DoubleWord only; no Claude cascade (cost optimization).
- **SPECULATIVE**: call DoubleWord batch; tolerate high discard rate.

The `CandidateGenerator` owns cascade mechanics. It wraps each provider call in a `FailbackStateMachine` that classifies failures and decides recovery timing. If the primary provider fails with `TIMEOUT`, the FSM enters `FALLBACK_ACTIVE` and the next operation prefers the fallback. If it fails with `CONNECTION_ERROR` (unreachable host), the FSM enters `QUEUE_ONLY` and waits for a health-probe success before retrying.

### §12.2 The Tool Loop

Each provider's `generate()` method accepts an optional `tool_loop: ToolLoopCoordinator`. When provided, `generate()` delegates to the coordinator instead of making a single API call.

The coordinator's `run()` method is the multi-turn loop:

1. Send the prompt (plus accumulated tool results) to the provider.
2. Parse the provider's response for tool calls.
3. For each tool call:
   - `GoverningToolPolicy.evaluate()` — check the call against the Iron Gate (Part XI).
   - If allowed: `AsyncProcessToolBackend.execute()` runs the tool in a subprocess sandbox.
   - If denied: emit a `tool_denied` result back to the provider.
4. Append tool results to the conversation.
5. Loop until the provider produces a response with no tool calls (the final answer).

The loop is bounded by `JARVIS_GOVERNED_TOOL_MAX_ROUNDS` (default `5`) and by the generation deadline.

### §12.3 The 16 Tools

The full tool manifest is the subject of Part IV (Venom). In brief, the tools cover:

- **Comprehension:** `read_file`, `search_code`, `list_symbols`.
- **Discovery:** `glob_files`, `list_dir`.
- **Call graph:** `get_callers`.
- **History:** `git_log`, `git_diff`, `git_blame`.
- **Mutation:** `edit_file`, `write_file`, `delete_file` (Iron-Gate-protected).
- **Execution:** `bash` (blocklist-gated), `run_tests` (policy-gated).
- **Web:** `web_fetch`, `web_search` (domain-allowlisted).
- **Human:** `ask_human` (risk-tier-gated).

Plus MCP external tools discovered from connected servers at prompt construction time.

### §12.4 The Iron Gate at GENERATE

Two Iron Gates fire in the GENERATE phase:

1. **Exploration-first gate.** Before emitting any patch, the model must have called at least two exploration tools (`read_file`, `search_code`, `get_callers`). Violating this produces a `GENERATE_RETRY` with targeted feedback.

2. **ASCII-strictness gate.** The candidate's content must contain only ASCII codepoints. Non-ASCII characters trigger automatic repair (replacing the character with an ASCII approximation) or, if repair fails, rejection.

These gates flow through the GENERATE retry loop — they are enforced post-generation, pre-VALIDATE, and violations result in a regeneration rather than a fall-through to APPLY. Part XI details the full Iron Gate philosophy.

### §12.5 Context Auto-Compaction

During long tool-loop runs, the accumulated prompt grows. Older tool results are compacted into a deterministic summary when the prompt exceeds 75% of the maximum budget (default 98,304 characters). The compaction preserves the most recent six tool chunks and summarizes older ones as:

```
[CONTEXT COMPACTED]
Compacted 12 earlier tool results (45,230 chars): 5 read_file, 4 search_code, 3 bash.
Recent results preserved below.
[END CONTEXT COMPACTED]
```

No model inference is used for the summary — it is pure deterministic counting and string manipulation. This keeps the loop viable on long runs without spending extra tokens.

### §12.6 The Candidate Produced

At the end of GENERATE (whether single-shot or tool-loop), the provider returns a `GenerationResult`:

- `candidates`: a list of candidate patches. Usually length 1; some providers support multiple candidates.
- `rationales`: per-candidate model reasoning (for observability).
- `tool_execution_records`: audit log of every tool call made during the loop.
- `usage`: token counts and cost.

The candidate is a structured object with `file_path` + `full_content` (single-file) or a `files: [{file_path, full_content, rationale}, ...]` list (multi-file). Multi-file candidates unlock coordinated changes across several files in a single atomic APPLY (see §15).

## §13. VALIDATE — Tests and Iron Gates

> **Big Picture:** Generating a candidate is necessary but not sufficient. The candidate must *work* — it must compile, pass type checks, pass tests, and meet the project's structural requirements. The VALIDATE phase runs the candidate through a gauntlet of increasingly strict checks. Failures here don't end the operation; they route to VALIDATE_RETRY or L2 Self-Repair.

**Source:** `backend/core/ouroboros/governance/orchestrator.py` (VALIDATE phase), `validation_runner.py`.

### §13.1 What Gets Validated

For each candidate file:

1. **Syntax check:** parse the file with the language's AST (Python `ast`, etc.). Invalid syntax = immediate rejection.
2. **Type check:** run `mypy` or equivalent. Type errors are classified as recoverable (can be fixed by L2) or unrecoverable (structural issue that needs regeneration).
3. **Test run:** `JARVIS_VERIFY_TIMEOUT_S` (default 60s) test run on the affected files. Tests that pass in isolation but fail together are rare but possible; they're caught here.
4. **Iron Gate checks:** exploration ledger, ASCII strictness, multi-file coverage (see Part XI).

### §13.2 The VALIDATE_RETRY Loop

If validation fails, the operation enters `VALIDATE_RETRY` and regenerates. The retry budget is bounded by `JARVIS_MAX_VALIDATE_RETRIES` (default `2`). After the budget is exhausted, the operation escalates to L2 Self-Repair.

### §13.3 L2 Self-Repair

L2 is an iterative convergence loop with its own FSM (see Part IV, §23). It tries up to `JARVIS_L2_MAX_ITERS` (default `5`) iterations within a `JARVIS_L2_TIMEBOX_S` (default `120s`) wall-clock budget. Each iteration:

1. Generate a patch informed by the failure context.
2. Run validation in sandbox.
3. Classify the failure (syntax, test, environment, flaky).
4. Evaluate progress (new failures? same failures? oscillation?).
5. Decide to retry, stop, or converge.

Kill conditions: deadline exhaustion, timebox expiry, max iterations, no-progress streak (`2`), oscillation detection (signature hash matching).

### §13.4 Convergence

A successful L2 iteration transitions the operation out of VALIDATE_RETRY and into GATE. A failed L2 sequence routes to POSTMORTEM with `root_cause` reflecting the failure class.

## §14. GATE & APPROVE — The Safety Chokepoint

> **Big Picture:** GATE is the last safety checkpoint before a change is written to disk. It is the final "should we really do this?" moment. For low-risk changes, GATE auto-approves and the operation proceeds. For medium-risk changes, GATE emits a notification and proceeds after a brief delay. For high-risk changes, GATE blocks and waits for a human.

**Source:** `backend/core/ouroboros/governance/policy_engine.py`, `orchestrator.py` (Phase 5b).

### §14.1 The Four-Tier Escalator

This is the same risk-tier table from §9.1, repeated here because its operational meaning is at GATE:

| Tier | GATE Behavior |
|---|---|
| `SAFE_AUTO` (Green) | Auto-approve silently. Proceed to APPLY. |
| `NOTIFY_APPLY` (Yellow) | Emit `notify_apply` decision via CommProtocol. Render diff preview. Wait `JARVIS_NOTIFY_APPLY_DELAY_S` (default 5s) for human cancellation. Proceed to APPLY if no cancel. |
| `APPROVAL_REQUIRED` (Orange) | Block. Emit `awaiting_approval` decision. Wait up to `approval_timeout_s` (default 600s) for human Y/N. |
| `BLOCKED` (Red) | Already short-circuited at CLASSIFY. GATE is unreachable for BLOCKED ops. |

### §14.2 The Orange PR Reviewer

For `APPROVAL_REQUIRED` ops, the default approval provider is a CLI prompt. The human types Y/N at the SerpentFlow REPL. But a second provider is available: `OrangePRReviewer`.

**Source:** `backend/core/ouroboros/governance/orange_pr_reviewer.py`.

When `JARVIS_ORANGE_PR_ENABLED=true`, Orange-tier operations are async-reviewed instead of blocking. The reviewer:

1. Creates a branch `ouroboros/review/<op-id>`.
2. Commits the candidate to that branch.
3. Pushes the branch to origin.
4. Files a GitHub PR via `gh pr create` with an evidence body and review checklist.
5. **The autonomous loop continues immediately** — it does not block on the PR.

The human reviews the PR asynchronously. If approved and merged, the review is retroactively validated. If rejected, the branch is deleted and a `FEEDBACK` memory entry is recorded with the rejection reason.

This is **Manifesto §7 (Absolute Observability)** at work: the PR is the auditable artifact. The operation is not hidden behind a REPL interaction; it is a reviewable unit of work the human can engage with on their own schedule.

### §14.3 The Diff Preview

Before any Yellow auto-apply, the diff is rendered in the CLI with five seconds of delay. During that window, the operator can type `cancel <op-id>` at the REPL to abort. This is Refinement #17 from Edge Case Hardening — a trust-building mechanism that lets the operator veto decisions they disagree with without requiring a full approval workflow.

## §15. APPLY — Writing Changes to Disk

> **Big Picture:** APPLY is the moment of truth. The patches have been validated. Approval has been secured. Now the changes are actually written to the file system. The ChangeEngine performs this with full rollback capability — if anything goes wrong mid-write, the pre-APPLY state is restored.

**Source:** `backend/core/ouroboros/governance/change_engine.py`, `orchestrator.py` (APPLY phase).

### §15.1 Single-File APPLY

For single-file candidates:

1. `RollbackArtifact.capture()` snapshots the target file's pre-APPLY state. If the file is new, the artifact records "create" semantics.
2. `ChangeEngine.execute()` writes the candidate's `full_content` to disk atomically (write to temp, then rename).
3. The operation's `APPLY` state entry is written to the ledger with pre- and post-hash metadata.
4. Success: transition to VERIFY. Failure: `RollbackArtifact.restore()` is called to revert, and the operation routes to POSTMORTEM.

### §15.2 Multi-File APPLY

For multi-file candidates (the `files: [...]` schema), APPLY iterates the list:

```python
for idx, file_spec in enumerate(candidate.files):
    pre_snapshots[idx] = RollbackArtifact.capture(file_spec.file_path)
    try:
        ChangeEngine.execute(file_spec)
    except Exception:
        # Batch-level rollback: revert all already-applied files in this batch.
        for j in range(idx - 1, -1, -1):
            pre_snapshots[j].restore()
        raise
```

Every file has its own `::NN` sub-op identifier (`op-<uuid>::00`, `::01`, `::02`, ...) for per-file observability. If any file fails, the batch is rolled back atomically — all already-applied files are reverted via the captured snapshots. This preserves the atomic-update guarantee for multi-file operations.

### §15.3 Stale Exploration Guard

At APPLY, the target files' current SHA-256 hashes are recomputed and compared against the hashes that were snapshotted at GENERATE time (`ctx.generate_file_hashes`). If any differ, the candidate was built on stale file state. This is a soft gate today (warning + ledger entry) rather than a hard reject, on the theory that concurrent operations are rare and the cost of false positives is worse than the cost of occasional stale writes. The stale-exploration guard exists to catch the failure; L2 or the next-operation sensors will repair it.

### §15.4 The REPL `/cancel`

Between GATE and APPLY, a cooperative cancellation check fires. If `serpent_flow.py:SerpentREPL._handle_cancel` has set the cancellation flag for this op-id (via the operator typing `cancel <op-id>` at the REPL), the orchestrator transitions to `CANCELLED` with `reason=user_cancelled` instead of proceeding to APPLY. This is a last-chance abort mechanism — even after approval, the human can still stop the write.

## §16. VERIFY — Post-Apply Verification Loop

> **Big Picture:** Writing the patch to disk is not the end. The test suite must be re-run with the patch applied — validation in isolation is not enough; validation in situ is what actually matters. If the post-apply tests fail, L2 Repair gets one more chance. If L2 also fails, the operation rolls back.

**Source:** `backend/core/ouroboros/governance/orchestrator.py` (Phase 8a).

### §16.1 Scoped Test Run

VERIFY runs `_validation_runner.run(changed_files, timeout=JARVIS_VERIFY_TIMEOUT_S)`. This is a **scoped** test run — only tests that exercise the changed files are executed. Running the entire test suite would be slow; running a scope targeted to the diff catches regressions without burning the wall clock.

### §16.2 Outcomes

- **PASS:** Continue to the benchmark gate (if enabled) and COMPLETE.
- **FAIL:** Route to L2 Repair. L2 is given the post-apply test failure context and attempts to fix the regression. If L2 converges, the fix is APPLY'd (via ChangeEngine) on top of the already-applied change, and VERIFY re-runs. If L2 fails, the operation transitions to POSTMORTEM with the `RollbackArtifact` stack rolling back all applied changes.

### §16.3 Heartbeat Observability

During VERIFY, SerpentFlow renders:

```
⏺ Verify(test_foo.py, test_bar.py)  →  2/2 passed  (3.4s)
```

Pass/fail counts are visible in real time. An operator watching the CLI sees precisely when verification passes or fails.

## §17. POSTMORTEM, COMPLETE, and Terminal States

> **Big Picture:** Every operation ends somewhere. COMPLETE is the happy path. POSTMORTEM is the failure path — but crucially, POSTMORTEM is not silent; it is the mechanism by which the organism *learns* from what went wrong. The terminal state is the most important state for the organism's long-term development.

**Source:** `backend/core/ouroboros/governance/comm_protocol.py` (POSTMORTEM emission), `orchestrator.py` (terminal transitions).

### §17.1 COMPLETE

The COMPLETE state is reached when VERIFY passes and the benchmark gate (if enabled) passes. The terminal state record includes:

- Final operation status.
- Total wall-clock duration.
- Total cost.
- Provider breakdown.
- File hash pairs (pre vs post).
- Cost-governor summary.

COMPLETE triggers the AutoCommitter (Phase 8b) to create a structured git commit with the O+V signature.

### §17.2 POSTMORTEM

POSTMORTEM is reached on any failure path. It is **always reached** — the orchestrator's `__exit__` handler guarantees that every operation terminates in a terminal state, POSTMORTEM included. A POSTMORTEM record includes:

- `failed_phase`: which phase produced the terminal failure.
- `root_cause`: classified cause (`infra`, `test`, `lsp`, `timeout`, `user_cancelled`, etc., or `none` if the postmortem closes without a specific cause).
- `artifacts`: logs, diffs, and state snapshots useful for debugging.

The POSTMORTEM record is published via `CommProtocol.emit_postmortem()`, which feeds it into the ConversationBridge for cross-op episodic visibility (see Part V, §31).

### §17.3 CANCELLED

`CANCELLED` is the user-initiated terminal state, reachable from GATE or APPLY via the REPL `cancel <op-id>` command. The cancellation is cooperative — the orchestrator checks the flag at phase boundaries, not mid-phase, so an in-flight model call is allowed to complete before transitioning. The cancelled record includes the phase where cancellation took effect and the reason string (default `user_cancelled`).

### §17.4 BLOCKED

`BLOCKED` is the pre-classification terminal state. It is reached only when CLASSIFY short-circuits because the target files match a hardcoded protected pattern (`.env`, `credentials.*`, `.git/`, supervisor core files). BLOCKED is recorded in the ledger but does no further work.

### §17.5 FAILED_PERMANENT

`FAILED_PERMANENT` is a sink state for unrecoverable errors — the kind that indicate a programmer mistake (invalid configuration, missing env var, schema violations that should have been caught earlier). It is terminal; further events for the op are no-ops.

### §17.6 The Ledger as Causal Record

Every terminal transition writes a `LedgerEntry` to `~/.jarvis/ouroboros/ledger/<op_id>.jsonl`. The ledger is append-only, file-backed, and deduplicated by `(op_id, state)`. A postmortem reader opens the ledger file, iterates the entries, and reconstructs the complete causal chain: when the op was CLASSIFIED, what the risk tier was, which route was stamped, which context files were expanded, what the plan was, what the candidate was, which Iron Gates fired, what the test results were, which phase terminated, what the root cause was.

This ledger is the foundation for Principle 7 (Absolute Observability). It is the data source that feeds cost analysis, failure-mode classification, convergence trend detection, and — ultimately — the capability-graduation mechanism (Manifesto §6).

<!-- engage:begin -->
#### Check your understanding: PART III — The Eleven-Phase Pipeline

<div class="engage" id="engage-part-iii">
<p class="engage-kicker">Conceptual questions</p>
<details class="cq"><summary>1. The Part's opening says GENERATE's content is probabilistic but the decision to proceed is deterministic. Where does that boundary show up in the phases, and why does it make autonomy safe?</summary>
<p>GENERATE is the only place the model shapes the change, through a multi-turn tool loop (§12). Everything that decides whether that output reaches disk is deterministic: the exploration and ASCII gates after GENERATE (§12.4), syntax, type and test checks in VALIDATE (§13.1), the tier table at GATE (§14.1), and the scoped tests at VERIFY (§16.1). A model can produce a bad patch, but it cannot argue its way through a failing test or a tier rule. Transitions follow explicit conditions enforced by the orchestrator's contract, so the system can be autonomous without trusting the model's judgement about its own work (§8, §8.2).</p>
</details>
<details class="cq"><summary>2. Planning failures are "soft" and the stale-exploration guard is also soft, while the Iron Gates at GENERATE are hard. What principle seems to decide which checks may fail open?</summary>
<p>Soft checks are ones whose failure costs quality or efficiency but not safety. A failed plan just means GENERATE runs without one, and an incoherent plan is downgraded to "default approach" (§11.3, §11.5). The stale guard is soft because concurrent operations are rare and false positives are judged worse than occasional stale writes, with L2 or later sensors repairing the damage (§15.3). The Iron Gates protect against things the system has decided must never happen without exploration, or that could corrupt files (non-ASCII), so violations force regeneration (§12.4). The paper is candid that the stale guard is a trade-off "today", not a guarantee.</p>
</details>
<details class="cq"><summary>3. Why does VERIFY re-run tests after APPLY when VALIDATE already ran them on the candidate?</summary>
<p>VALIDATE checks the candidate in isolation; VERIFY checks it in situ, with the patch actually on disk alongside everything else (§16). The paper's point is that "validation in isolation is not enough". Problems such as the stale-file case in §15.3, where a candidate was built on outdated file state, only show up once the real tree is involved. VERIFY keeps cost down by running only tests that exercise the changed files (§16.1). If those fail and L2 cannot repair it, the RollbackArtifact stack undoes the applied changes, so the safety net covers the write itself (§16.2).</p>
</details>
<p class="engage-kicker">Quiz</p>
<div class="quiz" id="quiz-part-iii">
<div class="mcq" data-answer="4">
<p class="mcq-q">1. A <code>todo_scanner</code> signal of ordinary complexity arrives marked high urgency. According to §9.2, which route does it get?</p>
<ol class="mcq-options" type="A">
<li>IMMEDIATE, because urgency is high</li>
<li>STANDARD, the fall-through default</li>
<li>SPECULATIVE, as proactive exploration</li>
<li>BACKGROUND, regardless of urgency</li>
</ol>
<details class="mcq-why"><summary>Show answer</summary>
<p><strong>D.</strong> §9.2 lists <code>todo_scanner</code> in <code>_BACKGROUND_SOURCES</code>, whose signals "always route to BACKGROUND regardless of urgency". Only the three sources in <code>_IMMEDIATE_SOURCES</code> get IMMEDIATE on high urgency.</p>
</details>
</div>
<div class="mcq" data-answer="2">
<p class="mcq-q">2. A model emits a patch after calling only <code>list_dir</code> and one <code>read_file</code>. What happens?</p>
<ol class="mcq-options" type="A">
<li>The patch goes to VALIDATE with a warning attached</li>
<li>GENERATE_RETRY with targeted feedback to explore more</li>
<li>The operation is BLOCKED and ends at once</li>
<li>The ASCII gate repairs the patch and lets it pass</li>
</ol>
<details class="mcq-why"><summary>Show answer</summary>
<p><strong>B.</strong> §12.4 requires at least two calls to exploration tools (<code>read_file</code>, <code>search_code</code>, <code>get_callers</code>) before any patch. One <code>read_file</code> is not enough, and <code>list_dir</code> is not on that list, so the gate triggers a regeneration.</p>
</details>

<div class="mcq" data-answer="1">
<p class="mcq-q">3. When does context auto-compaction kick in during a tool loop, and what does it keep?</p>
<ol class="mcq-options" type="A">
<li>Above 75% of a 98,304-character budget; it keeps the six newest tool chunks</li>
<li>Above 50% of the budget; a model summarises all prior tool results</li>
<li>After five tool rounds; it drops every result except the final one</li>
<li>Above 90% of the budget; it keeps only the <code>read_file</code> results</li>
</ol>
<details class="mcq-why"><summary>Show answer</summary>
<p><strong>A.</strong> §12.5 sets the threshold at 75% of a default 98,304-character budget, keeps the six most recent tool chunks, and summarises older ones by deterministic counting with no model inference.</p>

<div class="mcq" data-answer="3">
<p class="mcq-q">4. An operator types <code>cancel &lt;op-id&gt;</code> while a model call is still streaming. When does the operation become CANCELLED?</p>
<ol class="mcq-options" type="A">
<li>Immediately; the model call is killed mid-stream</li>
<li>Only after VERIFY, so the change can be rolled back</li>
<li>At the next phase boundary, after the in-flight call finishes</li>
<li>Never; cancellation applies only to Orange-tier operations</li>
</ol>
<details class="mcq-why"><summary>Show answer</summary>
<p><strong>C.</strong> §17.3 says cancellation is cooperative: the orchestrator checks the flag at phase boundaries, not mid-phase, so an in-flight model call completes before the transition. §15.4 describes the last such check, between GATE and APPLY.</p>

<p class="engage-kicker">Problem set</p>
<div class="pset" id="pset-part-iii">
<div class="problem">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Problem 1 (trace).</strong> At 03:00 a test fails in a single, non-core, non-security file, and the signal arrives with high urgency from <code>test_failure</code>. Walk the operation through every phase to COMPLETE. For each phase, name the decision taken and one thing that could stop or divert the operation there.</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>Decide the risk tier and route first, then check which bracketed phases a trivial operation skips. Do not forget the consciousness bridge at CLASSIFY or the budget clause in §8.2.</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p>CLASSIFY: a single non-core, non-security file is <code>SAFE_AUTO</code> (§9.1). It could be diverted to BLOCKED if the file matched a protected path, or bumped to <code>NOTIFY_APPLY</code> if the consciousness bridge rates regression risk HIGH. ROUTE: <code>test_failure</code> with high urgency goes IMMEDIATE, so Claude is called directly (§9.2). If the daily budget is exhausted, the op is queued instead (§8.2).</p>
<p>CONTEXT_EXPANSION and PLAN may be skipped for a trivial single-file op (§10, §11.2); a failed plan would be soft anyway (§11.3).</p>
<p>GENERATE: the tool loop runs for up to five rounds; the exploration-first and ASCII gates can force GENERATE_RETRY (§12.2, §12.4).</p>
<p>VALIDATE: syntax, type check, a 60-second test run and Iron Gate checks. Failure uses up to two VALIDATE_RETRY attempts, then L2 with five iterations in 120 seconds; if L2 fails, the op goes to POSTMORTEM (§13).</p>
<p>GATE: <code>SAFE_AUTO</code> auto-approves silently (§14.1). A cancel flag checked before APPLY would end it as CANCELLED (§15.4).</p>
<p>APPLY: snapshot, then an atomic temp-then-rename write; a write failure restores the snapshot and goes to POSTMORTEM (§15.1). VERIFY: scoped tests; a failure goes to L2, and if L2 fails everything is rolled back (§16.2).</p>
<p>COMPLETE: the terminal record is written and the AutoCommitter creates the signed commit (§17.1).</p>
</details>
</div>
<div class="problem">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Problem 2 (design).</strong> Someone proposes making the stale-exploration guard a hard reject: if any target file's SHA-256 at APPLY differs from its GENERATE-time hash, the operation fails. Using §15.3 and the governance contract in §8.2, weigh the benefit against the cost and say what you would need to know before adopting it.</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>The paper states its own reasoning for keeping the guard soft. What assumption does that reasoning rest on?</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p>Benefit: no candidate built on outdated file state would ever be written, closing the window §15.3 admits exists ("occasional stale writes").</p>
<p>Cost: today the guard only warns and writes a ledger entry because the paper judges concurrent operations rare and false positives worse than stale writes. A hard reject would send every mismatch to POSTMORTEM, wasting the generation and validation spend already incurred, which the cost clause of §8.2 tracks.</p>
<p>The decision rests on an empirical question: how often hashes actually differ, and how often those cases are harmless. The ledger records every stale-guard warning, so you could measure the rate before deciding. If stale writes turned out common or damaging, the assumption behind the soft gate would fail and a hard reject would be justified. See §15.3 and §17.6.</p>
</details>
</div>
<div class="problem">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Problem 3 (code reading).</strong> Open <code>backend/core/ouroboros/governance/urgency_router.py</code>. Find <code>_IMMEDIATE_SOURCES</code>, <code>_BACKGROUND_SOURCES</code> and <code>_COMPLEX_COMPLEXITIES</code>, then the routing method that uses them. (a) List entries in each set that are not in the paper's §9.2 description. (b) Is it exactly true in code that a background source routes to BACKGROUND "regardless of urgency"?</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>Search for <code>source in _BACKGROUND_SOURCES</code> and read the condition on the second such check.</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p>(a) <code>_IMMEDIATE_SOURCES</code> now also includes <code>operator_chat</code>, a goal typed by the operator, justified in a comment as the same class as <code>voice_human</code>. <code>_BACKGROUND_SOURCES</code> adds <code>memory_hygiene</code>, <code>cage_hygiene</code>, <code>capability_severance</code> and <code>audit_regression</code>. <code>_COMPLEX_COMPLEXITIES</code> adds <code>architectural</code>; its comment says leaving it out made architectural single-file ops fall through to STANDARD.</p>
<p>(b) Not exactly. The code first routes a background source with low urgency (the only member of <code>_BACKGROUND_URGENCIES</code>) to BACKGROUND, and then routes any other background source to BACKGROUND only if its complexity is not in <code>_COMPLEX_COMPLEXITIES</code>. A background source with <code>heavy_code</code>, <code>complex</code> or <code>architectural</code> complexity therefore falls through to the COMPLEX check. Also note IMMEDIATE checks come first in the method, so their ordering matters.</p>
<p>The lesson matches §9.2's core claim: routing is a fixed, ordered set of pure-code checks you can read and replay, and the paper's table is a summary of that ordering, which has grown since it was written.</p>
</details>
</div>
</div>
<p class="engage-kicker engage-kicker-adv">Advanced conceptual questions</p>
<details class="cq-adv"><summary>A1. The governance contract (§8.2) guarantees every transition is logged, every exception reaches POSTMORTEM, and every retry is bounded. Yet §93.8 reports 524 byte-identical VALIDATE_RETRY iterations re-validating a frozen pool, and 532 micro-fix runs that made zero repairs. What does the contract guarantee, and what does it not?</summary>
<p>The five clauses are about <em>termination and visibility</em>. No operation leaks (§8.1). No crash is silent. No loop runs forever. No pre-rejected op wastes work. Cost is always tracked. Every one of those held during the 524 retries: they were bounded, logged and ended in a terminal state.</p>
<p>What the contract does not promise is <em>efficacy</em>: that a rung, once reached, actually changes anything. A retry that re-validates the same frozen candidate is reachable, bounded and logged, and it still does nothing. That is exactly the "brute-force retries without diagnosis" the Zero-Shortcut Mandate forbids (§3), and the contract cannot see it, because it checks the shape of the run, not its effect.</p>
<p>§93.12 names the missing dimension. The reachability ledger tracks each capability through registered, invoked and <em>effective</em>, and a full scan found 131 features "DARK". The evidence needed per rung is simple: did the retry produce a different candidate, and did the repair change the verdict? A rung that runs often but never changes the candidate or the verdict is inert, however clean its ledger looks.</p>
</details>
<details class="cq-adv"><summary>A2. The exploration-first gate (§12.4) is hard: a patch without at least two exploration calls goes to GENERATE_RETRY. What happens when that hard gate meets a model that cannot reliably satisfy it, and why was the October fix not to soften the gate?</summary>
<p>A hard gate turns non-compliance into retries, and repeated non-compliance into zero throughput. §93.6 shows this live: before the fix, the local 30B produced 106 in-loop rejections and zero candidates in <code>bt-2026-08-31-155308</code>. The gate did its safety job perfectly and stopped the pipeline completely.</p>
<p>Softening the gate would have bought throughput by giving up the property the gate exists for: patches written by a model that had read the code first (§12.4, Part VII §47). That would be a bypass, which the Zero-Shortcut Mandate rules out (§3).</p>
<p>The fix was structural instead. Stateful tool masking (lever 3, <code>tool_masking.py</code>) changes the constrained-decoding grammar so that only tool calls are allowed until the minimum exploration is met. With nothing else changed, the full tool union explored 0/3, {tool, noop} gave 3/3 noop, and {tool} explored 3/3 (§93.6). The gate stayed hard. The model was simply made unable to violate it. The general lesson is that a hard gate on a weak generator should be enforced at the point of generation, not only checked after it.</p>
</details>
<details class="cq-adv"><summary>A3. VERIFY runs only tests that exercise the changed files (§16.1). §93.10 reports that 84 of 91 autonomous landings were new test files. What does a VERIFY "pass" actually tell you for such a landing, and is the Test Reality Gate the right fix?</summary>
<p>When the candidate is itself a new test file, the scoped run is mostly the candidate testing itself. A test that asserts nothing, or never imports the module it claims to test, passes trivially. For this class of landing, VERIFY's pass is close to vacuous: it shows the file runs, not that it checks anything.</p>
<p>The paper records this failure happening. A hollow landing (<code>c985ccaee4</code>) reached <code>main</code> and was reverted (<code>fcc50352f0</code>). The Test Reality Gate followed: it rejects candidate tests that cannot execute, assert nothing, or never import their subject (§93.8). Separately, the Antivenom audit added a detector for tautological ("quine") tests (§93.12).</p>
<p>A reasonable position is that the Reality Gate is necessary but not sufficient. It rules out tests that are hollow in form, but a test can import its subject and assert something true without being able to catch a real bug. The evidence that would settle it is a mutation check on the subject module. Proposal (not in the paper): plant a small fault in the subject and require the new test to fail. If a meaningful share of Reality-Gate-passing tests still pass against the mutant, the gate is too weak for a corpus that is 92% tests.</p>
</details>
<p class="engage-kicker engage-kicker-adv">Challenge problems</p>
<div class="pset pset-adv">
<div class="problem problem-adv">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Challenge 1 (quantitative).</strong> Use only the April defaults to test whether the budgets fit together. Givens: STANDARD worker watchdog 120 s and COMPLEX 180 s, "plus grace and tool-loop overhead" (§2); test runs time out at <code>JARVIS_VERIFY_TIMEOUT_S</code> = 60 s (§13.1, §16.1); <code>JARVIS_MAX_VALIDATE_RETRIES</code> = 2 (§13.2); L2 timebox 120 s (§13.3); Orange approval wait 600 s (§14.1). Assume every test run uses its full timeout and ignore generation time. (a) Compute a lower bound for the test-and-repair time of a STANDARD op that uses every rung in VALIDATE and VERIFY. (b) Compare the Orange approval wait with the COMPLEX watchdog. (c) Say what §93.12 did about this.</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>VALIDATE is one run plus two retries, then L2. VERIFY is one run, then L2, then a re-run of VERIFY (§16.2).</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p>Assumptions: each test run takes its full 60 s timeout, generation and grace are left out, and L2 uses its full 120 s timebox. Leaving out generation makes this a lower bound.</p>
<p>(a) VALIDATE: the first run plus two retries is 3 × 60 = 180 s. Escalating to L2 adds 120 s, for 300 s. VERIFY: one run is 60 s. On failure L2 adds 120 s, and the re-run of VERIFY adds 60 s, for 240 s. The total is 300 + 240 = 540 s, which is 4.5 times the 120 s STANDARD watchdog. Even the minimum path, one VALIDATE run and one VERIFY run, is 120 s at full timeout: the whole watchdog, with nothing left for generation.</p>
<p>(b) An Orange op can wait 600 s for a human. That is 600 / 180 ≈ 3.3 times the COMPLEX watchdog. A watchdog that is not suspended during the approval wait would fire long before the human answered.</p>
<p>(c) The paper does not say how April resolved these overlaps; the unspecified "grace and tool-loop overhead" may have absorbed some of them. What §93.12 records is the structural fix. About 40 run budgets are now derived from one wall-clock figure instead of being set independently, with tests that pin them against drift. The inline approval wait now has a deadline below the pipeline budget and fails closed.</p>
<p>Conclusion: independently set timeouts can each be sensible and still contradict each other. Deriving them from one figure makes the contradiction impossible to write down. Check: re-add the sums (180 + 120 + 60 + 120 + 60 = 540) and confirm that every term is a default quoted in Part III or §2.</p>
</details>
</div>
<div class="problem problem-adv">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Challenge 2 (cross-Part trace).</strong> §93.10 lists landing <code>f97f8195d6</code> (2026-09-07) on <code>governance/candidate_generator.py</code>. It was meant to make the generator decline multi-file swarm ops, but only a punctuation rewrite landed, and it was reverted (<code>c8430f9b6a</code>). Trace a change like this through the Part III phases and the October path to <code>main</code> (§93.7, §93.8). At each gate, say whether it would catch "valid code that does not do what the goal asked". Then say what kind of check would catch it, labelling anything new as a proposal.</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>Every gate you will meet checks safety, syntax, tests or structure. Look for one that compares the diff with the goal's intent.</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p>Trace the phases.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>CLASSIFY and ROUTE (§9).</strong> The path is not protected, so the op is not BLOCKED. A governance file may raise the tier, but tiering is about risk, not intent.</li>
<li><strong>GENERATE (§12.4).</strong> Exploration-first and ASCII checks look at behaviour and bytes. A punctuation edit passes both.</li>
<li><strong>VALIDATE (§13.1).</strong> Syntax, types and tests all pass, because punctuation changes nothing they measure. The Test Reality Gate (§93.8) only applies to candidate tests.</li>
<li><strong>GATE and APPROVE (§14).</strong> With the Sentinel, approval is automatic up to a tier ceiling. BLOCKED work, Order-2 self-modification and anything touching the cage escalate (§93.7). This file was none of those, so nothing escalated.</li>
<li><strong>APPLY and VERIFY (§15, §16).</strong> The write succeeds and the scoped tests still pass.</li>
<li><strong>Promotion gate (§93.7).</strong> It checks provenance, coverage, and that no public symbol vanished. A punctuation edit keeps every symbol. It passes.</li>
</ul>
<p>So every gate described would let this through, because each one asks "is it safe and well-formed?" and none asks "did it do the task?" The paper says this was reverted by hand. It does not say which gates were active on 2026-09-07, so this trace uses the gates as described.</p>
<p>What exists nearby: the declared-symbol contract carries the goal's target symbol to GENERATE (§93.8), and §93.4 mentions a "candidate value gate" from July without describing its rule. The paper does not show either one judging a diff against intent.</p>
<p>Proposal (not in the paper): a deterministic post-VALIDATE check that the diff touches the declared target symbol, and that it is not whitespace or punctuation only. Ops failing it would go to VALIDATE_RETRY with that feedback. It is pure code, so it keeps Principle 5's rule that deterministic code decides (§3). To check it, replay <code>f97f8195d6</code>'s candidate and confirm it is rejected while <code>e7b3bdfec2</code>, the +9-line retry that stands, passes.</p>
</details>
</div>
</div>
<p class="engage-kicker engage-kicker-x">Connections</p>
<div class="pset pset-x">
<div class="problem problem-x">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Connection 1 (Graph theory).</strong> §11.5 validates a <code>plan.1</code> before injecting it. Planned files must overlap the targets, the declared dependencies must be acyclic, and the file order must be a topological sort. An operation targets <code>service.py</code> and <code>api.py</code>. The model declares: <code>service.py</code> needs <code>models.py</code>; <code>api.py</code> needs <code>service.py</code>; <code>test_api.py</code> needs <code>api.py</code> and <code>models.py</code>. (a) Plan A orders the changes as models, api, service, test_api. Run Kahn's algorithm to find the valid order(s) and decide whether Plan A passes. (b) Plan B adds "<code>models.py</code> needs <code>test_api.py</code>". What does Kahn's algorithm report? (c) Plan C lists only <code>README.md</code> and <code>docs.md</code>. Which check fails? (d) What does the pipeline do in each failing case, and how expensive are these checks?</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>Draw an edge from each prerequisite to the file that needs it. Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes a node with in-degree 0. If it gets stuck before removing every node, there is a cycle.</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p>(a) The edges are models to service, service to api, api to test_api, and models to test_api. The in-degrees are models 0, service 1, api 1, test_api 2. Only models has in-degree 0, so remove it. Service drops to 0 and test_api to 1. Remove service, and api drops to 0. Remove api, and test_api drops to 0. Remove it. The queue never held more than one node, so the order is unique: models, service, api, test_api. Plan A puts api before service, but api needs service, so the ordering check fails.</p>
<p>(b) The new edge test_api to models closes the loop models, service, api, test_api, models. Now every node has in-degree at least 1, so Kahn's algorithm cannot start: 0 of 4 nodes are removed. That proves a cycle, and the acyclicity check fails.</p>
<p>(c) Neither target file appears, so the overlap check fails: "a plan that omits all target files is incoherent".</p>
<p>(d) In all three cases the plan is downgraded to "default approach", and GENERATE goes ahead without it (§11.5). Kahn's algorithm runs in O(V + E) time, here 4 nodes and 4 or 5 edges, and the overlap check is a set intersection.</p>
<p>What this says about the architecture: the model produces the plan, but deterministic graph checks decide whether it is coherent. They cost microseconds and no tokens. A model that contradicts itself (a cycle, or an order that breaks its own dependencies) is caught before its plan can mislead GENERATE, and the failure stays soft, consistent with §11.3.</p>
</details>
</div>
<div class="problem problem-x">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Connection 2 (Markov chains).</strong> Model the validation ladder of §13 as an absorbing Markov chain. An operation makes an initial validation attempt, then up to 2 VALIDATE_RETRY attempts (<code>JARVIS_MAX_VALIDATE_RETRIES</code>), then up to 5 L2 iterations (<code>JARVIS_L2_MAX_ITERS</code>). Ignore the 120 s timebox. The two absorbing states are GATE (a pass) and POSTMORTEM (the ladder is exhausted). Assume each attempt passes with probability p = 0.3. This is an illustrative figure, not a measurement. (a) If attempts are independent, what is the probability of reaching POSTMORTEM, and how many attempts are used on average? (b) Now suppose the attempts are perfectly correlated: every retry produces a candidate that fails or passes exactly as the first did. What is P(POSTMORTEM), and how many attempts are wasted when it fails? (c) Which mechanisms in §13.3 act on case (b), and which part of the ladder has none?</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>With independent attempts, the chain is a line of 8 transient states, and each one either absorbs into GATE with probability p or moves to the next. The expected number of steps is a geometric series cut off at 8.</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p>(a) The run ends in POSTMORTEM only if all 8 attempts fail: 0.7^8. Squaring step by step, 0.7^2 = 0.49, 0.7^4 = 0.2401 and 0.7^8 = 0.0576. So the chance of reaching GATE is about 94%. The expected number of attempts is the sum of 0.7^k for k = 0 to 7, which equals (1 - 0.7^8) / 0.3 = 0.9424 / 0.3, about 3.14. Most operations that pass do so early.</p>
<p>(b) If the attempts are identical, the first one decides everything. P(POSTMORTEM) = 0.7 no matter how long the ladder is, and a failing operation uses all 8 attempts, 7 of them pure waste. Depth then buys nothing.</p>
<p>(c) L2 is built for case (b). Each iteration generates a patch informed by the failure context, which aims to decorrelate it from the last attempt. It also classifies progress, and it stops on a no-progress streak of 2 or on oscillation (a matching signature hash), instead of running all 5 iterations. As §13.2 describes the two VALIDATE_RETRY regenerations, they have no progress or repetition detector, so correlated failures there are paid for in full.</p>
<p>What this says about the architecture: a retry ladder helps only to the extent that its attempts are independent. Real gains come from changing the input between attempts and from detecting when the input has not changed. That is the Zero-Shortcut Mandate (§3) in numbers: "no brute-force retries without diagnosis".</p>
</details>
</div>
</div>
</div>
<!-- engage:end -->

# PART IV — Venom: The Agentic Execution Layer

> **Big Picture:** The original O+V pipeline was a one-shot code generator — send a prompt, get a patch back. That design could not plan. It could not read target files before writing. It could not run tests and revise. Venom is what transforms the pipeline into a multi-turn agentic loop — the same capability that makes Claude Code powerful, but wrapped inside the deterministic Ouroboros skeleton. This Part describes Venom's design, its 16-tool manifest, the MCP forwarding architecture, and the L2 Self-Repair Engine that rescues operations when first-pass validation fails.

## §18. Why Venom Exists — The Phone-Call vs Letter Analogy

> **Analogy:** Imagine asking a friend to plan a week-long trip to Japan. In a one-shot arrangement, you write one letter: "please plan my trip." Your friend replies with a complete itinerary — but they had no way to ask you clarifying questions mid-planning, no way to check flight prices, no way to verify that your preferred hotel is available. In a multi-turn arrangement, you have a phone conversation. Your friend asks "what's your budget?" mid-planning. They say "let me check — the hotel you mentioned is fully booked, can I suggest an alternative?" The conversation is iterative, responsive, and produces a better itinerary because the planner could explore before committing.
>
> Venom is the phone-call version of code generation. The model can read files mid-generation, search for related code mid-generation, run tests mid-generation, and revise its patch based on what it finds. Without Venom, O+V is writing letters. With Venom, O+V is having conversations.

### §18.1 What Venom Adds

Four specific capabilities:

1. **Pre-patch exploration.** Before writing code, the model reads the target files, searches for related code, and inspects the call graph. This prevents patches generated from stale parameter-weight memory — "senior engineer behavior" replacing "junior engineer guessing."

2. **Intra-generation verification.** The model can run `run_tests` mid-generation to verify its own work. A test that fails after the first draft informs the second draft. The model iterates on its output before submitting it to VALIDATE.

3. **Agentic tool use.** The model uses tools the way a human engineer uses tools — not as a black box, but as a set of instruments that extend reach. `edit_file` lets the model make targeted changes. `bash` lets it run commands (under Iron Gate supervision). `web_fetch` lets it consult external documentation.

4. **Self-repair when validation fails.** If VALIDATE rejects the candidate, L2 Self-Repair takes over — iterating up to five times within a 120-second wall-clock budget, classifying failures, building repair prompts, and converging on a fix.

### §18.2 Why the Name

Venom is named after the Marvel symbiote — a creature that attaches to a host and grants abilities the host could not exercise alone, while the host grants the symbiote a vessel. The analogy holds: Ouroboros is the governance skeleton (the host); Venom is the agentic intelligence (the symbiote). Without Ouroboros, Venom would be unconstrained — an unsupervised model making uncaged changes to disk. Without Venom, Ouroboros would be rigid — a pipeline that cannot explore before acting. Together, they are disciplined self-improvement.

### §18.3 Tool Defaults — Unshackled Under Governance

All 15 primary tools are **enabled by default**. The safety perimeter is not env-var opt-in — it is the Iron Gate (AST parser, command blocklist, path protection), the risk engine, and the approval gates. Quoting `OUROBOROS.md` on this choice:

> *"The Iron Gate (AST parser, command blocklist) is the deterministic skeleton. The tools are the nervous system. The skeleton does not think; the nervous system does not hold weight."*

This is a deliberate architectural inversion of the industry default. Most agentic frameworks disable tools by default and require opt-in. O+V enables tools by default and requires opt-out — because the containment guarantees are structural, not configurational.

## §19. The ToolLoopCoordinator

> **Big Picture:** The ToolLoopCoordinator is the engine room of Venom. It is the loop that sends a prompt, parses the model's response for tool calls, gates each tool call through the Iron Gate, executes approved tools in subprocess sandboxes, feeds the results back into the conversation, and iterates until the model produces a final answer. Everything in this Part is about what happens inside that loop.

**Source:** `backend/core/ouroboros/governance/tool_executor.py`.

### §19.1 The Loop

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ToolLoopCoordinator.run(prompt, deadline, max_rounds)  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                          │
│  Round 1:                                                │
│    ├─ Provider.stream(prompt) → response                 │
│    ├─ parse_fn(response) → List[ToolCall]                │
│    ├─ For each ToolCall:                                 │
│    │    ├─ GoverningToolPolicy.evaluate(call)            │
│    │    │    ├─ Allowed  → execute                       │
│    │    │    └─ Denied   → inject tool_denied result     │
│    │    └─ AsyncProcessToolBackend.execute(call)         │
│    └─ Append tool results to conversation                │
│                                                          │
│  Round 2..N: (same pattern)                              │
│                                                          │
│  Termination:                                            │
│    - No tool calls in response → final answer            │
│    - max_rounds reached → system nudge "produce answer"  │
│    - deadline exceeded → abort with partial candidate    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### §19.2 Configuration

| Variable | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `JARVIS_GOVERNED_TOOL_USE_ENABLED` | `true` | Master switch — `false` disables the loop |
| `JARVIS_GOVERNED_TOOL_MAX_ROUNDS` | `5` | Max tool iterations per generation |
| `JARVIS_GOVERNED_TOOL_TIMEOUT_S` | `30` | Per-tool execution timeout |
| `JARVIS_GOVERNED_TOOL_MAX_CONCURRENT` | `2` | Concurrent tool executions |
| `JARVIS_TOOL_OUTPUT_CAP_BYTES` | `4096` | Max tool output size in prompt |

The five-round default is conservative. Most generations complete in 2–3 rounds; a fifth round is the last-chance budget. The max rounds is hard — after round 5, a system message nudges the model: *"You have enough context. Produce your final code change now."*

### §19.3 Provider Integration

Both `ClaudeProvider` and `PrimeProvider` accept a `tool_loop: Optional[ToolLoopCoordinator]` parameter. When provided, their `generate()` method delegates to `tool_loop.run()` instead of making a single API call. The coordinator handles:

- Deadline enforcement (per-round and aggregate).
- Token-budget management (prompt growth, compaction triggering).
- Audit trail recording via `ToolExecutionRecord` objects — every tool call becomes a ledger entry.

### §19.4 MCP Forwarding Inside the Loop

External MCP tools are discovered at prompt-construction time via `GovernanceMCPClient.discover_tools()`. The discovered tools are injected into the prompt's tool manifest under an `**External MCP tools:**` section. When the model calls `mcp_{server}_{tool}`, the coordinator dispatches to `AsyncProcessToolBackend._run_mcp_tool()`, which makes a JSON-RPC `tools/call` to the external server.

MCP tools bypass the standard manifest check (policy Rule 0) and are auto-allowed by Rule 0b (`tool.allowed.mcp_external`). External servers handle their own authentication and authorization. The Iron Gate still applies to the invocation transport: `create_subprocess_exec` arrays for stdio, TLS for SSE. No shell injection surface.
