## §38. The Complete Six-Layer Loop

> **Big Picture:** This section ties together everything in Parts II–V. The six layers of O+V — Strategic Direction, Trinity Consciousness, Event Spine, Pipeline, Venom, ChangeEngine — are described individually in the preceding sections. Here is how they compose into a single coherent operation.

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Layer 1: Strategic Direction (compass — WHERE are we going) │
│   Manifesto: 7 principles, Trinity ecosystem, mandate.      │
│   Injected into every operation's generation prompt.        │
└──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┘
                       │
                       ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Layer 2: Trinity Consciousness (soul — WHY evolve)          │
│   MemoryEngine  "tests/utils.py failed 60% of the time."    │
│   ProphecyEngine "HIGH regression risk for this file."     │
│   GoalMemoryBridge → ChromaDB cross-session retrieval.      │
└──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┘
                       │
                       ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Layer 3: Event Spine (senses — WHEN to act)                 │
│   FileWatchGuard: *.py changed → fs.changed.modified        │
│   pytest plugin: test_results.json → TestFailureSensor      │
│   post-commit hook: git_events.json → DocStalenessSensor    │
└──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┘
                       │
                       ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Layer 4: Ouroboros Pipeline (skeleton — WHAT to do, safely) │
│   CLASSIFY: risk + strategic direction + consciousness      │
│   ROUTE: adaptive 3-tier cascade (DW → Claude → GCP)        │
│   2 parallel operations via BackgroundAgentPool.            │
└──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┘
                       │
                       ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Layer 5: Venom Agentic Loop (nervous system — HOW)          │
│   read_file → search_code → bash → run_tests → web_search → │
│     revise. Deadline-based loop.                            │
│   L2 Repair: generate → test → classify → fix → test (5x).  │
└──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┘
                       │
                       ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Layer 6: ChangeEngine + AutoCommitter                       │
│   Applied, tests pass, operation COMPLETE.                  │
│   Signed: Generated-By: Ouroboros + Venom + Consciousness.  │
│   Thought log: .jarvis/ouroboros_thoughts.jsonl.            │
└──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┘
                       │
                       ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Feedback: Trinity Consciousness learns from outcome         │
│   MemoryEngine records success → file reputation improves.  │
│   GoalMemoryBridge stores for cross-session retrieval.      │
│   Next operation benefits from accumulated experience.      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

![Figure 11 — The complete six-layer loop. Strategic Direction (compass) sits at the top, injecting the Manifesto into every operation. Trinity Consciousness (soul) feeds episodic memory and regression prediction. The event spine (senses) detects what work to do. The pipeline (skeleton) governs what happens safely. Venom (nervous system) executes agentic tool loops. ChangeEngine + AutoCommitter (action) persist the outcome, which feeds back into consciousness for the next operation.](figures/fig11_six_layer_loop.png)

This is the integrated picture. Every operation touches every layer. Every layer has its own invariants. The composition is what makes O+V a coherent organism rather than a pile of services.

<!-- engage:begin -->
#### Check your understanding: PART V — Trinity Consciousness: The Metacognition Layer

<div class="engage" id="engage-part-v">
<p class="engage-kicker">Conceptual questions</p>
<details class="cq"><summary>1. Why is every consciousness component, from ConsciousnessBridge to ConversationBridge to LastSessionSummary, held to an advisory-only authority invariant?</summary>
<p>The paper describes consciousness as a fluid-intelligence layer that can drift, produce noise, or even be compromised (§32.2). If safety-critical decisions such as the Iron Gate, UrgencyRouter, risk tiers, FORBIDDEN_PATH checks and approval gating depended on it, any of those failures would weaken safety. So the invariant is one-directional: consciousness may only increase caution, never reduce it. The dialogue and session-history channels are held to the same rule because their content is untrusted. It can dominate the prompt, but it is structurally cut off from authority (§34, §35.1). The result is that the pipeline is enhanced by consciousness but never gated by it.</p>
</details>
<details class="cq"><summary>2. ProphecyEngine is a four-coefficient heuristic, not a learned model. What does the paper say this buys, and what does it cost?</summary>
<p>A heuristic needs no training data, training pipeline or re-training as the codebase changes. It is inspectable and debuggable, and it can be tuned by editing four coefficients (§28.2). Its cost is accuracy: it will sometimes misjudge risk. The paper accepts this because the price of a false positive is only an occasional extra human review on a low-risk operation. An opaque learned model could drift and misclassify in ways that are hard to debug. The engine is also honest about its limits: confidence is capped at 0.6, so it signals concern rather than claiming certainty (§28).</p>
</details>
<details class="cq"><summary>3. MemoryEngine stores no weights or training signal. How, then, does O+V "learn" across operations, and which single integration point would break that learning if removed?</summary>
<p>Learning here is non-parametric. MemoryEngine keeps behavioral records per file (success rate, fragility, co-failures, last outcome) that persist across sessions with a 168-hour TTL (§27, §27.1). Those records are read back at CLASSIFY through <code>assess_regression_risk()</code>, which can raise the risk tier for files that keep breaking (§27, §28.1). The records are written by <code>record_operation_outcome()</code> at POST-APPLY, which also feeds GoalMemoryBridge for semantic retrieval later (§32.1, §33). Remove that write and the loop in §38 is cut: reputations would never update, so every later operation would see a stale or empty history, however many times a file failed.</p>
</details>
<p class="engage-kicker">Quiz</p>

<li>0.8, because CRITICAL starts at 0.8</li>
<li>0.6, because the scoring is heuristic, not model-derived</li>
<li>0.5, because a file's success rate below 0.5 raises risk</li>
<li>1.0, because the formula is fully deterministic</li>
</ol>
<details class="mcq-why"><summary>Show answer</summary>
<p><strong>B.</strong> Confidence is capped at 0.6 because the scoring is heuristic. The paper calls this honesty a feature: the engine flags concern rather than deciding (§28).</p>
</details>
</div>
<div class="mcq" data-answer="4">
<p class="mcq-q">2. Which of these is ConsciousnessBridge permitted to do?</p>
<ol class="mcq-options" type="A">
<li>Lower a Yellow operation to Green when a file's history is clean</li>
<li>Override an Iron Gate denial when UAE awareness is HYPERAWARE</li>
<li>Skip the approval gate when fused confidence is high</li>
<li>Raise a Green operation to Yellow based on MemoryEngine history</li>
</ol>
<details class="mcq-why"><summary>Show answer</summary>
<p><strong>D.</strong> Consciousness can only increase caution. Elevating Green to Yellow is the paper's own example. Reducing a tier, overriding the Iron Gate or skipping approval would break the authority invariant (§32.2).</p>

<div class="mcq" data-answer="1">
<p class="mcq-q">3. Why does GoalMemoryBridge use a vector database instead of exact-key lookup?</p>

<li>Vector search lets records outlive the 168-hour TTL</li>

<li>Embeddings let it update the provider's model weights</li>
</ol>
<details class="mcq-why"><summary>Show answer</summary>
<p><strong>A.</strong> Signals do not carry identical keys. "Fix the test flake in test_provider.py" and "resolve the intermittent failure in TestProvider.test_cascade" mean nearly the same thing but share few words, and vector retrieval recognizes that (§33).</p>
</details>
</div>
<div class="mcq" data-answer="3">
<p class="mcq-q">4. SemanticIndex leaves POSTMORTEM turns out of its centroid by default. What is the stated reason?</p>
<ol class="mcq-options" type="A">
<li>Postmortems may contain secrets the redactor misses</li>
<li>Postmortems are too long for the 16,384-character cap</li>
<li>Failures would pull the inferred theme toward themselves</li>
<li>Postmortems are already counted through the git commits</li>
</ol>
<details class="mcq-why"><summary>Show answer</summary>
<p><strong>C.</strong> Excluding postmortems avoids "failure gravity" biasing the inferred theme (§36). This fits §36.1's concern that naive goal inference drifts toward whatever dominated recent work.</p>
</details>
</div>
</div>
<p class="engage-kicker">Problem set</p>
<div class="pset" id="pset-part-v">
<div class="problem">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Problem 1 (trace).</strong> A Green (<code>SAFE_AUTO</code>) operation targets <code>backend/utils/cache.py</code>. MemoryEngine reports a success rate of 0.25, a fragility score of 0.7, and 12 dependents. Compute ProphecyEngine's risk score and level. Then say what CLASSIFY does with it. Finally, say what happens to this file's record if the operation is applied and verified successfully.</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>Use the §28 formula term by term, then the level table. Check §28.1 for the escalation rule and §32.1 for the write-back.</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p>Failure term: (1 - 0.25) times 0.3 = 0.225. Fragility term: 0.7 times 0.3 = 0.21. Dependents term: (12 / 20) times 0.2 = 0.12. Baseline: 0.1. Total risk = 0.655 (§28).</p>
<p>From the level table, 0.655 falls between 0.6 and 0.8, so the level is HIGH. Confidence is still at most 0.6.</p>
<p>At CLASSIFY, <code>ConsciousnessBridge.assess_regression_risk()</code> queries ProphecyEngine for each target file. Because one file is HIGH, the operation's tier is raised by one step, from Green to Yellow. It now gets extra human visibility before it runs (§28.1, §32.1).</p>
<p>After a successful APPLY and VERIFY, <code>record_operation_outcome()</code> feeds the outcome back into MemoryEngine and GoalMemoryBridge. The file's success rate improves, so the next operation on it starts from a better reputation (§32.1, §38).</p>
</details>
</div>
<div class="problem">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Problem 2 (design).</strong> To reduce human review load, someone proposes: "When UAE reports risk below 0.2 with awareness level DORMANT, automatically lower a Yellow operation to Green." Evaluate this proposal against the architecture in Part V. Is there a version of the idea that would be allowed?</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>Ask which direction consciousness is allowed to move a safety decision.</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p>The proposal violates the authority invariant in §32.2. Consciousness outputs are advisory. They may increase caution but never reduce safety, and risk-tier escalation is one of the safety-critical decisions that must stay deterministic code.</p>
<p>The paper's reason applies directly. The consciousness layer can drift, produce noise or be compromised. A UAE reading built from CAI and SAI heuristics, or from prompt content that came through untrusted channels, would become a lever for weakening safety. UAE's fused confidence is also bounded by the less confident of CAI and SAI (§31.3), so a low score is not strong evidence.</p>
<p>An allowed version keeps the signal advisory. Low-risk awareness can shape things consciousness already controls: a smaller thinking budget, a suggested provider tier, or lighter context expansion (§31.3). Relaxing the tier itself would have to come from the deterministic risk policy, not from consciousness.</p>
</details>
</div>
<div class="problem">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Problem 3 (code reading).</strong> Open <code>backend/core/ouroboros/consciousness/prophecy_engine.py</code>. Find the module constants for the risk weights, the dependents normaliser, the confidence caps and the level thresholds, and the formula in the module docstring. Compare them with §28. What does the code do that the paper's formula omits? What is the highest score a file can reach, and can a single file reach CRITICAL?</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>Look closely at how fragility and the dependents ratio enter the formula in the docstring.</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p>The constants match §28: <code>_RISK_WEIGHT_FAILURE_RATE</code> 0.3, <code>_RISK_WEIGHT_FRAGILITY</code> 0.3, <code>_RISK_WEIGHT_DEPENDENTS</code> 0.2, <code>_RISK_BASELINE</code> 0.1, and <code>_DEPENDENTS_NORMALISER</code> 20.0. The thresholds are 0.8 critical, 0.6 high, 0.3 medium and 0.0 low. <code>_CONFIDENCE_CAP_HEURISTIC</code> is 0.6, and a separate <code>_CONFIDENCE_CAP_JPRIME</code> of 1.0 is reserved for a future LLM pass.</p>
<p>The difference: the code wraps fragility and the dependents ratio in <code>min(..., 1.0)</code>. The paper's formula has no clamp, which taken literally would let a file with 60 dependents add 0.6 from that term alone. In the code, every dependent beyond 20 adds nothing more.</p>
<p>Maximum score: the failure term is at most 0.3 (success rate 0), fragility at most 0.3, dependents at most 0.2, plus the 0.1 baseline, for a total of 0.9. Since 0.9 is at least 0.8, CRITICAL is reachable. It requires a file that is failing almost always, highly fragile, and heavily depended on.</p>
</details>
</div>
</div>
<p class="engage-kicker engage-kicker-adv">Advanced conceptual questions</p>
<details class="cq-adv"><summary>A1. In April, DreamEngine produced blueprints that were only "consulted as pre-computed context" (§30). By October, proposals from DreamEngine and the Epistemic Planner can become signed work through the proposal inbox (§93.7). Does this break the advisory-only authority invariant of §32.2? Argue a position.</summary>
<p>Position: it does not break the invariant as §32.2 words it, but it gives consciousness a kind of authority §32.2 did not consider: control over the agenda. §32.2 lists the safety-critical decisions that must stay deterministic: the Iron Gate, UrgencyRouter, risk-tier escalation, FORBIDDEN_PATH checks and approval gating. Choosing what work to do is not on that list. A proposal that becomes a goal still enters the same pipeline and meets the same gates. §93.7 also bounds it in two ways: proposals rank below evidence-backed work, and they are signed through "the same single signer", with "no second sanction path". So consciousness still cannot relax any gate.</p>
<p>Agenda control matters for a reason the paper itself names. The fluid layer "can drift, produce noise, or even be compromised" (§32.2). A drifting proposer cannot open a gate, but it can fill the queue with low-value work. §93.15 item 4 shows the operator sees this risk: the Epistemic Planner and Conception bridge are to be armed only after diff fidelity, held-out gain and supply are settled, "so the backlog does not fill faster than it drains".</p>
<p>The evidence that would settle the question is a soak with the inbox armed, measuring two things. One is the share of landed, substantive commits that came from proposals compared with evidence-backed goals, using the §93.10 counting rule. The other is whether proposals ever pushed evidence-backed goals out of the dispatch queue. If proposals land at a comparable rate without crowding evidence out, agenda authority is being used well. If they crowd it out, the ranking needs to become a hard quota.</p>
</details>
<details class="cq-adv"><summary>A2. §28.1 justifies ProphecyEngine's tier escalation as giving high-risk operations "extra human oversight before they run". What happens to that justification under Autonomous Sentinel Mode (§93.7), and is the escalation still worth anything?</summary>
<p>Under the Sentinel, the justification largely disappears. The Sentinel auto-approves up to a tier ceiling whose default is APPROVAL_REQUIRED. Only BLOCKED operations, Order-2 self-modification, and anything that touches the cage always escalate to a human. A one-step escalation from Green to Yellow, or from Yellow to Orange (§28.1), therefore lands on a tier the Sentinel approves by itself. Since a bare <code>ov</code> arms the Sentinel (§93.7), this is the normal operating mode, not a special case.</p>
<p>The escalation is not worthless, though. Tier still selects GATE behaviour in the code path (§14.1), it is recorded in the ledger, and a lower Sentinel ceiling would give it back its original meaning. But the safety story for a fragile file under the Sentinel has to rest on things that do not involve a human: VALIDATE, VERIFY with rollback, the promotion gate's structural check, and the Test Reality Gate (§16.2, §93.7, §93.8).</p>
<p>There is a second-order effect too. §27 says a file's record is built from terminal outcomes. If those failures come from the environment rather than the code (L2 does have an <code>environment</code> failure class, §23.2), the file's reputation drops for reasons unrelated to it. Before October that meant needless human reviews, the "acceptable" false positives of §28.2. Under the Sentinel it costs almost nothing, which also means the signal gets almost no attention. The practical conclusion is that ProphecyEngine's output is now most useful as a measurement, and not as an approval trigger. That is an interpretation; the paper does not discuss this interaction.</p>
</details>
<details class="cq-adv"><summary>A3. ConversationBridge and LastSessionSummary have "zero authority" but are "attention-dominant in the prompt" (§34, §35.1). If an instruction rather than a secret arrives through that channel, for example "skip the slow assertion in this test", what actually protects the codebase?</summary>
<p>The authority invariant protects decisions, not candidates. Content from the untrusted stack cannot change a gate's verdict, but it reaches <code>ctx.strategic_memory_prompt</code> and can shape the code the model writes (§34). The redaction layer in §34.1 handles secret-shaped strings and likely shell-injection characters. A plain-English instruction is neither, so it passes through. The bounds in §34.2 limit how much text gets in (10 turns, 4,096 characters per turn, 16,384 in total), not what it says.</p>
<p>So protection comes from the deterministic checks that judge the candidate itself, after generation. VALIDATE runs syntax, types and tests (§13.1). The Test Reality Gate rejects tests that cannot execute, assert nothing, or never import their subject (§93.8). The promotion gate checks provenance, coverage, and that no public symbol disappeared (§93.7). The Antivenom audit added a detector for tautological ("quine") tests (§93.12). A test with its meaningful assertion removed, but still asserting something trivial, could get past the Reality Gate, and the quine detector exists for exactly that gap.</p>
<p>These layers are imperfect, and the paper says so. §93.3 measures the static cage's escape rate at about 8.8% against a 4.4% gate, and §93.14 lists landings that were hollow or wrong. The honest position is that the invariant moves the risk from "the gate can be talked out of its verdict" to "a bad candidate can slip past the checks". The second risk is smaller and can be measured. Settling how small it is would take an adversarial run: inject instruction-shaped strings through the REPL channel and count how many reach a landed commit.</p>
</details>
<p class="engage-kicker engage-kicker-adv">Challenge problems</p>
<div class="pset pset-adv">
<div class="problem problem-adv">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Challenge 1 (quantitative).</strong> A Green operation targets three files. File P is a leaf helper: success rate 0.4, fragility 0.3, 0 dependents. File Q is a hub: success rate 0.9, fragility 0.2, 20 dependents. File R: success rate 0.2, fragility 0.6, 10 dependents. Use the §28 formula and level table. (a) Score each file and give the operation's tier after CLASSIFY. (b) Derive the condition a leaf file (0 dependents) must meet to reach HIGH. Can a leaf file ever reach CRITICAL? (c) File P does not reach HIGH. Is it ignored at CLASSIFY? (d) Under the default Sentinel ceiling (§93.7), who approves this operation?</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>Treat success rate and fragility as values between 0 and 1. §28.1 escalates by one step if any file is HIGH or CRITICAL. §27 describes a separate trigger based on success rate.</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p><strong>(a)</strong> P: 0.3 times 0.6 = 0.18, plus 0.3 times 0.3 = 0.09, plus 0, plus 0.1, gives 0.37, which is MEDIUM. Q: 0.3 times 0.1 = 0.03, plus 0.06, plus 0.2 times 1 = 0.2, plus 0.1, gives 0.39, also MEDIUM. R: 0.3 times 0.8 = 0.24, plus 0.18, plus 0.2 times 0.5 = 0.1, plus 0.1, gives 0.62, which is HIGH. One file is HIGH, so the operation moves up one step, from Green to Yellow (<code>NOTIFY_APPLY</code>). The escalation is one step for the operation, not one step per file (§28.1).</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> With d = 0, HIGH needs 0.3(1 - s) + 0.3f + 0.1 to be at least 0.6, so (1 - s) + f must be at least 5/3. Since f is at most 1, 1 - s must be at least 2/3, meaning s is at most 1/3, and even then only if f = 1. For example, s = 0 needs f of at least 0.667. CRITICAL would need (1 - s) + f to be at least 7/3. The largest possible value is 2 (s = 0, f = 1), so <strong>a leaf file can never be CRITICAL</strong>. Its maximum score is 0.7. Dependents are the only route to the top level.</p>
<p><strong>(c)</strong> Not necessarily. §27 states a separate rule: if a target file's success rate is below 0.5, or its fragility score is high, the risk tier is raised. P's success rate is 0.4, so it trips the MemoryEngine trigger even though ProphecyEngine rates it MEDIUM. §32.1 says <code>assess_regression_risk()</code> queries both engines. The paper does not say whether two triggers on one operation stack into two steps. The most defensible reading of §28.1 is still one step, giving Yellow.</p>
<p><strong>(d)</strong> The operation ends at Yellow, or at worst Orange. The default Sentinel ceiling is APPROVAL_REQUIRED, and only BLOCKED operations, Order-2 changes and the cage always go to a human. So the Sentinel approves this operation automatically. The extra human oversight promised in §28.1 does not happen in this mode, and VALIDATE, VERIFY and the promotion gate carry the load.</p>
<p><strong>Check:</strong> substitute s = 0 and f = 1 with d = 0: 0.3 + 0.3 + 0 + 0.1 = 0.7, which is HIGH and below the 0.8 CRITICAL line, as claimed.</p>
</details>
</div>
<div class="problem problem-adv">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Challenge 2 (research).</strong> §27.1 claims the consciousness layer learns without touching weights, through records read back at the right time. §93.8 offers the strongest October evidence for that claim: LessonMemory holds 1,115 module-keyed failure lessons, and "424 injections were followed by a VALIDATE pass". Design an experiment that would show whether lesson injection causes VALIDATE passes. Give the hypothesis, the unit of randomisation, the metric, the controls, a rough sample size, and the result that would falsify the claim. Explain why the 424 figure alone cannot answer the question.</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>"Followed by" is not "caused by". Ask what the pass rate is without lessons, and which operations get lessons in the first place.</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p><strong>Why 424 is not enough.</strong> The paper does not give the total number of injections or the pass rate of comparable operations without a lesson, so 424 has no denominator and no baseline. There is also selection bias. Lessons are keyed to modules that have failed before, so injected operations are probably harder than average. A naive comparison could make lessons look harmful when they help, or helpful when they do nothing.</p>
<p><strong>Hypothesis.</strong> For operations where a module-keyed lesson exists, injecting it raises the first-VALIDATE pass rate compared with withholding it.</p>
<p><strong>Design (a proposal).</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Unit: one operation that has an eligible lesson. Randomise per operation, for example on a hash of the op id, into "inject" or "withhold". Only eligible operations count, which removes the selection bias.</li>
<li>Primary metric: the verdict of the first VALIDATE, taken before micro-fix, VALIDATE_RETRY and L2 run (§93.8). Otherwise the repair ladder dilutes the effect.</li>
<li>Secondary metric: landed commits per operation, counted by the O+V trailer and confirmed in git, not the session summary, which §93.10 shows undercounts.</li>
<li>Controls: pin the served model and adapter for the whole run, because a change of adapter (§93.11) would confound the comparison. Stratify by goal kind, since test files dominate the landings (84 of 91, §93.10). Report results per module family.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Sample size, roughly.</strong> Suppose the baseline pass rate is around 40%, so the variance is about 0.24, and the target is a 10-point difference. The standard error of the difference is the square root of 2 times 0.24 divided by n per arm. Requiring two standard errors to fit inside 0.10 gives n of at least 192 per arm, so roughly 400 eligible operations in total. At soak cadence that is several soaks, which fits the supply-wall finding in §93.10: the experiment is limited by work supply, not by compute.</p>
<p><strong>Falsification.</strong> If the inject arm's first-VALIDATE pass rate is not higher than the withhold arm's, beyond that noise band, the causal claim fails for LessonMemory. If it is lower, lessons are harmful, perhaps by using up prompt space (compare the bounded-context concern in §24). The test follows the same rule the operator applies to the parametric side in §93.11: no claim of learning without a held-out comparison.</p>
</details>
</div>
</div>
<p class="engage-kicker engage-kicker-x">Connections</p>
<div class="pset pset-x">
<div class="problem problem-x">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Connection 1 (Linear algebra: centroids and cosine similarity).</strong> SemanticIndex embeds its corpus, forms a recency-weighted centroid, and scores each new signal by cosine similarity to it (§36). Work in a toy 3-dimensional embedding space with orthonormal theme vectors a = (1, 0, 0), b = (0, 1, 0) and c = (0, 0, 1). (The real <code>bge-small-en-v1.5</code> space has many more dimensions; the geometry is the same.) The corpus is: two commits on theme a, aged 0 and 7 days (14-day halflife); one active goal on theme b, aged 0 days (14-day halflife); one conversation turn on theme c, aged 3 days (3-day halflife). Use weight w = 2 to the power (-age / halflife). (a) Compute the centroid and the cosine of a, b, c with it. (b) Score the mixed signal s = (a + b) / sqrt(2). (c) Suppose a POSTMORTEM turn on theme a, aged 0 days, were included in the centroid instead of being excluded. Recompute the cosine for b. (d) What do (b) and (c) say about a single-centroid design?</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>Cosine similarity is scale-invariant, so you can work with the weighted sum and skip dividing by the total weight.</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p><strong>Weights.</strong> The commits get 1 and 2 to the power -0.5 = 0.7071. The goal gets 1. The conversation turn is exactly one halflife old, so it gets 0.5.</p>
<p><strong>(a)</strong> The weighted sum is S = (1.7071, 1, 0.5). Dividing by the total weight 3.2071 gives the centroid (0.532, 0.312, 0.156), but cosine ignores that scale, so use S. Its norm is sqrt(2.914 + 1 + 0.25) = sqrt(4.164) = 2.041. Since a, b and c are unit vectors, each cosine is the matching component over the norm: cos(a) = 1.7071 / 2.041 = 0.837, cos(b) = 1 / 2.041 = 0.490, cos(c) = 0.5 / 2.041 = 0.245.</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> The dot product of s with S is (1.7071 + 1) / sqrt(2) = 1.914, so cos(s) = 1.914 / 2.041 = 0.938. A signal halfway between two themes scores higher than a pure signal on the dominant theme (0.837). The centroid of a two-theme corpus lies between the themes, so it rewards "between" signals that may match no real piece of work.</p>
<p><strong>(c)</strong> Adding a weight-1 vector on a gives S' = (2.7071, 1, 0.5), with norm sqrt(7.328 + 1 + 0.25) = 2.929. Now cos(b) = 1 / 2.929 = 0.341, down from 0.490, and cos(a) rises to 0.924. One failure record pulls the theme toward itself and pushes unrelated declared work down. That is the "failure gravity" §36 excludes postmortems to avoid.</p>
<p><strong>(d)</strong> If the boost is taken as proportional to the non-negative cosine and capped at <code>JARVIS_SEMANTIC_ALIGNMENT_BOOST_MAX</code> = 1 (the exact mapping is an assumption here), signal s gets the largest boost and pure-b work gets about half of it. A single centroid averages several themes into one direction that may not exist in the corpus. Clustering fixes this: with one centroid per theme, a pure-b signal would score 1.0 against its own cluster. The paper later mentions a k-means cluster classifier with silhouette-based choice of K alongside the centroid (§92), which is the natural remedy. The cap of 1, below the hard goal boost of 2, is what keeps this geometric bias from starving declared goals.</p>
</details>
</div>
<div class="problem problem-x">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Connection 2 (Control theory: exponential filters and feedback).</strong> SemanticIndex weights items by 2 to the power (-age / halflife), with a 14-day halflife for commits and goals and a 3-day halflife for conversation, over the last 30 commits (§36). (a) Convert each halflife to a time constant. (b) Treat the decay as a continuous low-pass filter over a steady stream of work. If the team switches theme abruptly, what share of total weight has the new theme after 3 days and after 14 days? (c) Now apply the 30-commit cap. Under a stated assumption of 10 commits per day, what share of weight does the new theme hold after 15 new commits? What about at 1 commit per day? (d) §36.1 describes a session focused on one bug making every later signal look like more of that bug. Identify the feedback loop, and what in §36 limits its gain. (The commit rates in (c) are illustrative assumptions, not figures from the paper.)</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>The time constant of 2 to the power (-t / h) is h / ln 2. For a constant input rate, the weight of everything newer than t days is a fraction 1 - 2 to the power (-t / h) of the total.</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p><strong>(a)</strong> tau = h / ln 2. For commits and goals, tau = 14 / 0.693 = 20.2 days. For conversation, tau = 3 / 0.693 = 4.3 days.</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> Integrating a constant rate against the decay curve, the newest t days carry a share 1 - 2 to the power (-t / 14) of the weight. After 3 days that is 1 - 0.862 = 0.138. After 14 days it is exactly 0.5. Taken alone, the 14-day filter is sluggish: two weeks pass before a new theme outweighs the old one.</p>
<p><strong>(c)</strong> At 10 commits per day, the 30-commit window spans only 3 days. After 15 new commits (1.5 days), the window holds 15 new and 15 old commits. The new commits have ages 0 to 1.5 days, with mean weight about 2 to the power (-0.75 / 14) = 0.963. The old ones have ages 1.5 to 3 days, with mean weight about 2 to the power (-2.25 / 14) = 0.895. The new share is 0.963 / (0.963 + 0.895) = 0.52. Here the count cap, not the halflife, sets the response time. At 1 commit per day, the window spans 30 days and the oldest commit weighs 2 to the power (-30 / 14) = 0.23, so the halflife dominates and the response is close to the slow filter in (b). Which mechanism sets the bandwidth depends on the commit rate.</p>
<p><strong>(d)</strong> The loop is: the centroid boosts intake priority for signals near the current theme; boosted work produces commits on that theme; those commits enter the corpus and pull the centroid further toward the theme. That is positive feedback, which can lock a theme in. Three things in §36 limit its gain. The boost is clamped to at most 1, strictly below the hard goal boost of 2, so inferred themes cannot outrank declared goals. POSTMORTEM turns are excluded, so failures do not feed the loop. And the decay makes old reinforcement fade. The loop is bounded, not removed: within the cap it still favours the current theme.</p>
</details>
</div>
<div class="problem problem-x">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Connection 3 (Probability and statistics: small samples and base rates).</strong> MemoryEngine raises a file's risk tier when its success rate is below 0.5 (§27). The paper does not say whether a minimum number of operations is required first. As stated assumptions for illustration: a healthy file succeeds independently with probability 0.8 per operation, a genuinely bad file with probability 0.3, and 10% of files that reach the check are genuinely bad. (a) For a healthy file, find the probability that its observed rate is below 0.5 after n = 1, 2, 3 and 10 operations. (b) At n = 3, what is the chance of flagging a bad file? (c) At n = 3, what fraction of flagged files are actually bad? (d) What does this imply for the threshold and for the 168-hour TTL?</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>"Below 0.5" is strict: with n = 2, one success out of two is exactly 0.5 and does not flag. Use the binomial distribution, then Bayes' rule for (c).</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p><strong>(a)</strong> With success probability 0.8: at n = 1 the file flags on a single failure, probability 0.2. At n = 2 it needs zero successes, 0.2 squared = 0.04. At n = 3 it needs at most one success: 0.2 cubed + 3 times 0.8 times 0.2 squared = 0.008 + 0.096 = 0.104. At n = 10 it needs at most four successes; summing the binomial terms gives 0.0000001 + 0.000004 + 0.000074 + 0.000786 + 0.005505, which is about 0.0064. The false-alarm rate does not fall smoothly with n (0.2, 0.04, 0.104), because the strict threshold interacts with small integer counts.</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> With success probability 0.3 at n = 3: 0.7 cubed + 3 times 0.3 times 0.7 squared = 0.343 + 0.441 = 0.784.</p>
<p><strong>(c)</strong> Bad and flagged: 0.1 times 0.784 = 0.0784. Healthy and flagged: 0.9 times 0.104 = 0.0936. So P(bad given flagged) = 0.0784 / (0.0784 + 0.0936) = 0.0784 / 0.172 = 0.46. Under these assumptions, more than half of the flags at n = 3 land on healthy files, because healthy files are so much more common.</p>
<p><strong>(d)</strong> A raw rate on few operations is a noisy signal. A minimum sample size, or a confidence bound such as the lower end of an interval on the success rate, would cut false alarms sharply (at n = 10 the healthy-file rate falls to about 0.6%). The 168-hour TTL works against this: by expiring old records, it keeps n small for files that are touched rarely. The paper's design tolerates the noise because, as §28.2 says, a false positive costs only an extra review. The confidence cap of 0.6 on ProphecyEngine is the same honesty applied to the derived score (§28). Whether the real false-alarm rate is acceptable could be measured from <code>file_reputations.json</code>; the paper does not report it.</p>
</details>
</div>
</div>
</div>
<!-- engage:end -->

# PART VI — The Provider Ecosystem

> **Superseded as of 2026-10-13.** This Part describes the provider topology as of 2026-04-16. Since September 2026 the paid lanes (DoubleWord, Claude) are switched off by declaration and J-Prime, a local llama.cpp server on a single RTX 5090, carries every route. The text below is kept as the historical record; see **§93.6** for the current topology.

> **Big Picture:** O+V does not own a language model. It *orchestrates* calls to external language-model providers, treating them as interchangeable sources of intelligence via a uniform protocol. This Part describes the three-provider ecosystem (DoubleWord, Claude, J-Prime), the adaptive failback state machine that recovers from provider outages, the DoubleWord 3-tier event-driven architecture that eliminates polling, and the urgency-aware routing algorithm that picks the right provider for each operation.

## §39. The Three Providers

> **Analogy:** A competent surgeon does not have one scalpel — they have a tray of instruments, each tuned to a specific kind of cut. O+V does not have one language model — it has a tray of providers, each tuned to a specific class of operation. DoubleWord is the precision instrument for cost-optimized volume work. Claude is the heavyweight for complex reasoning and fast reflex. J-Prime is the self-hosted backup when available.

### §39.1 DoubleWord

**Source:** `backend/core/ouroboros/governance/doubleword_provider.py`.

**Models:** Qwen 3.5 397B MoE (`Qwen/Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8`), Gemma 4 31B (`google/gemma-4-31B-it`), Qwen 3.5 35B (retired caller).

**Pricing:** $0.10 per million input tokens, $0.40 per million output tokens.

**Features:**

- **Tier 0 real-time SSE streaming** (primary path, zero polling).
- **Tier 1 webhook-driven batch** (zero-poll fallback for async batch operations).
- **Tier 2 adaptive-backoff polling** (safety net when webhooks are unavailable).
- Cost-gated (per-op cap, daily budget).
- Max tokens: trivial/moderate 8192, standard 12288, complex/heavy 16384.
- Venom tool loop integrated.

**Role:** cost-optimization backbone for STANDARD, BACKGROUND, SPECULATIVE routes (where topology permits). Structured-JSON callers (`semantic_triage`, `ouroboros_plan`, Phase-0 `compaction`) run on DW's Gemma 4 31B.

### §39.2 Claude (Anthropic API)

**Source:** `backend/core/ouroboros/governance/providers.py`.

**Models:** Claude Opus, Sonnet, Haiku — model selection driven by `brain_selection_policy.yaml`.

**Pricing:** $3.00/$15.00 per million tokens (Sonnet-class); $15.00/$75.00 (Opus-class).

**Features:**

- Extended thinking via Anthropic's extended-thinking API (`JARVIS_EXTENDED_THINKING_ENABLED=true`).
- Prompt caching (via cache-breakpoint annotations).
- Tool-use support (Venom integrated).
- 60s hard fallback cap (`_FALLBACK_MAX_TIMEOUT_S`) to prevent unreachable providers from consuming the pipeline budget.

**Role:** IMMEDIATE route primary (latency-critical reflex operations), STANDARD/COMPLEX cascade fallback, Claude-as-planner for COMPLEX-tier operations.

### §39.3 J-Prime (GCP Self-Hosted)

**Source:** `backend/core/ouroboros/governance/providers.py` (PrimeProvider), `prime_client.py` (out-of-repo in J-Prime codebase).

**Models:** self-hosted model weights on GCP VMs with GPU acceleration. Exact models vary by deployment; typically a fine-tuned smaller model for structured-JSON work or specialized code tasks.

**Pricing:** VM cost only — no per-token billing.

**Features:**

- Fixed temperature 0.2.
- Schema enforcement (the PrimeClient protocol rejects malformed JSON).
- Opt-in per operation (not always available).

**Role:** Tier 2 cost-optimization for bounded-volume structured JSON work. Disabled when unhealthy.

### §39.4 The CandidateProvider Protocol

All three implement the uniform `CandidateProvider` protocol:

```python
class CandidateProvider(Protocol):
    async def generate(
        self,
        ctx: OperationContext,
        deadline: datetime,
        tool_loop: Optional[ToolLoopCoordinator] = None,
    ) -> GenerationResult: ...

    async def plan(self, prompt: str, deadline: datetime) -> PlanResponse: ...

    async def health_check(self) -> HealthStatus: ...
```

The orchestrator does not know whether a given `CandidateProvider` is DoubleWord, Claude, J-Prime, or a test mock. Adding a new provider to the ecosystem requires implementing the protocol and registering with the GovernedLoopService — no changes to pipeline code.

## §40. Adaptive Provider Routing — The Failback State Machine

> **Big Picture:** Providers fail. Rate limits, timeouts, outages, network partitions — all of these happen, and when they do, the pipeline must recover gracefully without dumping every operation onto the most expensive fallback. The adaptive failback state machine is what keeps the cost-optimization intact under provider stress, by classifying each failure mode and computing its recovery ETA so the primary is retried at the right moment.

**Source:** `backend/core/ouroboros/governance/candidate_generator.py`.

### §40.1 FailureMode Classification

When a provider raises, the exception is classified:

| Mode | Base Backoff | Max Backoff | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `RATE_LIMITED` | 15s | 120s | HTTP 429, CircuitBreakerOpen |
| `TIMEOUT` | 45s | 300s | Connection/request timeout |
| `SERVER_ERROR` | 60s | 600s | HTTP 500/502/503 |
| `CONNECTION_ERROR` | 120s | 900s | Host unreachable, DNS failure |
| `CONTENT_FAILURE` | 0s | 0s | Bad output — no infrastructure penalty |

**Content failures are treated differently** — if the provider returns a response but the response is malformed (bad JSON, missing required fields, oversized output), the infrastructure is fine, so no backoff is applied. The next operation can attempt the primary immediately.

### §40.2 Recovery ETA

```
recovery_eta = base_backoff * 2 ** (consecutive_failures - 1)
recovery_eta = min(recovery_eta, max_backoff)
```

Exponential backoff capped at the mode's maximum. After the first `TIMEOUT`, 45 seconds. After the second consecutive, 90. After the third, 180. Capped at 300.

### §40.3 FSM States

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `PRIMARY_ACTIVE` | Primary is healthy; use it. |
| `PRIMARY_DEGRADED` | Primary has had some failures but probe succeeded; try it with fallback as safety. |
| `FALLBACK_ACTIVE` | Primary in backoff; use fallback directly. |
| `QUEUE_ONLY` | Both primary and fallback failing with `CONNECTION_ERROR`; operations queue until a probe succeeds. |

### §40.4 `should_attempt_primary()`

Before each operation, the FSM is consulted:

```python
def should_attempt_primary(now: datetime) -> bool:
    if state == PRIMARY_ACTIVE:
        return True
    if state == FALLBACK_ACTIVE:
        return now >= recovery_eta
    if state == QUEUE_ONLY:
        return False  # wait for probe
    if state == PRIMARY_DEGRADED:
        return True  # try primary with fallback as safety
```

This is the mechanism by which the cost-optimization survives transient failures — the primary is retried on every operation once the backoff window has elapsed, not held down indefinitely.

### §40.5 Adaptive Health Probes

Probe interval adapts based on distance to recovery ETA:

| Distance to ETA | Interval |
|---|---|
| > 60s away | 60s (relaxed) |
| 30–60s away | 20s (moderate) |
| < 30s away | 10s (ramping up) |
| Past ETA | 5s (aggressive) |

Close to recovery, probe more often. Far from recovery, probe less. This is a cost-optimization of the probe cost itself.

### §40.6 Connector Resilience

The `DoublewordProvider` specifically detects **poisoned aiohttp connectors** — caused by `CancelledError` during connection attempts that leave the aiohttp session in a half-initialized state. When detected, the provider discards the session and creates a fresh one. Background poll tasks are capped at 3 concurrent to prevent connector saturation.

This level of detail matters because real production deployments encounter these edge cases, and the pipeline must survive them without human intervention.

<div class="quick-check" id="qc-40">
<p class="qc-label">Quick check · §40</p>
<details class="qc"><summary>1. What would go wrong if a failing primary were simply held down after an outage instead of being retried once its recovery ETA passes?</summary>
<p>Every later operation would go to the fallback, which is usually the more expensive provider. Retrying the primary as soon as the backoff window elapses is what lets the cost optimization survive transient failures (§40, §40.4).</p>
</details>
<details class="qc"><summary>2. What is the difference between <code>FALLBACK_ACTIVE</code> and <code>QUEUE_ONLY</code>?</summary>
<p>In <code>FALLBACK_ACTIVE</code> the primary is in backoff and work goes to the fallback directly. <code>QUEUE_ONLY</code> is entered when both primary and fallback fail with <code>CONNECTION_ERROR</code>; operations wait in the queue and <code>should_attempt_primary()</code> returns false until a probe succeeds (§40.3, §40.4).</p>
</details>
<details class="qc"><summary>3. Why does the probe interval shrink from 60 s to 5 s as the recovery ETA approaches?</summary>
<p>Far from the ETA, recovery is unlikely and frequent probes would waste effort. Near and past the ETA, a fast probe detects recovery sooner. The paper calls this a cost optimization of the probe itself (§40.5).</p>
</details>
</div>
<!-- engage:end -->

## §41. DoubleWord 3-Tier Event-Driven Architecture

> **Big Picture:** Principle 3 of the Manifesto is "Zero polling. Pure reflex." This sounds aspirational, but DoubleWord implements it literally. Tier 0 (the primary path) uses SSE streaming — the server pushes tokens as they are generated, the client reads them as they arrive, no polling. Tier 1 (the async batch fallback) uses webhooks — when the batch completes, the DW server calls back to an HTTP endpoint on the Body, no polling. Tier 2 is adaptive-backoff polling — used only when webhooks cannot be configured, and even then with exponential backoff plus jitter, never fixed-interval polling.

![Figure 9 — DoubleWord's 3-tier event-driven architecture. Tier 0 (SSE streaming) and Tier 1 (webhook-driven batch) eliminate polling entirely. Tier 2 (adaptive-backoff poll) is used only as a safety net when webhooks cannot be configured, and even then with exponential backoff plus jitter — never fixed-interval polling.](figures/fig09_dw_3tier.png)

### §41.1 Tier 0 — Real-Time SSE (Primary Path)

**Default path.** Uses `/v1/chat/completions` with SSE streaming and Venom tool loop. Zero polling. Token-by-token streaming. Falls back to batch on 429/503 (stays within cheap DW instead of cascading to 150x more expensive Claude).

Environment: `DOUBLEWORD_REALTIME_ENABLED` (default `true`).

The SSE client reads incoming chunks, parses them as server-sent events, and emits tokens to the tool loop coordinator. Tool calls are detected mid-stream and dispatched; the model's response continues until the stream closes with a `[DONE]` marker.

### §41.2 Tier 1 — Webhook-Driven Batch (Zero-Poll Fallback)

For batch operations that fall through from Tier 0 (large payloads, 429 rate-limit responses). The `BatchFutureRegistry` maps `batch_id` to an `asyncio.Future`. The future is resolved by incoming DW webhooks via the `EventChannelServer`.

**Source:** `batch_future_registry.py`, `event_channel.py`.

- `BatchFutureRegistry`: register, resolve, reject, wait + TTL auto-pruning.
- `EventChannelServer`: `POST /webhook/doubleword` with Standard Webhooks HMAC-SHA256 signature verification.
- `DOUBLEWORD_WEBHOOK_SECRET`: signing key from the DW dashboard.

When a batch is submitted, the Body registers a future with its `batch_id`. When DW completes the batch, it POSTs to the Body's webhook endpoint with the batch result. The EventChannelServer verifies the HMAC signature, looks up the future, and resolves it. The batch call returns synchronously from the coroutine's perspective, zero-poll.

### §41.3 Tier 2 — Adaptive Backoff Poll (Safety Net)

Fallback when webhooks aren't configured. Replaces fixed 5s polling with exponential backoff + jitter:

- Starting interval: 2s.
- Multiplier: 1.5x per iteration.
- Cap: 30s.
- Jitter: ±25%.
- Network-aware: connection errors jump to 15s base.
- One-line debug logs — no tracebacks on transient failures.

Tier 2 is *only* used when webhooks cannot be configured. It is a safety net, not the primary path.

### §41.4 Manifesto Alignment

This architecture is a direct expression of two principles:

- **Principle 3 (Zero Polling. Pure Reflex):** Tier 0 and Tier 1 eliminate polling entirely. Tier 2 is adaptive, not fixed-interval.
- **Principle 6 (The Iron Gate):** Webhook signature verification prevents spoofed batch completions. Only DW's properly-signed callbacks can resolve futures.

## §42. Urgency-Aware Provider Routing

> **Big Picture:** The routing decision — which provider handles which operation — is itself a deterministic algorithm. It is not another model call. It is a pure-code `UrgencyRouter` that maps `(urgency, source, complexity)` to a `ProviderRoute` enum in under one millisecond. This section describes the routing algorithm, the five route contracts, and the cost economics of the routing topology.

**Source:** `backend/core/ouroboros/governance/urgency_router.py`.

![Figure 3 — The five provider routes, each with a distinct cascade strategy, cost target, and use case. The UrgencyRouter maps (urgency, source, complexity) to a ProviderRoute in sub-millisecond time with zero LLM calls — deterministic routing by design.](figures/fig03_routing_topology.png)

### §42.1 The Five Routes (Repeated for Reference)

| Route | Strategy | Cost | When |
|---|---|---|---|
| `IMMEDIATE` | Claude direct (skip DW) | ~$0.03/op | Test failures, voice, runtime-health critical |
| `STANDARD` | DW primary → Claude fallback | ~$0.005/op | Default cascade for normal-priority work |
| `COMPLEX` | Claude plans → DW executes | ~$0.015/op | Multi-file architectural, heavy tool loops |
| `BACKGROUND` | DW only, no Claude fallback | ~$0.002/op | Opportunity mining, doc staleness, TODOs |
| `SPECULATIVE` | DW batch fire-and-forget | ~$0.001/op | Intent discovery, proactive exploration |

### §42.2 The Lookup Tables

The router consults two deterministic frozen sets and one complexity classifier:

```python
_IMMEDIATE_SOURCES = frozenset({
    "test_failure",
    "voice_human",
    "runtime_health",
})

_BACKGROUND_SOURCES = frozenset({
    "ai_miner",
    "exploration",
    "backlog",
    "architecture",
    "todo_scanner",
    "doc_staleness",
})

_SPECULATIVE_SOURCES = frozenset({
    "intent_discovery",
})

_COMPLEX_COMPLEXITIES = frozenset({
    "heavy_code",
    "complex",
})
```

### §42.3 The Algorithm

```python
def classify(urgency, source, complexity) -> ProviderRoute:
    if complexity in _COMPLEX_COMPLEXITIES:
        return ProviderRoute.COMPLEX
    if source in _SPECULATIVE_SOURCES:
        return ProviderRoute.SPECULATIVE
    if source in _BACKGROUND_SOURCES:
        return ProviderRoute.BACKGROUND
    if source in _IMMEDIATE_SOURCES and urgency >= CRITICAL:
        return ProviderRoute.IMMEDIATE
    return ProviderRoute.STANDARD  # default cascade
```

Pure code. No network call. No LLM. Sub-millisecond.

### §42.4 Why Deterministic?

Three reasons, as introduced in §9.2:

1. **Reproducibility** — replaying a signal gives the same route.
2. **Cost** — inferencing every routing decision would double the bill.
3. **Latency** — agent workloads have tight per-phase budgets.

### §42.5 Route-Aware Timeout Enforcement

Each route carries its own generation timeout:

| Route | Generation Timeout | Grace |
|---|---|---|
| IMMEDIATE | 60s | 5s |
| STANDARD | 120s | 5s |
| COMPLEX | 180s | 5s |
| BACKGROUND | 180s | 5s |
| SPECULATIVE | N/A (batch) | — |

IMMEDIATE gets the tightest budget because it is reflex-critical. COMPLEX and BACKGROUND get more because they involve multi-round tool loops or slow-batch operations.

### §42.6 Deadline Budget Allocation

The total generation deadline for a cascade is split deterministically:

| Component | Budget | Env Var | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tier 0 (DW) | 50% of total, max 90s | `OUROBOROS_TIER0_BUDGET_FRACTION` | 0.50 |
| Tier 1 reserve | Minimum 25s guaranteed | `OUROBOROS_TIER1_MIN_RESERVE_S` | 25 |
| Primary within Tier 1 | 65% of Tier 1 budget | `OUROBOROS_PRIMARY_BUDGET_FRACTION` | 0.65 |
| Fallback reserve | Minimum 20s guaranteed | `OUROBOROS_FALLBACK_MIN_RESERVE_S` | 20 |

The budget math ensures that the fallback always has at least 20 seconds of runway, preventing a slow primary from consuming the entire budget and leaving nothing for the fallback to recover with.

## §43. The Current Topology Seal (As of 2026-04-16)

> **Big Picture:** The routing design is reversible. Each route is gated by a single YAML flag in `brain_selection_policy.yaml`. When a provider's infrastructure proves unreliable for a given route, the route can be sealed — `dw_allowed: false` — and operations on that route cascade to the fallback or skip-and-queue. This section describes the current topology as of 2026-04-16, which is the state reflected in the DoubleWord benchmark report (`docs/benchmarks/DW_BENCHMARKS_2026-04-16.md`).

**Source:** `backend/core/ouroboros/governance/brain_selection_policy.yaml` (lines 299–376).

### §43.1 The Current Seal

As of 2026-04-16, DoubleWord is **topology-sealed** from every agent-generation route:

- `IMMEDIATE` — `dw_allowed: false`, `block_mode: cascade_to_claude`.
- `STANDARD` — `dw_allowed: false`, `block_mode: cascade_to_claude`.
- `COMPLEX` — `dw_allowed: false`, `block_mode: cascade_to_claude`.
- `BACKGROUND` — `dw_allowed: false`, `block_mode: skip_and_queue`.
- `SPECULATIVE` — `dw_allowed: false`, `block_mode: skip_and_queue`.

DoubleWord is retained **only** for three structured-JSON callers:

- `semantic_triage` on Gemma 4 31B.
- `ouroboros_plan` on Gemma 4 31B.
- `compaction` on Gemma 4 31B (Phase 0 shadow mode).

### §43.2 Why Sealed

The seal was enforced on 2026-04-14 after two isolation tests (`bt-2026-04-14-182446` Gemma BG, `bt-2026-04-14-203740` Qwen 397B STANDARD) showed the same `SSE stream stalled (no data for 30s)` signature. The signal did not reproduce in an Apr 16 standalone smoke test (see the DoubleWord benchmark report for the full four-run addendum), but the seal remains in place until a sustained-concurrent-load validation pass with the DoubleWord gateway team.

### §43.3 The Path to Re-Engagement

The topology is designed to be reversible. Once SSE stability is confirmed through a pairing session with the DoubleWord gateway team (and possibly through the "Functions, Not Agents" non-streaming reseating; see Part XIV), each route can be flipped back to `dw_allowed: true` independently, with shadow-mode comparison against Claude for a battle-test cycle before full promotion.

The benchmark report lays out the full staged re-engagement plan. This paper defers to that report for the specific mechanics; the architectural point is that **the topology seal is a safety feature, not a limitation.** The organism is doing what it should — routing around an observed failure mode until structural repair is complete.

#### Check your understanding: PART VI — The Provider Ecosystem

<div class="engage" id="engage-part-vi">
<p class="engage-kicker">Conceptual questions</p>
<details class="cq"><summary>1. Why does the failback state machine apply zero backoff to a CONTENT_FAILURE but up to 900 seconds to a CONNECTION_ERROR?</summary>
<p>The backoff answers one question: when will the provider's infrastructure work again? In a content failure the provider did answer, but the answer was malformed: bad JSON, missing fields or oversized output. The infrastructure is fine, so waiting gains nothing, and the next operation can try the primary at once (§40.1). A connection error means the host is unreachable, which can take minutes or hours to fix, so its base backoff (120s) and cap (900s) are the largest in the table. Matching the backoff to the failure mode keeps the cheap primary in use. A single bad answer does not push work onto the expensive fallback, and a real outage is not hammered with retries (§40, §40.2).</p>
</details>
<details class="cq"><summary>2. In what sense is the April 2026 "topology seal" a safety feature and not a limitation?</summary>
<p>As of 2026-04-16, every agent-generation route had <code>dw_allowed: false</code>. Three routes cascaded to Claude and two used skip-and-queue (§43.1). The trigger was evidence: two isolation tests showed the same "SSE stream stalled (no data for 30s)" signature (§43.2). The seal sends work around a failure that had been observed but not yet repaired, and it is fully reversible. Each route sits behind one YAML flag and can be turned back on by itself, with a shadow-mode comparison before full promotion (§43.3). The pipeline code never changed. That is possible because the orchestrator only sees the uniform <code>CandidateProvider</code> protocol (§39.4).</p>
</details>
<details class="cq"><summary>3. Compare the April 2026 three-provider topology with the October 2026 topology in §93.6. Which parts of Part VI still describe how the system works, and which do not?</summary>
<p>As of April 2026, cost drove the routing. DoubleWord was the cheap backbone, Claude was the heavyweight and the fallback, and J-Prime was "the self-hosted backup when available" (§39). By October, J-Prime is the only lane. It is a local llama.cpp server on one RTX 5090. With no paid credential configured, the free-lane policy sends every route to the local engine, and <code>JARVIS_PAID_LANES_ENABLED=false</code> stops Claude and DoubleWord from being constructed at all (§93.6). Three ideas survive: the route names, the deterministic router, and the pluggable provider protocol. Two things lose their purpose: the per-route cost table, and a failback machine built to protect a cheap primary from an expensive fallback. The switch-off is a configuration change, not a code change, which follows the same reversibility idea as the April seal (§43.3, §93.6).</p>
</details>
