</ol>
<details class="mcq-why"><summary>Show answer</summary>
<p><strong>C.</strong> TIMEOUT has a 45s base, so 45 times 2 to the power 2 is 180s. That is below the 300s cap. The sequence runs 45, 90, 180, then caps at 300 (§40.2).</p>
</details>
</div>
<div class="mcq" data-answer="4">
<p class="mcq-q">2. A signal arrives from <code>test_failure</code> with urgency CRITICAL and complexity <code>heavy_code</code>. Which route does the §42.3 algorithm return?</p>
<ol class="mcq-options" type="A">
<li><code>IMMEDIATE</code>, because test failures are reflex-critical</li>
<li><code>STANDARD</code>, the default cascade</li>
<li><code>BACKGROUND</code>, because the source is a sensor</li>
<li><code>COMPLEX</code>, because complexity is checked first</li>
</ol>
<details class="mcq-why"><summary>Show answer</summary>
<p><strong>D.</strong> The first branch of <code>classify</code> tests complexity against <code>_COMPLEX_COMPLEXITIES</code>. <code>heavy_code</code> matches, so the IMMEDIATE check is never reached (§42.3).</p>
</details>
</div>
<div class="mcq" data-answer="1">
<p class="mcq-q">3. In DoubleWord's Tier 1 webhook path, what stops an attacker from resolving a pending batch future with a fake result?</p>
<ol class="mcq-options" type="A">
<li>HMAC-SHA256 signature verification on each incoming webhook</li>
<li>A TTL that prunes futures older than a few minutes</li>
<li>Adaptive-backoff polling that re-checks every result</li>
<li>The 60s hard fallback cap on the Claude provider</li>
</ol>
<details class="mcq-why"><summary>Show answer</summary>
<p><strong>A.</strong> <code>EventChannelServer</code> checks the Standard Webhooks HMAC-SHA256 signature before it resolves a future. The paper ties this to Principle 6, the Iron Gate (§41.2, §41.4).</p>
</details>
</div>
<div class="mcq" data-answer="2">
<p class="mcq-q">4. Under the seal in force on 2026-04-16, what was DoubleWord still used for?</p>
<ol class="mcq-options" type="A">
<li>Only the SPECULATIVE batch route</li>
<li>Three structured-JSON callers on Gemma 4 31B</li>
<li>BACKGROUND work, with no Claude fallback</li>
<li>Nothing; it was removed from the code base</li>
</ol>
<details class="mcq-why"><summary>Show answer</summary>
<p><strong>B.</strong> Every agent-generation route had <code>dw_allowed: false</code>. DoubleWord kept only <code>semantic_triage</code>, <code>ouroboros_plan</code> and the Phase 0 <code>compaction</code>, all on Gemma 4 31B (§43.1).</p>
</details>
</div>
</div>
<p class="engage-kicker">Problem set</p>
<div class="pset" id="pset-part-vi">
<div class="problem">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Problem 1 (trace).</strong> As of April 2026, DoubleWord is the primary on the STANDARD route, and its FSM is in <code>PRIMARY_ACTIVE</code>. At time 0 a DW call times out. Trace the next few minutes. What state does the FSM enter? When does <code>should_attempt_primary()</code> return true again? How often is the primary probed as that time approaches? What happens if the retry also times out?</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>Combine three tables: failure modes (§40.1), FSM states (§40.3) and probe intervals (§40.5).</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p>The exception is classified as <code>TIMEOUT</code>, with a 45s base and a 300s cap. One consecutive failure gives a recovery ETA of 45 times 2 to the power 0, which is 45s (§40.1, §40.2). The primary is now in backoff, so the FSM moves to <code>FALLBACK_ACTIVE</code>, and operations go straight to the fallback (§40.3).</p>
<p><code>should_attempt_primary()</code> returns <code>now &gt;= recovery_eta</code> in that state, so it becomes true at t = 45s (§40.4). Probes follow the distance to the ETA (§40.5). At t = 0 the ETA is 45s away, which falls in the 30 to 60s band, so the interval is 20s. After t = 15s the ETA is under 30s away, so the interval drops to 10s. Past the ETA it drops to 5s.</p>
<p>If the retry also times out, the failure count becomes 2 and the ETA becomes 90s. The doubling continues to 180s and then stops at the 300s cap. A content failure on the retry would add no backoff (§40.1).</p>
</details>
</div>
<div class="problem">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Problem 2 (design).</strong> The October 2026 system (§93.6) has a single local lane, J-Prime on one RTX 5090. Paid lanes are switched off and never constructed. Someone proposes deleting the failback state machine (§40) and the per-route deadline split (§42.6), since "there is nothing to fail back to." Argue for and against. Use §93.5 to explain why a failure classifier still matters when every lane is free.</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>Ask what each mechanism protected. Then ask what §93.5 says happened when a 402 response was read as an outage.</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p>For the proposal: much of Part VI exists to protect a cheap primary from an expensive fallback. The route cost table (§42.1), the Tier 0/Tier 1 split (§42.6) and the probe-cost tuning (§40.5) all assume two paid lanes with different prices. With one local lane and the free-lane policy routing everything locally (§93.6), the cost argument goes away. A fallback reserve has nothing to reserve for.</p>
<p>Against the proposal: the system still has to tell kinds of failure apart. §93.5 shows the cost of getting this wrong. When the paid credit ran out, the classifier read HTTP 402 as an outage, and one session produced 125 false awaken triggers. The fix was a table-driven ECONOMIC state that separates "out of money" from rate limits and outages. Classifying failures, and not penalising a lane for a content failure (§40.1), is about telling the truth about causes, not only about cost.</p>
<p>Two more reasons to keep it. Re-enabling paid lanes is "a configuration change, not a code change" (§93.6), and that relies on the machinery still existing. The uniform provider protocol (§39.4) is what lets J-Prime be swapped in without changing the pipeline. A sound answer keeps classification and the protocol, and accepts that the cost tables are dormant.</p>
</details>
</div>
<div class="problem">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Problem 3 (code reading).</strong> Open <code>backend/core/ouroboros/governance/candidate_generator.py</code> and find <code>class FailureMode</code> and the <code>_RECOVERY_PARAMS</code> table below it. Compare them with the five-row table in §40.1. Which modes exist in code but not in the paper? What backoff profile does each get? What does the set <code>_PRIMARY_INNOCENT_MODES</code> add to the paper's description of CONTENT_FAILURE?</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>Read the comments next to each extra enum member. They say whose fault each failure is.</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p>The five modes in the paper are all present, with the same base and max values: RATE_LIMITED 15/120, TIMEOUT 45/300, SERVER_ERROR 60/600, CONNECTION_ERROR 120/900 and CONTENT_FAILURE 0/0 (§40.1). The code adds four more. <code>CONTEXT_OVERFLOW</code> means the prompt exceeded the size limit, and it has a zero profile. <code>TRANSIENT_TRANSPORT</code> covers HTTP/2 disconnects and early stream closes, with a 5s base and 30s cap. <code>TEMPORAL_SHED</code> is a routing refusal, not a fact about DW's health, and it has a zero profile. <code>LOCAL_DEFECT</code> covers TypeError, AttributeError and similar bugs in O+V's own call path, also with a zero profile.</p>
<p><code>_PRIMARY_INNOCENT_MODES</code> takes the idea behind CONTENT_FAILURE ("the infrastructure is fine, so no backoff") and makes it a named set. The set contains CONTENT_FAILURE, TEMPORAL_SHED and LOCAL_DEFECT. For these, the operation still cascades, but the provider's FSM is not penalised.</p>
<p>The LOCAL_DEFECT comment explains why. Unrecognised exceptions used to fall through to the TIMEOUT default. One signature drift in O+V's own code then locked DoubleWord out and sent every later operation to Claude, while the logs blamed an upstream provider that was never called. The point of §40.1 is that the backoff should match the real cause. The code applies that idea to failure causes the April paper did not list.</p>
</details>
</div>
</div>
<p class="engage-kicker engage-kicker-adv">Advanced conceptual questions</p>
<details class="cq-adv"><summary>A1. DoubleWord's Tier 0 falls back to batch on 429/503 "to stay within cheap DW" instead of cascading to Claude (§41.1). §93.2 later reports that the batch path never completed inside its 180 s budget. What is the second-order effect of a cost-protecting fallback that never completes?</summary>
<p>The design in §41.1 is a cost argument. Claude is described as about 150 times more expensive, so a 429 or 503 is answered by staying inside DoubleWord and switching to the webhook batch path (§41.2). That choice is sound only if the batch path returns inside the operation's deadline. §93.2 records that it did not: the batch path "never completed inside its 180 s budget" (<code>1fa295394d</code>).</p>
<p>The second-order effect is that money is traded for time, and the time is lost for nothing. The route timeouts in §42.5 are 120 s for STANDARD and 180 s for COMPLEX and BACKGROUND, so a batch call that cannot finish in 180 s uses up the whole generation window. On BACKGROUND the effect is worse, because that route has no Claude fallback at all (§42.1). The operation ends with no candidate and no spend, which looks cheap in the ledger but produces nothing. The deadline split in §42.6 protects the Claude reserve only on cascading routes, so it cannot rescue a route whose only lane is the slow one.</p>
<p>The lesson is that a fallback has to be judged by its completion rate inside the budget, not by its unit price. The evidence that settles it is the one §93.2 supplies: measured completion times against the route deadline.</p>
</details>
<details class="cq-adv"><summary>A2. §42.4 justifies deterministic routing by reproducibility: "replaying a signal gives the same route." Under the October free-lane policy (§93.6), the route a signal actually takes depends on whether a paid credential is configured. Has reproducibility been lost?</summary>
<p>Not in the sense §42.4 means, but its scope has narrowed. The <code>classify</code> function in §42.3 is still a pure function of <code>(urgency, source, complexity)</code>, and it still returns the same <code>ProviderRoute</code> on replay. What changed is the step after it. In April a route named a provider strategy (for example "DW primary, Claude fallback"). In October the free-lane policy sends every route to the local engine when no paid credential is configured (§93.6), and <code>paid_lanes.py</code> decides whether a paid lane is switched on, configured and allowed. The last of these also consults the economic ledger.</p>
<p>So the provider that serves a replayed signal is a function of the signal <em>and</em> of configuration and ledger state. Two replays of the same signal on two days can reach different providers if the ledger changed in between. A fair position is that reproducibility now holds for the route and not for the provider. Full replay needs the configuration and the ledger verdict recorded alongside the route.</p>
<p>The cost and latency arguments in §42.4 survive unchanged: no model call is made to decide either step. The evidence that would settle whether this matters in practice is how often the paid-lane verdict changes during a session. With <code>JARVIS_PAID_LANES_ENABLED=false</code> declared, that rate should be zero.</p>
</details>
<details class="cq-adv"><summary>A3. §39.4 claims that adding a provider "requires implementing the protocol and registering with the GovernedLoopService — no changes to pipeline code." Does the August to October move to a local 30B on the RTX 5090 (§93.6, §93.8) vindicate that claim or refute it?</summary>
<p>It vindicates the claim at the interface level and refutes a stronger reading of it at the behaviour level. The interface held. J-Prime replaced DoubleWord and Claude on every route, the pipeline phases stayed the same (§93.8 says the phase set is unchanged since §92), and paid lanes can come back by configuration alone (§93.6).</p>
<p>But a working pipeline needed far more than a working <code>generate()</code>. §93.6 lists defects that each had to be found in a live run. The 5090 was sized as a 24 GiB L4, which halved context to 16,896 tokens. The client cache was keyed by URL alone, so a model swap kept the old weights. <code>JARVIS_LOCAL_MODEL_NAME</code> was ignored. The model would not explore until a constrained-decoding grammar forced tool calls. §93.8 then adds an AST-Signature Anchor, a diff output schema and a test reality gate, all because a smaller model behaved differently behind the same interface.</p>
<p>The protocol in §39.4 specifies call shapes (<code>generate</code>, <code>plan</code>, <code>health_check</code>). It does not specify context size, grammar support, or how reliably the model follows the output contract. Those are the properties that broke. A fair conclusion is that the protocol makes providers swappable but not interchangeable. The evidence for this is the §93.6 defect list and §93.14 item 3: diff fidelity is still the leading way operations die.</p>
</details>
<p class="engage-kicker engage-kicker-adv">Challenge problems</p>
<div class="pset pset-adv">
<div class="problem problem-adv">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Challenge 1 (quantitative).</strong> Use the deadline split in §42.6: Tier 0 gets 50% of the total, at most 90 s. Tier 1 is guaranteed at least 25 s. The primary within Tier 1 gets 65%, and the fallback is guaranteed at least 20 s. Compute the four components for a cascade with a total of 120 s (STANDARD), 180 s (COMPLEX), and 50 s. Then use the stall signature in §43.2 ("no data for 30s") to say how much of the 120 s Tier 0 budget a stalled DoubleWord stream wastes before it is detected.</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>The paper gives fractions and floors but not how they interact. State a rule: compute the fraction first, then let a floor take time from the larger share when it binds. Check that the four parts always add up to the total.</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p><strong>Assumptions.</strong> Tier 0 = min(0.5 × T, 90 s), cut back if it would leave Tier 1 below 25 s. Tier 1 = T − Tier 0. Primary = 0.65 × Tier 1, cut back if it would leave the fallback below 20 s. Fallback = Tier 1 − primary. §42.6 does not spell out this precedence, so it is an assumption.</p>
<p><strong>T = 120 s.</strong> Tier 0 = min(60, 90) = 60 s. Tier 1 = 60 s, which is above 25. Primary = 0.65 × 60 = 39 s. Fallback = 21 s, which is above 20. Check: 60 + 39 + 21 = 120. No floor binds, with one second to spare on the fallback.</p>
<p><strong>T = 180 s.</strong> Tier 0 = min(90, 90) = 90 s. Tier 1 = 90 s. Primary = 58.5 s. Fallback = 31.5 s. Check: 90 + 58.5 + 31.5 = 180. The 90 s cap is exactly at its limit here. Any total above 180 s sends all extra time to Tier 1. The fallback stays under Claude's 60 s hard cap (§39.2) up to a total of about 261 s (Tier 1 about 171 s, fallback about 60 s).</p>
<p><strong>T = 50 s.</strong> Tier 0 = 25 s, which leaves Tier 1 at exactly its 25 s floor. Primary = 0.65 × 25 = 16.25 s, which would leave the fallback at 8.75 s, below its 20 s floor. The floor binds, so the fallback gets 20 s and the primary only 5 s. Check: 25 + 5 + 20 = 50. Below 50 s, Tier 1 stays pinned at 25 s (primary 5 s, fallback 20 s) and only Tier 0 shrinks. Below 25 s, Tier 0 gets nothing at all.</p>
<p><strong>The stall.</strong> On a 120 s STANDARD cascade, Tier 0 has 60 s. A stream that stalls is declared stalled after 30 s with no data (§43.2), so in the worst case half of the Tier 0 budget, and a quarter of the whole operation, goes to waiting. If the stall begins late in the stream, detection can land at the 60 s Tier 0 limit and the stall detector never fires before the budget does.</p>
<p><strong>Conclusion.</strong> The split works as designed at 120 s and 180 s. At short totals the floors invert the 65/35 intent and starve the primary. The 30 s stall window is large compared with a 60 s Tier 0 share, which is consistent with the April decision to seal the routes rather than tune timeouts (§43.1). To check, recompute with your own precedence rule. The sums must equal T. Under this rule the fallback floor first binds just below 120 s, where the fallback share is 0.35 × 0.5 × T, which drops under 20 s once T is below about 114 s.</p>
</details>
</div>
<div class="problem problem-adv">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Challenge 2 (adversarial).</strong> The April router (§42.3) sends a <code>test_failure</code> signal at CRITICAL urgency to IMMEDIATE: Claude direct, about 0.03 US dollars per operation (§42.1). Construct the cheapest event sequence you can that turns this into a sustained spend leak. Twenty test files each flip red then green once a minute (a flaky suite), and every flip to red emits a critical signal. Estimate the hourly spend. Then go through Part VI and the relevant mechanisms in Parts VII and VIII and decide which layer, if any, stops the leak.</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>Look at where cost caps are actually attached. §39.1 lists a per-op cap and a daily budget, but for which provider? Then check whether coalescing (§52.8) and the file DAG (§46) apply to critical signals.</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p><strong>The rate.</strong> Twenty files each produce one red flip per minute, so 20 critical signals arrive per minute. Each targets one file, so the DAG (§46) allows one active operation per file at a time. The IMMEDIATE timeout is 60 s plus 5 s grace (§42.5), so each file can sustain about one operation per minute. That gives about 20 operations per minute, 1,200 per hour, and at about 0.03 US dollars each, roughly 36 US dollars per hour, or about 864 US dollars per day. For comparison, the same volume on BACKGROUND (about 0.002 per op) would be about 2.40 US dollars per hour.</p>
<p><strong>Layer by layer, April design.</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Router (§42.3): it does what it was built to do. The signal really is a critical test failure, so IMMEDIATE is the correct output.</li>
<li>Failback FSM (§40): it reacts to provider <em>failures</em>. Every call here succeeds, so it never engages.</li>
<li>DoubleWord's per-op cap and daily budget (§39.1): attached to DoubleWord. IMMEDIATE skips DW entirely (§42.1), so those caps never see the spend.</li>
<li>Coalescing (§52.8): HIGH-urgency signals bypass the 30 s window. Assume CRITICAL is treated at least as HIGH, so there is no merging.</li>
<li>Priority (§50.1): critical urgency subtracts 3, so the flood goes to the front of the queue and pushes other work back. It makes the leak worse, not better.</li>
<li>File DAG (§46): this is the one thing that bounds the leak. It holds concurrency to one operation per file, which is why the estimate is 20 per minute and not unbounded.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Honest verdict.</strong> Nothing in Part VI stops the leak. The April paper contains no route-level spend ceiling for IMMEDIATE. The first mechanism in the paper that sits on every paid call is Aegis (§93.2): an out-of-process spend proxy where each paid call is admitted, reserved and reconciled. That gives an admission point where a ceiling can refuse calls. In October the dollar leak disappears because paid lanes are never constructed (§93.6). The same flood would then take over the single local lane instead (one GPU, §93.14 item 7), so the cost becomes starved throughput rather than money.</p>
<p><strong>A proposal (not in the paper).</strong> Detect flapping per test identity, for example the same test going red, green, red inside a window, and demote it from IMMEDIATE to a quarantine or BACKGROUND route. Pair this with a per-route spend ceiling at the admission point. To check the estimate, recompute with your own flip rate. Spend scales linearly with files multiplied by flips per minute, capped at one operation per file per IMMEDIATE timeout.</p>
</details>
</div>
</div>
<p class="engage-kicker engage-kicker-x">Connections</p>
<div class="pset pset-x">
<div class="problem problem-x">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Connection 1 (Economics).</strong> Use the April 2026 prices in §39: DoubleWord charges 0.10 US dollars per million input tokens and 0.40 per million output tokens; Claude Sonnet-class charges 3.00 and 15.00, Opus-class 15.00 and 75.00. Assume an operation with 20,000 input tokens and 2,000 output tokens (an assumption, not a paper figure). (a) Compute that operation's cost on each provider, and check the "150x more expensive Claude" claim in §41.1. (b) Take an assumed daily mix of 100 operations: 10 IMMEDIATE, 60 STANDARD, 10 COMPLEX, 15 BACKGROUND, 5 SPECULATIVE, priced at the per-op figures in §42.1. Compute the total. (c) Recompute it under the §43.1 seal, pricing every Claude-direct operation at the IMMEDIATE figure of about 0.03. What happens to the marginal cost of one more STANDARD operation?</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>The 150x claim only holds against one price class and one direction of tokens. Under the seal, two routes cost nothing because their work is not done.</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p>(a) DoubleWord: 20,000 × 0.10 / 1,000,000 = 0.002, plus 2,000 × 0.40 / 1,000,000 = 0.0008, total 0.0028 US dollars. Sonnet-class: 0.06 + 0.03 = 0.09, about 32x DoubleWord. Opus-class: 0.30 + 0.15 = 0.45, about 161x. Per token, Sonnet is 30x (input) to 37.5x (output) and Opus is 150x to 187.5x. So "150x" matches the Opus-class input ratio; against Sonnet-class the gap is roughly 30 to 38x.</p>
<p>(b) April mix: 10 × 0.03 = 0.30; 60 × 0.005 = 0.30; 10 × 0.015 = 0.15; 15 × 0.002 = 0.03; 5 × 0.001 = 0.005. Total about 0.79 US dollars per 100 operations.</p>
<p>(c) Sealed: IMMEDIATE, STANDARD and COMPLEX all cascade to Claude (§43.1). At about 0.03 each that is 80 × 0.03 = 2.40. BACKGROUND and SPECULATIVE are <code>skip_and_queue</code>, so they cost nothing and produce nothing. The bill rises about 3x while 20 of the 100 operations are no longer done. The marginal cost of one more STANDARD operation goes from about 0.005 to about 0.03, a factor of 6. These are estimates built from the paper's approximate per-op figures, not measured spend.</p>
<p>The lesson for the architecture: route choice in April was an economic decision, and the seal was a deliberate trade of cost for reliability. The October topology (§93.6) removes the per-token price entirely, so the marginal dollar cost of an operation becomes zero. The scarce resource then becomes GPU time, which is the subject of Connection 2.</p>
</details>
</div>
<div class="problem problem-x">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Connection 2 (Queueing theory and economics).</strong> In October (§93.6), J-Prime on one RTX 5090 serves every route. A slot sweep measured aggregate decode throughput of 124, 165 and 177 tokens per second at 1, 2 and 3 slots. Assume each operation decodes 2,000 output tokens and that prefill time is small enough to ignore (both assumptions). For each slot count, compute the decode time per operation and the operations per hour. Use Little's law to check the 2-slot numbers. Then say what "cost" means for routing when the marginal dollar price is zero.</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>Aggregate throughput is shared across the slots, so each stream gets the aggregate divided by the slot count. Little's law is L = λW.</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p>1 slot: each operation takes 2,000 / 124 = 16.1 s, so 3,600 / 16.1 = about 223 operations per hour.</p>
<p>2 slots: each stream gets 165 / 2 = 82.5 tokens per second, so an operation takes 24.2 s. Throughput is 165 × 3,600 / 2,000 = about 297 operations per hour.</p>
<p>3 slots: each stream gets 59 tokens per second, so an operation takes 33.9 s. Throughput is about 319 operations per hour.</p>
<p>The second slot adds about 74 operations per hour (+33%) for a 50% longer per-operation latency. The third adds only about 22 per hour (+7%) for a further 40% latency increase. That is why the paper places the knee at 2 slots.</p>
<p>Little's law check at 2 slots: λ = 297 / 3,600 = 0.0825 operations per second, W = 24.2 s, so L = 0.0825 × 24.2 = 2.0 operations in service, matching two busy slots. If work arrives faster than about 297 operations per hour, utilization exceeds 1 and the queue grows without bound, however many routes the router distinguishes.</p>
<p>Note that the paper also reports a decode p50 of 172 tokens per second at one slot on real O+V traffic, a different measurement from the 124 in the sweep. Mixing the two would give wrong ratios, so the calculation uses the sweep alone.</p>
<p>What this says about the architecture: in April, routing traded dollars against latency across providers (§42.1). In October every route lands on the same GPU, so the price of an operation is the GPU-seconds it occupies and the delay it imposes on everything queued behind it. The useful decisions move from "which provider" to admission and concurrency, which is why local concurrency now follows the engine's reported slot count (§93.6).</p>
</details>
</div>
<div class="problem problem-x">
<p class="problem-q"><strong>Connection 3 (Markov chains).</strong> Model the §40 failback state machine for <code>TIMEOUT</code> failures as an absorbing Markov chain. After the k-th consecutive failure the primary waits b_k = min(45 × 2^(k−1), 300) seconds (§40.2), then is retried. Assume each retry fails independently with probability p (an assumption; real outages are correlated, and the paper gives no p). Let the transient states be F1, F2, F3 and F4+ (four or more consecutive failures, where the backoff stays at 300 s), and let success be the absorbing state. Starting just after a first failure, find the expected number of visits to each transient state, then the expected total backoff time for p = 0.2 and p = 0.5. Finally, show what happens to that expectation without the 300 s cap.</p>
<details class="problem-hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
<p>Each state moves forward with probability p and absorbs with probability 1 − p, except F4+, which loops on itself. The fundamental matrix N = (I − Q)^−1 gives expected visits; its first row here can be read off directly.</p>
</details>
<details class="problem-sol"><summary>Worked solution</summary>
<p>The transient block Q has F1 → F2, F2 → F3 and F3 → F4+ with probability p, and F4+ → F4+ with probability p. Every state goes to success with probability 1 − p. The first row of N = (I − Q)^−1 gives the expected visits from F1: F1 once, F2 p times, F3 p² times, and F4+ p³ / (1 − p) times (a geometric number of self-loops).</p>
<p>Expected backoff is E = 45 + 90p + 180p² + 300p³ / (1 − p).</p>
<p>For p = 0.2: 45 + 18 + 7.2 + 300 × 0.008 / 0.8 = 45 + 18 + 7.2 + 3 = about 73 s. For p = 0.5: 45 + 45 + 45 + 300 × 0.125 / 0.5 = 135 + 75 = 210 s. The expected number of retries before success is 1 / (1 − p): 1.25 and 2 respectively.</p>
<p>Without the cap, b_k = 45 × 2^(k−1) for all k, so E = Σ 45 × (2p)^(k−1). That geometric series converges only when 2p &lt; 1. At p = 0.5 every term equals 45 and the sum diverges; for p &gt; 0.5 it diverges faster. So the cap is not cosmetic: it is what keeps the expected time in fallback finite when the primary fails at least half the time.</p>
<p>During that backoff, work goes to the fallback (<code>FALLBACK_ACTIVE</code>, §40.3), which in April was the more expensive provider. The expected backoff is therefore also an expected period of paying fallback prices. The mode-specific caps in §40.1 (120 s to 900 s) bound that exposure per failure mode. The independence assumption is the weak point of the model: correlated outages make p rise after each failure, which lengthens the real stay in F4+ beyond these figures. These are model outputs, not measurements.</p>
</details>
</div>
</div>
</div>
<!-- engage:end -->

---

# PART VII — Autonomous Developer Intelligence (Seven Capabilities)

> **Big Picture:** A pipeline that only *generates patches* is still not an autonomous developer. A real autonomous developer has *intelligence about being a developer* — understanding that certain changes warrant human escalation, that the same files being touched twice concurrently is a conflict, that exploring before writing is non-negotiable, that mistakes should be remembered, and that cost matters. This Part describes the seven capabilities that turn O+V's pipeline into a proactive autonomous developer rather than an autonomous patch factory.

## §44. Capability 1 — Operation Intent Visibility

> **Big Picture:** Every operation the organism performs has a *reason*. The model's rationale for *why* it made a specific change is captured at GENERATE and displayed prominently in the operator's terminal. This is what makes the autonomy legible. You can watch a real operation happen and understand the model's thinking, not just the diff.

**Source:** `serpent_flow.py` (`set_op_reasoning`, `show_diff`), `orchestrator.py` (GENERATE phase rationale capture).

Every operation displays the model's reasoning for why it made a specific change. The rationale is captured from `candidate_rationales` at GENERATE and stored per-op via `set_op_reasoning(op_id, reasoning)`. It is displayed as a `reasoning:` line under each `Update(path)` block in the SerpentFlow CLI:

```
⏺ Update(tests/test_failure_sensor.py)
   ├── reasoning: The current sensor does not handle the case where two identical
   │   signals arrive in the same tick. Adding a dedup guard via (signal_id,
   │   timestamp_bucket) fixes the storm-after-reset bug observed in
   │   bt-2026-04-14-022414.
   ├── +42 -3 (test module, new test cases)
   └── [APPLIED]
```

The operator sees not just what changed, but *why* — in the model's own words, captured at the moment of decision. This is Principle 7 (Absolute Observability) at the op level.

## §45. Capability 2 — Severity-Based Human Escalation Protocol

> **Big Picture:** Not every change deserves human review. A one-line test fix does not need a human approver. A breaking API change does. The four-tier risk escalator is the mechanism that makes this judgment structurally, not heuristically. Different risk tiers follow different paths through the pipeline — and crucially, the organism communicates visibly which tier each operation is on.

**Source:** `risk_engine.py` (`RiskTier.NOTIFY_APPLY`), `orchestrator.py` (Phase 5b).

The four-tier escalator (repeated from §9.1 because it matters at every phase):

| Tier | Color | Auto-Apply? | Trigger Rules |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SAFE_AUTO` | Green | Yes, silent | Single-file, non-core |
| `NOTIFY_APPLY` | Yellow | Yes, visible | New files (Rule 10), multi-file changes (Rule 11), core orchestration paths (Rule 12) |
| `APPROVAL_REQUIRED` | Orange | No, blocks | Security-sensitive, breaking API |
| `BLOCKED` | Red | Rejected | Supervisor, credentials, governance engine |

![Figure 5 — The four-tier risk escalator. Each tier determines whether the operation auto-applies, blocks for a notification window, blocks for human approval, or is rejected outright. Consciousness-driven escalation can elevate the tier by one step when regression risk is high.](figures/fig05_risk_escalator.png)

### §45.1 NOTIFY_APPLY Behavior

The Yellow tier is the pragmatic innovation. Rather than forcing every multi-file change through a human approval wait, the orchestrator emits a `notify_apply` decision via CommProtocol. SerpentFlow renders it prominently as:

```
⚠ NOTIFY_APPLY  op-abc123  reason=multi_file  files=4  auto-applying in 5s
```

During the 5-second window, the operator can type `cancel op-abc123` at the REPL to abort. If no cancellation is issued, the operation continues to APPLY. This is a **trust-building mechanism**: the human is informed of the change before it lands, has a window to intervene, but is not required to do so. Over many operations, the operator's vigilance can relax as trust builds; if a problematic Yellow op slips through, the operator intervenes, and the rules are refined.

### §45.2 BLOCKED Short-Circuit

Red tier ops short-circuit at CLASSIFY. The orchestrator does not attempt GENERATE on a BLOCKED op — it writes a BLOCKED ledger entry and emits a BLOCKED POSTMORTEM. This is **structural refusal**, not advisory warning.

<p>The refusal is structural, not advisory: the orchestrator never attempts GENERATE, writes a BLOCKED ledger entry and emits a BLOCKED POSTMORTEM. No candidate for a forbidden target (supervisor, credentials, governance engine) is ever produced (§45.2).</p>

## §46. Capability 3 — Operation Dependency Chains (DAG-Based Signal Merging)

> **Big Picture:** When two sensors detect opportunities targeting the same files, the organism does not run them as two uncoordinated operations — one would trample the other's changes, producing a merge conflict with itself. The intake router is DAG-aware: it recognizes file-overlap conflicts and queues the second operation behind the first, releasing it only when the first completes. This prevents the organism from fighting itself.

**Source:** `unified_intake_router.py` (`_active_file_ops`, `_queued_behind`, `release_op`).

### §46.1 The Mechanism

```
Signal A arrives, targets [foo.py]
  → _active_file_ops[foo.py] = op_id_A
  → operation A proceeds

Signal B arrives, targets [foo.py]
  → _find_file_conflict([foo.py]) returns op_id_A
  → B is queued in _queued_behind[op_id_A]

Operation A completes
  → release_op(op_id_A)
    → removes foo.py from _active_file_ops
    → re-ingests Signal B automatically
```

### §46.2 Multi-File Conflict Resolution

If a new signal targets `[foo.py, bar.py]` and `foo.py` is already active under op A, the new signal is queued behind A — even though `bar.py` is free. The conservative choice: wait for the conflict to clear, then re-plan from the new state (which includes A's patch).

### §46.3 TTL for Stale Locks

Active file locks carry timestamps. If an operation crashes and leaves a file locked, subsequent signals would queue forever. Refinement #11 (Edge Case Hardening) adds a TTL: locks older than `JARVIS_FILE_LOCK_TTL_S` (default 300 seconds) are force-released with a warning log. This prevents starvation behind crashed operations.

## §47. Capability 4 — Exploration-First Enforcement

> **Big Picture:** The difference between a senior engineer and a junior engineer is not just experience — it is *the discipline to read the code before changing it*. Junior engineers write patches from memory. Senior engineers read the target file first. Exploration-first enforcement makes the organism act like a senior engineer, by requiring at least two exploration tool calls before any code-change tool call.

**Source:** `providers.py` (`_build_tool_section`), `orchestrator.py` (Iron Gate call site), `exploration_engine.py` (ExplorationLedger).

### §47.1 The Prompt-Level Nudge

The generation prompt includes an explicit **Exploration-first protocol** section:

```
### CRITICAL: Exploration-first protocol

Before proposing ANY code change, you MUST verify the current state using
at least 2 exploration tools:
1. Read the target file — read_file to see the actual current code.
   NEVER generate a patch from parametric memory alone.
2. Check dependents — search_code or get_callers to find code that
   imports/calls the function you're changing.
```

This prevents patches generated from stale weights. The model reads first, then writes.

### §47.2 The Runtime Gate

Prompting alone is not enough — a model can ignore instructions. The Iron Gate enforces exploration-first at the post-GENERATE, pre-VALIDATE checkpoint. It scans `GenerationResult.tool_execution_records` for exploration tool calls (`read_file`, `search_code`, `get_callers`) and verifies that at least `JARVIS_MIN_EXPLORATION_CALLS` (default `2`) were made.

Violations produce a `GENERATE_RETRY` with targeted feedback:

```
Your previous attempt did not call any exploration tools before proposing
the patch. Required minimum: 2 exploration tool calls (read_file,
search_code, get_callers). Please explore the target file and its call
graph before writing a patch.
```

The model retries with the feedback, typically produces correct exploration depth on the retry, and the operation proceeds.

### §47.3 The ExplorationLedger (Diversity-Weighted Scoring)

The raw counter floor (`tool_calls >= _min_explore`) is being phased out in favor of **diversity-weighted scoring**. An `ExplorationLedger` classifies every exploration tool call into one of five categories:

| Category | Tools |
|---|---|
| `COMPREHENSION` | `read_file`, `list_symbols` |
| `DISCOVERY` | `glob_files`, `list_dir` |
| `CALL_GRAPH` | `get_callers` |
| `STRUCTURE` | (future) Oracle-graph introspection |
| `HISTORY` | `git_log`, `git_diff`, `git_blame` |

Duplicate calls (same tool + same `arguments_hash`) get **zero credit** — forward progress is measured as new files/queries, not repeated fetches.

The gate passes when all three conditions hold:

- `diversity_score ≥ min_score`
- `|categories_covered| ≥ min_categories`
- `required_categories ⊆ categories_covered`

Floors are env-driven per complexity:

| Complexity | Min Score | Min Categories | Required Categories |
|---|---|---|---|
| `trivial` | 0 | 0 | — (bypass) |
| `simple` | 4.0 | 2 | — |
| `moderate` | 8.0 | 3 | — |
| `architectural` | 14.0 | 4 | `{call_graph, history}` |

Architectural operations **must** read call graphs and git history — you cannot rewrite the orchestrator without understanding who calls what and why it was written the way it was.

### §47.4 Anti-Gaming Invariant

**Failed tool calls accrue *score* but not *category coverage*.** A failed grep is still signal — the model learned something from the failure. But it cannot count toward category coverage, because otherwise a model could fake exploration by flooding failing calls and reaching the score floor without genuinely exploring.

### §47.5 Battle-Test Evidence

The ExplorationLedger was validated in Sessions A–G (2026-04-14) — see Part XII, §73 for the full arc. Session C demonstrated shadow-mode scoring that flagged a `4× read_file` shallow exploration at `score=3.00, categories=comprehension`. Session G then demonstrated the full adaptation loop: retry feedback → model diversifies tools → second ledger decision passes at `score=25.50, categories=5`.

## §48. Capability 5 — Post-Apply Verification Loop

> **Big Picture:** Validation in isolation (before APPLY) is not sufficient. Tests can pass in a sandbox but fail after APPLY because of filesystem interactions, import ordering, or state the sandbox did not reproduce. The post-apply VERIFY phase re-runs a scoped test suite after the changes are on disk, catching regressions before they close the operation.

**Source:** `orchestrator.py` (Phase 8a), `serpent_flow.py` (`op_verify_start`, `op_verify_result`).

### §48.1 The Scoped Test Run

After APPLY succeeds, VERIFY runs only the tests that exercise the changed files. Running the full test suite would be slow; running a scope targeted to the diff catches regressions without burning the wall clock.

```
Phase 8a: Scoped post-apply test run
  ├── _validation_runner.run(changed_files, timeout=60s)
  ├── Emit heartbeat with verify_test_starting / verify_test_passed
  ├── SerpentFlow renders ⏺ Verify(files) with pass/fail counts
  │
  ├── On PASS → continue to benchmark gate → COMPLETE
  └── On FAIL → route to L2 repair engine
      ├── Build synthetic ValidationResult
      ├── _l2_hook(ctx, synth_val, deadline)
      ├── If L2 converges → continue to COMPLETE
      └── If L2 fails → combine with benchmark result → rollback
```

Budget: `JARVIS_VERIFY_TIMEOUT_S` (default 60 seconds).

### §48.2 The Scope Fix (Refinement #10)

An early version of post-apply L2 Repair had a bug: when the scoped test suite failed after APPLY, L2 would generate a fix candidate, but the candidate was not actually written to disk. It stayed in memory, was re-validated against the sandbox (which passed), and the operation "completed" without the fix landing. Refinement #10 closes this gap — the L2 repair candidate is now actually written via `change_engine.execute()` before VERIFY re-runs.

### §48.3 Why VERIFY Is Distinct from VALIDATE

VALIDATE runs against a sandbox copy of the candidate. VERIFY runs against the applied disk state. The distinction matters because:

- Some tests read from the filesystem.
- Import ordering can differ between sandbox and live process.
- Concurrent state (e.g., database connections) is real in VERIFY, simulated in VALIDATE.

Running a post-apply verification turns "passes validation" into "passes verification on disk" — a stricter guarantee.

## §49. Capability 6 — Cumulative Session Intelligence

> **Big Picture:** Within a single session, the organism accumulates lessons. Every operation produces either a success lesson ("this worked, here's what it was") or a failure lesson ("this failed, here's why"). The next operation in the session sees these lessons in its generation prompt. The organism learns from its own behavior across a session.

**Source:** `orchestrator.py` (`_session_lessons`), `providers.py` (prompt injection), `op_context.py` (`session_lessons` field).

### §49.1 The Lessons Buffer

An ephemeral `_session_lessons` buffer on `GovernedOrchestrator` accumulates compact insights:

- **Success**: `[OK] Fix assertion error in test_provider.py (test_provider.py)`
- **Failure**: `[FAIL:test] Add type hints to config loader (config_loader.py)`

Capped at 20 lessons (`JARVIS_SESSION_LESSONS_MAX`).

### §49.2 Prompt Injection

Before each GENERATE phase, the lessons are injected into the `OperationContext.session_lessons` field and rendered into the generation prompt:

```
## Session Lessons (from prior operations this session)

Use these to avoid repeating mistakes and build on successes:

- [OK] Fix off-by-one in provider parser (providers.py)
- [FAIL:build] Add async wrapper — missing await (event_channel.py)
- [OK] Suppress PyPI timeout tracebacks (runtime_health_sensor.py)
```

The model reads these before generating. Lessons shape the current operation's approach.

### §49.3 Infra Poisoning Guard (Refinement #8)

Not all lessons are equal. An operation that failed because of a DoubleWord outage produces a lesson like `[FAIL:infra] ... DoubleWord timeout`. That lesson is not about code — it is about infrastructure. If injected into the prompt, the model might try to avoid the failing behavior (e.g., avoid calling DW) when the real fix is just to retry.

Refinement #8 tags infrastructure failures as `"infra"` and excludes them from the session-lessons injection. Only `"code"` lessons (actual logic failures, test regressions) reach the model. This prevents transient infrastructure noise from teaching the model false patterns.

### §49.4 Convergence Metric (Refinement #18)

The lessons buffer also tracks success rates before and after the first lesson was recorded (`_ops_before_lesson`, `_ops_after_lesson`). Every `JARVIS_LESSON_CONVERGENCE_CHECK_INTERVAL` (default `10`) post-lesson operations, the success rates are compared. If post-lesson success rate is *lower* than pre-lesson, the lessons are considered **misleading** and the buffer is cleared.

This is self-correcting intelligence. If the lessons are helping, keep them. If they are hurting, discard them. The organism does not commit to guidance that is not working.

## §50. Capability 7 — Cost-Aware Operation Prioritization

> **Big Picture:** The intake router holds a priority queue. When multiple signals are pending, the router chooses the next one to dispatch based on a composite score that factors in source tier, urgency boost, file-count penalty, confidence bonus, and dependency credit. The effect: focused, high-urgency, high-confidence operations are processed first; sprawling, low-urgency, low-confidence operations wait.

**Source:** `unified_intake_router.py` (`_compute_priority`).

### §50.1 The Formula

```python
def _compute_priority(envelope):
    base = _PRIORITY_MAP.get(envelope.source, 99)      # source tier
    urgency = _URGENCY_BOOST.get(envelope.urgency, 0)  # critical=3, high=1
    cost_penalty = 0 if files <= 1 else (1 if files <= 4 else 2)
    confidence_bonus = 1 if envelope.confidence >= 0.9 else 0
    dep_credit = min(len(queued_behind_this_file_set), 3)  # Refinement #9
    return base - urgency + cost_penalty - confidence_bonus - dep_credit
```

Lower priority number = higher priority. The formula pushes:

- High-urgency signals up (critical urgency = -3).
- Focused single-file signals up (cost_penalty = 0).
- High-confidence signals up (confidence_bonus = -1).
- Signals that would unblock other queued signals up (dep_credit up to -3).

### §50.2 Example

Suppose three signals are pending:

| Signal | Source | Urgency | Files | Confidence | Dep credit | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | test_failure | critical | 1 | 0.95 | 0 | 2 - 3 + 0 - 1 - 0 = -2 |
| B | opportunity_miner | normal | 4 | 0.70 | 0 | 5 - 0 + 1 - 0 - 0 = 6 |
| C | doc_staleness | low | 1 | 0.85 | 2 | 6 - 0 + 0 - 0 - 2 = 4 |

Order: A (-2) → C (4) → B (6). Signal A goes first (it's a critical test failure). Signal C goes second (it's low-urgency but unblocks other queued work). Signal B goes last (opportunity mining is low-priority by default).

### §50.3 All Enqueue Paths

The composite score is computed for all three enqueue paths:

1. Initial enqueue (first time a signal is seen).
2. Retry enqueue (an operation deferred due to conflict, now re-ingesting).
3. WAL replay (restart recovery).

This ensures prioritization is consistent regardless of how a signal enters the queue.

<!-- engage:begin -->
<div class="quick-check" id="qc-50">
<p class="qc-label">Quick check · §50</p>
<details class="qc"><summary>1. In the <code>_compute_priority</code> formula, is a larger number served sooner or later? Which terms push a signal earlier?</summary>
<p>Later: a lower number means higher priority. Urgency boost, the confidence bonus and dependency credit are subtracted, so they move a signal earlier; the file-count cost penalty is added, so sprawling signals move later (§50.1).</p>
</details>
<details class="qc"><summary>2. Why is the score computed on retry enqueue and WAL replay, not only on first enqueue?</summary>
<p>So that a signal's place in the queue does not depend on how it entered it. A deferred or recovered signal is ordered by the same rule as a fresh one (§50.3).</p>
</details>
</div>
<!-- engage:end -->

## §51. The Seven Capabilities in Concert

These seven capabilities are not independent — they compose.

- Intent visibility (§44) + session intelligence (§49) means the operator can read the thought log and understand what the organism has been learning.
- Severity escalation (§45) + cost-aware priority (§50) means high-risk operations with high value get processed first, under appropriate human oversight.
- Dependency DAG (§46) + exploration-first (§47) + post-apply verify (§48) means concurrent operations do not conflict, each operation reads before writing, and each operation's changes are verified in situ.

Together, these seven capabilities are the difference between a pipeline that executes operations and an **autonomous developer** that acts with judgment. Every capability is battle-test validated (Part XII). Every capability is observable (Principle 7). Every capability is reversible via env vars if needed.
